“Old enough to understand when a record is being altered,” Caedmon replied.
Silence fell hard.
Morwenna felt the danger shift. Not toward Caedmon. Toward the document.
She lifted it and held it near the lamp. The writing had been scraped in one place, the fibers raised like white hairs. Beneath the correction, a different number showed through.
“Read the erased line,” she said.
Caedmon came closer. “The original count was—”
He stopped.
“Say it.”
His eyes moved across the page. “The original count was 2,483.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
“That is the current garrison.”
“Yes.”
“Then what was added?”
Caedmon breathed through his nose. “Nothing. The number was replaced, not amended.”
Sabelle’s attention sharpened. “By whom?”
“No signature remains.”
“Signatures can be removed,” Morwenna said. “Intent is harder to scrape away.”
She set the parchment down.
A memory rose unbidden: broken banners sodden in black water, drowned radiance under a sky without stars. The War of Drowned Light had begun in 225 AS and ended in 235 AS, with 64617 casualties. It had collapsed into a decade of guerrilla reprisals. The Silent Choir was recorded as the victor, though the war’s spark had secretly been staged by them.
No triumph had survived that war. Only the habit of vengeance.
The old report was still read in academies and council chambers, where men argued over formations and supply lines. Morwenna remembered the margins better than the victories. Every correction had concealed a corpse. Every official number had been a door locked against the dead.
“The record says the war ended,” Caedmon said quietly.
“The record says many things.”
“The Silent Choir is recorded as the victor.”
Sabelle’s gaze remained upon Morwenna. “And the spark was secretly staged by them.”
The lamps burned low. The words seemed to drink the light.
Morwenna placed both hands upon the table. “You say that as though the distinction matters.”
“It matters to those who still believe victory absolves the hand that struck the match.”
“Belief is not jurisdiction.”
“No,” Sabelle said. “Jurisdiction is what remains after belief has been stripped away.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Beyond the shutters, something struck the fortress wall. A gull, perhaps. Or a hand.
Morwenna did not look.
The five powers had learned to sit at the same table without calling it peace. The Ashen Vanguard wanted roads and oaths. House Morvain wanted inheritance recognized where armies had failed. The Silent Choir wanted silence to mean obedience. The Iron-Ring Cartel wanted every hunger made profitable. The Bleeding Crown wanted the realm to remember that crowns could bleed and still command.
Morwenna served none of them cleanly.
She had been born in 288 AS, and the sea had taught her that loyalties were vessels: useful only while they held. Secretly, she sold intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel. The admission lived beneath her ribs with the steady pressure of a second heart.
Sabelle touched the corner of the report.
“Cindermere Hold,” they said.
Morwenna looked down.
The name stood among the mountain marks: a blackened fortress among the peaks.
“Why bring it into this?”
“Because the body was wearing a clasp stamped with its seal.”
Caedmon bent over the map. “Cindermere Hold was founded in 246 AS among The High Spires.”
“Was,” Sabelle said.
“Though its garrison once numbered 8878,” Morwenna continued, “the hold is now abandoned and is not a core holding.”
Caedmon traced the mountain road with one ink-stained finger. “The route from Cindermere Hold to the coast is impassable.”
“According to the record,” Morwenna said.
“According to the cliffs,” Caedmon answered.
Morwenna studied him.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
He had not meant to be insolent. That was what made it dangerous. Men who feared their own words learned to speak truth as though it were an accident.
Sabelle drew one glove back over their hand. “Then someone crossed the cliffs.”
“Or the clasp was planted,” Morwenna said.
“By whom?”
The question waited, polished and patient.
Morwenna’s mind moved through possibilities. The Cartel would plant a seal if it bought them access. The Silent Choir would plant one if it wished to make an old war speak again. House Morvain would plant one if the corpse served a claim. The Ashen Vanguard would deny planting anything. The Bleeding Crown would call the evidence treasonous and demand it be burned.
She could tell Sabelle none of this.
Not yet.
Caedmon lifted the report’s lower edge. “There is another mark.”
Morwenna leaned in.
A smear of reddish wax clung to the parchment. Not a seal. Not quite. A thumbprint pressed through it, thin and ridged.
Caedmon whispered, “Someone touched this while the wax was warm.”
Sabelle’s face went still.
In the corridor, the guard outside made a sound of surprise.
Then came a second sound: the dragging scrape of something heavy against the stone.
Morwenna reached for the sword at her side, though her hand had not yet closed around the hilt when the door began to open again—and from the darkness beyond it came the wet, patient breathing of a thing that had no living lungs.
The door opened by the width of a hand.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
A pale limb slid through the gap and rested against the stone. The fingers were too long, the nails split and dark beneath them. Moisture shone along the knuckles. It dripped soundlessly onto the threshold.
The guard outside tried to speak.
Only a wet click came from his throat.
Morwenna drew her sword.
Steel whispered free. The sound seemed pitifully small against that breathing, which continued with the patient rhythm of bellows submerged in a cistern.
“Caedmon,” she said.
The scribe had already backed into the table. His shoulder struck the inkpot. Blackness spilled over the report, spreading toward the reddish wax mark like a second, hungrier stain.
“Do not move,” Morwenna told him.
“I was not intending to.”
“Then remain excellent at it.”
Sabelle stood between the door and the table. They had not drawn a weapon. Their hands hung loose at their sides, the fingers slightly curled, as if awaiting an object placed into them.
Morwenna watched their face.
Nothing.
Not fear. Not surprise. Only that severe stillness which had made petitioners lower their eyes before the High Inquisitor had spoken a word. The two crowns upon Sabelle’s authority were not visible in the dimness, but Morwenna felt them all the same: invisible weights laid upon the room, pressing every breath flatter.
The door opened another inch.
The thing beyond it bent.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Its head came through sideways first, scraping the lintel. What remained of its face had been wrapped in strips of dark cloth, soaked until the weave clung to the shape beneath. One eye showed through. It was clouded, silver-white, and fixed upon the report.
Not upon them.
Upon the report.
Caedmon saw it too. His lips parted.
Morwenna moved before thought could make the decision cowardly.
She crossed the room in three strides and seized the parchment from the table. Ink ran over her glove. The page was warm. Not with life. With the residual heat of the wax, perhaps, or the heat of a hand that had pressed the mark.
The thing inhaled.
The sound came through its covered mouth like water dragged up through reeds.
“Give it back,” Sabelle said.
Morwenna turned her blade toward them. “You know what it is?”
“I know what it wants.”
“That is not what I asked.”
“No.” Sabelle’s gaze settled on the report in Morwenna’s hand. “It is not.”
Behind the door, the guard made a muffled choking sound. The creature’s shoulder entered the room. Its clothing was the color of old ash, stiff with salt or some paler crust. A metal clasp hung at its throat, pitted and dull.
Morwenna did not look at the guard.
“Caedmon,” she said, “is there anything on that page about Gloamreach?”
His eyes flicked to the parchment, then to the creature. “The quarantine records. Garrison returns. Supply losses. Nothing—”
“Read it.”
“Now?”
“Especially now.”
He bent over the table. His hands trembled once, then steadied. Reserved, meticulous, he began to read from memory where the ink had blurred.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
“Gloamreach. Pale Coast. Core location. Quarantined status maintained.” His voice thinned. “Garrison—two thousand four hundred and eighty-three.”
The creature stopped.
The breathing ceased.
For a moment the whole room held its silence with it.
Morwenna felt the page tighten in her hand.
Not physically. The parchment remained limp, stained, and half-curled. But some pressure gathered around it, the sense of attention narrowing to a point. She had known admirals who could quiet a deck with a glance. She had known storms that seemed to choose a single mast to break. This was neither. This was appetite given patience.
Sabelle’s eyes had moved to Caedmon.
“Continue,” they said.
Caedmon swallowed. “The last—”
“Continue.”
“The last notation is incomplete. The entry ends beneath the quarantine seal.”
The thing turned its head toward Sabelle.
Morwenna saw then that the cloth around its face was not tied. It had grown there. Threads disappeared beneath the skin, vanishing into a black seam at the jaw.
She should have been afraid.
Instead, a colder instinct rose through her: calculation.
A creature that came for a report had been sent, or summoned, or compelled. A creature that recognized a number might be following an order. An order meant an author. An author meant leverage.
Leverage was the only mercy power ever offered.
She stepped backward, bringing the parchment closer to the lamp. The reddish smear stood out beneath the ink. Not a seal. A thumbprint. The ridges caught the light.
Someone had touched this while the wax was warm.
Someone who had expected the mark to be found.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
“High Inquisitor,” she said, “did you bring this thing here?”
Sabelle’s expression did not change, but the skin beside one eye tightened.
“I did not bring it.”
“Then you know who did.”
“Do not mistake silence for knowledge.”
“I have never mistaken the two.”
The creature entered farther. Its arm dragged along the doorframe. Bits of stone broke away and struck the floor. It had a human shape, more or less, but the proportions had been stretched by some merciless hand. Its left foot angled inward. Its right knee refused to bend until the last instant, then folded with a crack.
Caedmon pushed himself away from the table.
Morwenna held out her free hand. “Stay there.”
He obeyed.
Sabelle watched the creature come into the room. There was something in their gaze that Morwenna had seen before—not compassion, not disgust. Recognition burdened by ownership.
The thought arrived unwanted and whole.
A bound revenant.
She had heard the phrase in sealed rooms, spoken by people who believed secrecy was a moral defense. They had never agreed on whether such things were weapons, prisoners, or witnesses. Sabelle Mournvale the Twice-Crowned had fought in The Leaden Accord, fighting for The Ashen Vanguard. That history had made them difficult to surprise and harder to intimidate. But history did not explain the wet breathing at the door.
A cellar might.
Morwenna’s grip tightened on the sword.
“You keep one,” she said.
Caedmon looked at her.
Sabelle did not.
The creature raised its hand.
“Do not,” Sabelle said.
It halted.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
The obedience was immediate. Not the obedience of fear. Not even the obedience of training. It stopped because the command had entered it and remained there.
Morwenna’s pulse gave one hard beat.
Sabelle moved toward the door. Their boots passed within reach of the thing’s fingers. The creature’s hand twitched, hungry or confused.
“Back,” Sabelle said.
It withdrew.
The guard outside collapsed against the wall. Morwenna heard the dull impact, then a small groan.
She should have sent for help. She should have shouted for the corridor to be sealed, for the chamber to be cleared, for every blade within hearing to come running.
But Caedmon had read the garrison number, and the creature had stopped.
And the report still lay in her hand.
A report concerning Gloamreach. A quarantined core location on the Pale Coast, held by a garrison of 2,483. Intelligence worth selling, if the right detail had been omitted from the proper copy. Intelligence worth killing for, if the quarantine concealed more than sickness.
The Iron-Ring Cartel would pay for certainty.
Morwenna felt the secret move inside her like a knife beneath cloth.
Sabelle saw it. Perhaps not the secret itself, but the hesitation around it.
“You are thinking of keeping the page,” they said.
“I am thinking of why it was sent.”
“Those are not separate thoughts.”
“No?”
“No. Not when the person thinking them is a Fleet Admiral.”
The title struck with more force than accusation. It carried the weight of fleets that did not exist in the room, of orders written in her hand and obeyed by distant mouths. Morwenna kept her face still.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Behind Sabelle, the creature’s wet breathing began again.
“Your servant is becoming impatient,” Morwenna said.
“They are not my servant.”
“Then what are they?”
Sabelle glanced toward the thing.
For the first time, something resembling weariness crossed their face.
“A consequence.”
The word hung between them.
Caedmon’s gaze fell to the ink spreading over the table. He had not touched the report again. His fingers were blackened at the tips.
Morwenna studied the creature’s exposed eye. The clouded sphere reflected the lamp without seeing it. A strand of cloth shifted over its mouth.
“Consequences can be redirected,” she said.
“Not this one.”
“Everything can be redirected.”
“That is the faith of the powerful.”
“It is the practice of the living.”
Sabelle looked at her then, fully. Their eyes were dark beneath the hard planes of their face, and the severity in them was no longer inquisitorial. It was older. More private.
“You should have stayed at the table,” they said.
Morwenna understood too late.
The creature moved.
It did not lunge at her. It crossed the room in a broken blur, one shoulder leading, the floor cracking beneath its weight. Morwenna raised her sword, but the blade met only a sleeve. The impact drove her backward into the wall. Stone struck her spine. The report flew from her hand.
Caedmon cried out.
The parchment spun once through the lamplight.
The creature caught it.
Its fingers closed around the page without tearing it. The wet breathing stopped again. It bowed its head, pressing the covered ruin of its face to the ink.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Morwenna saw the red wax smear vanish beneath its palm.
Sabelle whispered a word.
Not a command this time.
A name, perhaps—but no name Morwenna knew, and no name she could safely invent for the thing now crouched over the stolen report. The sound was low, shaped by grief or disgust.
The revenant shuddered.
Caedmon stumbled toward the far wall. “What is it doing?”
Morwenna pushed away from the stone. Pain flashed along her ribs. She ignored it and lifted her sword.
The creature unfolded.
The page clung to its hand.
Sabelle’s face had gone pale.
“Morwenna,” they said.
No title. No courtesy.
The creature turned toward her.
The clouded eye brightened from within, not with light but with the color of something burning beneath deep water.
Sabelle took one step forward. “Put down the report.”
The revenant did not obey.
Morwenna raised her sword higher, and from somewhere beneath the cloth around its mouth came the first word it had spoken.
“Morwenna Ashgrove.”
The name came wetly through the cloth, as if spoken by a throat lined with river mud.
Caedmon made a small sound behind her. His quill struck the floor. Morwenna heard it roll once, twice, and stop against the wall.
Sabelle did not move.
The revenant held the report between two blackened fingers. The page trembled, though nothing else in the chamber stirred. Its wrappings were dark with cellar damp, and beneath them something shifted with the slow patience of rot.
Morwenna kept her sword raised.
“Who taught it my name?” she asked.
“Names are not taught,” Sabelle said. “They are retained.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
The answer had the coldness of a door barred from within.
Morwenna watched the revenant’s clouded eye. “It has seen me before.”
“No.”
“You expect me to believe that?”
“I expect you to believe what is useful.”
Sabelle’s gaze remained fixed on the creature. They stood with the authority of their office still upon them: Sabelle Mournvale the Twice-Crowned, High Inquisitor, born in 263 AS, the crown-marks at their brow hidden beneath shadow and the ruinous light that leaked through the shutters. Their hands were empty. That frightened Morwenna more than a drawn blade would have.
The chamber smelled of wet stone, old ash, and the sharp medicinal stink rising from the revenant’s wrappings. Somewhere beneath the floor, water tapped against the foundation. The sound had a rhythm. A patient knock from the dark.
Morwenna knew this place now.
Sabelle kept a bound revenant in their cellar.
The knowledge had been forced into the open by the creature’s arrival, but it had not become less dangerous for being seen. Secrets did not die when uncovered. They changed owners.
“Give me the report,” Sabelle said.
The revenant turned its head toward them.
The paper sagged in its grasp. Ink bled across the page, black veins spreading through the writing.
Caedmon crouched beside the fallen quill. “It is destroying the record.”
“You are a Scribe,” Sabelle said without looking at him. “You should have secured it.”
Caedmon’s fingers closed around the quill. “I did secure it.”
“Then your security is inadequate.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Morwenna felt the room narrowing around them. The walls had always seemed close in Cindermere Hold, but now the black stone leaned inward like a tribunal. The abandoned hold had been founded in 246 AS among The High Spires, raised for a garrison that once numbered 8878. Its strength had gone the way of all old strength. No soldiers remained in its halls. It was abandoned now, and not a core holding of any power that still mattered.
Yet the dead had found a use for it.
The revenant lifted the report to its face.
Morwenna’s hand tightened on her sword.
“Stop it.”
The creature’s mouth opened beneath the cloth. Not wide. Not enough for a human jaw. The wrappings pulled apart, revealing darkness packed with glistening teeth.
The page vanished between them.
Caedmon lurched upright. “No—”
The revenant swallowed.
Paper rasped down its throat.
Then it spoke again.
“Gloamreach.”
Sabelle’s expression altered by less than a breath.
Morwenna saw it. She saw the calculation, the swift burial of alarm beneath inquisitorial calm. Gloamreach lay on the Pale Coast, a quarantined core location with a garrison of 2,483. A place sealed against the coast around it, guarded as much from within as from without.
A place about which the Iron-Ring Cartel had wanted information.
Her mouth went dry.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
The Cartel paid in secrets, not coin. They preferred intelligence because coin could be seized, counted, or traced. Intelligence merely entered the world and made men believe their choices were their own. Morwenna had sold intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel in silence, with discipline, and without forgiving herself for the ease of it.
The revenant faced her.
“Gloamreach,” it repeated. “Quarantined.”
Caedmon looked between them. “What does it mean?”
“It is reading the report,” Morwenna said.
“It ate the report.”
“Then it has a better memory than you.”
His face tightened, but he said nothing.
Sabelle extended one hand. “Come here.”
The revenant did not obey.
A thin line of dark fluid ran from beneath its wrappings and fell onto the floor. Where it struck the stone, frost flowered in a black ring.
Sabelle’s voice sharpened. “I bound you.”
The creature’s eye brightened.
Morwenna felt the pressure in the air before the revenant moved. Her skin prickled beneath her uniform. The sword in her hand seemed suddenly ceremonial, a strip of worked metal held against a force that had once possessed a body and now possessed only purpose.
“You bound it,” she said.
Sabelle did not glance at her. “That is what I said.”
“In your cellar.”
“Yes.”
The word fell between them.
Caedmon stared at Sabelle with the pale horror of a man discovering that the record he kept was smaller than the truth. His quill shook in his hand.
The revenant stepped forward.
Its foot made no sound.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Sabelle’s fingers closed into a fist. Beneath the floor, something answered: a chain drawn taut, links groaning in the dark. The revenant halted, its body jerking backward as invisible force took hold of it.
For the first time, Sabelle looked tired.
Morwenna saw the cost of the binding in the hollows beneath their eyes, in the rigid set of their shoulders. The Twice-Crowned High Inquisitor had not mastered death. They had made an agreement with it and mistaken the terms.
“What does it want?” Morwenna asked.
“It wants what all bound things want.”
“Freedom?”
“No.” Sabelle’s eyes went to the ruined mouth. “Recognition.”
The revenant twisted against the unseen chain.
The chamber filled with a low, grinding moan. Dust sifted from the ceiling. Caedmon dropped the quill again.
Morwenna took one step sideways, keeping both Sabelle and the creature in view. The report had contained intelligence concerning Gloamreach. That alone was dangerous. But if the revenant had spoken the name because it had read the page, then it could also speak what the page had not yet revealed.
The names of routes.
The disposition of ships.
The messages she had passed to the Iron-Ring Cartel.
Her secret had not been written in the report. She had been careful. She was always careful.
The revenant turned its clouded eye toward her, as if it had heard the thought.
“War,” it said.
Sabelle’s face went still.
Morwenna lowered the point of her sword by a fraction. “Which war?”
The answer came in pieces, dragged from somewhere beneath the creature’s tongue.
“The War of Drowned Light.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
The words seemed to darken the room.
Morwenna had learned the war as every officer learned it: in figures, losses, and maps where whole districts had been rubbed away. It began in 225 AS and ended in 235 AS. 64617 casualties. The Silent Choir was recorded as the victor.
But the old records lied by omission.
The spark had been secretly staged by The Silent Choir.
She had known that much only because a cipher had crossed her desk and a price had been offered for its contents. She had sold the intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel before any official archive could close around it. The Cartel had not told her why it wanted the truth. It had merely paid.
Now the revenant whispered it through ruined teeth.
“Spark... Choir.”
Sabelle’s fist trembled.
Caedmon looked at Morwenna. “What is it saying?”
Morwenna did not answer.
The War of Drowned Light had not ended when the banners fell. It had collapsed into a decade of guerrilla reprisals, each killing justified by an earlier killing, each corpse made into evidence for the next. The Silent Choir had won, according to the record. Victory had been the name given to whoever remained standing when the water stopped burning.
The revenant’s head snapped toward the door.
A sound came from beyond it.
Not footsteps.
A soft dragging, many times repeated, as if something outside were pulling a length of wet cloth along the corridor.
Sabelle released the binding.
The revenant surged forward.
Morwenna struck.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Her blade met its shoulder. The impact traveled up her arm with the shock of hitting submerged timber. The wrappings split. Beneath them lay no flesh she could recognize, only layers of grey matter veined with dim red light.
The revenant seized her wrist.
Its grip was cold enough to burn.
Morwenna drove her knee into its side. It did not yield. The clouded eye pressed close to her face, and within it she saw a shoreline beneath a drowned sky, banners drifting in dark water, mouths opening soundlessly below the surface.
Then she saw Gloamreach.
Pale stone. Sealed gates. A garrison of 2,483 standing beneath a sky without birds.
And beyond the quarantine wall, something waiting.
The revenant spoke against her cheek.
“Open.”
Morwenna tore her wrist free. Skin came away beneath its fingers. She stumbled backward, blood bright against the dimness.
Sabelle raised both hands.
The floor split.
Black chains burst from the cracks and wrapped around the revenant’s limbs. It thrashed, tearing stone loose in slabs. The chamber shook. Caedmon cried out and flattened himself against the wall, his precious quill crushed beneath his palm.
Sabelle’s voice became a command meant for the dead.
“Return below.”
The revenant’s mouth opened.
It did not look at Sabelle.
It looked at Morwenna.
“Morwenna Ashgrove,” it said. “The Cartel knows.”
The chains dragged it down.
Morwenna stood frozen as the black stone closed over the revenant’s body. One hand remained visible for a moment, fingers clawing at the edge of the broken floor. The report’s last scrap clung to one nail. Then that vanished too.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Silence fell hard.
Water tapped beneath them.
Caedmon slowly unfolded from the wall. Blood seeped across his palm where the quill had pierced it.
Sabelle lowered their hands.
Morwenna kept her sword up.
“The Cartel knows what?” Caedmon asked.
Sabelle turned toward her.
Their face held no accusation. That was worse. Accusation belonged to law, and law could be answered. What rested in Sabelle’s eyes was comprehension.
Morwenna felt the old discipline gather around her like armor. Fleet Admiral. Commanding station. Unbroken voice. No fear visible where fear could be used.
“The creature was damaged,” she said. “Its words were not reliable.”
Sabelle looked down at the sealed floor.
“No,” they said. “They were not.”
From beneath the stone came a single knock.
Then another.
The same patient rhythm as before.
But now it was answering someone below.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
The wind came through Cindermere Hold without asking leave.
It moved along the broken battlements, worried the loose stones, and descended through the arrow slits in thin, cold fingers. Halvard Vane the Grave-Sworn stood within the gatehouse and listened to it pass through the ruin. There was no fire in the brazier. No sentry called from the wall. Dust had gathered in the joints of the flagstones and lay there undisturbed except where boots had crossed it recently.
One pair of boots.
Halvard looked down.
The prints led toward the inner court, their edges still sharp. Whoever had made them had not come in from the mountain path. They had come from the dead barracks.
A place abandoned did not empty itself. It shed its people first, then its purpose, then its noise. The rest remained: doors hanging from one hinge, blackened stones, rust in the rain gutters, old straw turned the color of bruises. Cindermere Hold had been founded in 246 AS among The High Spires. Once, its garrison had numbered 8878. Now it was abandoned, no core holding, a great stone tooth left in the jaw of the heights.
Yet someone had swept the gatehouse floor.
Halvard stepped over the newest print and entered the inner court.
The sky pressed low between the peaks. Ash-colored light lay over the towers. Along the western wall, a standard without its device cracked softly in the wind, its cloth reduced to strips. Halvard watched it twist upon its pole, unable to decide whether it was trying to rise or fall.
Their cloak stirred behind them. The movement felt too loud.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
At the far side of the court, a door stood ajar.
Halvard did not touch the hilt of the knife concealed beneath their coat. The gesture would have been an admission, and admissions had weight. They had learned to carry weight without showing the strain. That was the first discipline of a Seneschal. The second was knowing which burdens belonged to the living and which had already been placed upon the dead.
Inside the building, something scraped.
Halvard entered.
A passage ran beneath the old keep, narrow and low-roofed. The walls had once been whitewashed. Smoke had darkened them in long vertical stains. Water fell somewhere beyond the stone, one drop at a time, with the patience of a clerk making entries in a ledger.
At the passage’s end, a room showed a stripe of lamplight.
Halvard paused before it.
The lamp flame did not flicker. That meant a shield had been placed around it, or the room had no draft. Neither possibility belonged in Cindermere Hold.
They pushed the door open.
A man sat at a table beneath the eastern wall. He had arranged papers in a neat fan, weighted at the corners with bits of broken masonry. A traveling case rested beside his chair. The room had been made habitable with ruthless economy: one blanket, one cup, one lamp, one narrow bed against the wall.
The man lifted his head.
“Halvard Vane the Grave-Sworn,” he said.
Halvard let the silence answer before they did. “You know my name.”
“I know the names that arrive with sealed orders.”
“Then you know I dislike being expected.”
“I expected the seal. Not you.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
His voice held no fear that Halvard could hear. That was not courage. Courage had heat in it. This was the flatness of someone who had been waiting too long for a danger and had grown tired of imagining its face.
Halvard looked at the papers. “You serve at Cindermere Hold.”
“I do.”
“Cindermere Hold is abandoned.”
The man’s mouth shifted, not quite into a smile. “Both statements remain true.”
The answer entered the room like a blade laid gently upon a table.
Halvard removed their gloves, finger by finger. “Your name.”
“Ignatz Marrowgate.”
The name belonged nowhere in Halvard’s memory, which did not mean it had never been spoken. Memory was a locked archive with corridors that changed when no one watched. Halvard had been born in 338 AS, and since then had learned that the world kept every record except the one a person most needed.
Ignatz Marrowgate inclined his head. “You are a major Seneschal.”
“I am.”
“Then the order is not routine.”
“Routine orders are carried by riders.”
“Riders do not come to abandoned holds?”
“Not unless someone has given them a reason.”
Ignatz glanced toward the door. “Someone did.”
Outside, the wind struck the walls. The whole keep answered with a deep, hollow groan.
Halvard crossed to the table. The papers were not military reports. Their margins bore columns of cramped writing, corrections, and small black marks made with a blunt nib. A scribe’s work, though not the work of an unpracticed hand.
“Where did you get these?”
“They were left here.”
“By whom?”
Ignatz’s eyes moved to the lamp. “By someone who did not want to be seen leaving them.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
“That is not an answer.”
“It is the answer I possess.”
Halvard placed one bare hand upon the nearest page. The ink had dried unevenly. Some lines had been written in haste; others had been copied with careful deliberation. There were references to stores, gates, sealed chambers, and a ward. No names appeared. No dates. Only the old notation of a place that had once been expected to withstand an enemy.
The Thrice-Bound Lantern.
The words had been written three times in the margin, each instance crossed through and written again below. The artifact was a ward forged in 72 AS, marked by three visible bindings. Its strength lay in restraint and containment. Halvard had seen its likeness only in old inventories: a severe lantern, made less to give light than to keep something from reaching it.
“What is it?” Ignatz asked.
“You already know.”
“I know the name. I want to know why it is written here.”
Halvard turned the page.
Behind them, a stone shifted in the corridor.
Ignatz did not move. His hand remained atop the papers. Halvard saw the tension gather in his wrist.
The sound came again.
Not the wind. Not water.
A foot placed carefully upon dust.
Halvard looked at the door.
Ignatz whispered, “There was no one in the court.”
“There is now.”
“Your people?”
“I came alone.”
That was true. It was also the kind of truth that could be made useless by what it concealed.
Halvard reached for the lamp and pinched the flame between two fingers. Darkness fell abruptly, carrying the smell of hot oil and old metal. Ignatz inhaled once through his nose.
“Do not speak,” Halvard murmured.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
The room became a sealed thing. The mountain wind withdrew behind the walls. Somewhere far below, the hidden water continued its measured dripping.
Halvard listened.
A scrape. Then another.
The door stood open by the width of a hand. Beyond it, the passage was black.
Their thoughts went, as they always did when danger presented itself, not toward survival but toward arrangement. The body was a temporary vessel. The consequences were not. If the intruder entered, Ignatz might die. If Ignatz died, the papers might vanish. If the papers vanished, an old ward might remain unaccounted for in a fortress that had outlived its purpose. None of those possibilities troubled Halvard equally.
The greatest danger was not discovery.
It was interruption.
For three nights, Halvard had carried the shape of their liege’s death within the mind. Not the act itself; acts were crude, and crude things invited witnesses. The sequence mattered more: the altered seal, the emptied cup, the servant dismissed, the door left unbarred at the proper hour. A death could be made to resemble misfortune if one respected misfortune’s habits.
Their own liege had trusted the gravity of Halvard’s silence.
That trust had been useful.
A shadow crossed the crack beneath the door.
Ignatz’s fingers tightened on the papers. Halvard saw the movement and lifted one hand, warning him still.
The shadow stopped.
For one breath, the room held.
Then someone outside said, “Open.”
The voice was muffled by the stone, but it was human.
Ignatz leaned close. “They know I am here.”
“They know someone is here.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
“They used my name before you came?”
“No.”
“Then they know.”
Halvard let their hand fall beneath the coat. The knife’s hilt met their palm, familiar as a vow. The epithet Grave-Sworn had been spoken of them in courts where candles burned cleanly and floors held no dust. People heard it and imagined devotion. They imagined a person chained to duty, a servant who had made the dead into witnesses.
Let them imagine.
“Open,” the voice said again.
Halvard looked at Ignatz. In the dimness, the scribe’s face was only a pale interruption in the dark.
“What do you serve?” Halvard asked.
“Cindermere Hold.”
“No. What do you serve?”
Ignatz’s breathing changed. “The record.”
“A record does not bleed.”
“It does when men alter it.”
The answer had the shape of an accusation, though Halvard could not tell against whom.
The latch moved.
Halvard stepped away from the table and into the angle beside the door. Ignatz gathered the papers against his chest. The lamp, extinguished, gave off its last warmth between them.
The door began to open.
Halvard raised the knife, and in the darkness their fingers found the first page where The Thrice-Bound Lantern had been written, as though the old ward itself had reached through the paper and taken hold of them—
The door opened wide enough for a blade of corridor-light to enter.
It was not lamplight. It had the thin, bluish pallor of moonlight reflected from snow, though no snow lay beyond the walls. Halvard saw a shoulder, a gloved hand, the dull rim of a helm. The stranger paused on the threshold.
Ignatz moved first.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
He flung the papers toward the table and stepped into the light.
Halvard’s knife touched the soft place beneath his jaw.
“Do not,” Halvard whispered.
Ignatz froze. The pages slid from his grasp. One turned in the air, its ink catching the pallor. The words were visible for only a breath.
The Thrice-Bound Lantern housed in Hollowvale.
Then the page struck the floor.
The stranger outside said, “You were ordered to open.”
Ignatz’s throat worked against the knife. “By whom?”
“By the one who gave the order.”
“Then carry back the answer.”
A silence settled between the room and the corridor. It was the silence of a house listening through its stones. Somewhere beyond the wall, something dripped at regular intervals. Halvard counted three falls before the stranger spoke again.
“You are not alone.”
“Neither are you,” Halvard said.
The gloved hand tightened on the door.
He had expected fear. Instead, he heard the faint rasp of metal being drawn.
Halvard pressed the knife harder. Ignatz made no sound, but the papers under his boots rustled. A bad place for them. A worse place for blood. Ink and blood did not mingle cleanly; the ink fled, the blood remained. That was one of the first truths taught to any servant of a ledger.
The stranger entered.
Halvard saw a narrow face beneath the helm, a mouth without a beard, eyes obscured by the shadow of the brow. No crest marked the cloak. No ring showed on the hand. The absence was deliberate. Men who wished to be unknown rarely managed it; men who wished to be unclaimed were more dangerous.
The door closed behind him.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Halvard kept the knife at Ignatz’s throat and turned his gaze toward the stranger. “You have come for the record.”
“I have come for the scribe.”
“I am no—”
“Quiet,” Halvard said.
Ignatz’s mouth shut.
The stranger’s attention shifted between them. “You know what he carries?”
“I know what men kill for.”
“That is not an answer.”
“It is the only one you have earned.”
The stranger took another step. The boards complained beneath his weight. His cloak smelled of wet stone and iron. Halvard knew the scent. It clung to the thresholds of places where decisions had been made before witnesses arrived.
Ignatz looked down at the page beneath his boot.
Halvard felt the movement and followed it with his eyes.
The page had folded over itself. Only a strip of writing remained visible, but the words were enough to summon a buried room: three bands around a dark lantern, each binding laid over the last; the old marks cut into the metal like scars that had healed badly. He had never seen the artifact. He had seen drawings, descriptions, a disputed inventory rendered in six hands. He had seen the same line repeated until repetition had made it sacred.
The Thrice-Bound Lantern housed in Hollowvale.
Not lost. Not destroyed. Housed.
A ward was not a weapon until someone opened what it restrained.
Ignatz shifted his weight.
The knife kissed skin.
“Do not reach for it,” Halvard said.
“I was not.”
“You were thinking of it.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
The scribe’s gaze lifted. In the dimness his face seemed reduced to angles and hollows. Halvard could not tell whether he was young or merely starved of sleep. “You read the line.”
“I read enough.”
“Then you know why they came.”
The stranger’s hand dropped to his side. “They?”
“Those who altered the record.”
“You accuse everyone who touches paper.”
“Only the careful ones.”
The stranger gave a short laugh. It held no amusement. “You speak like a man who has never had to choose between a lie and a grave.”
Halvard’s grip remained steady.
There were graves that waited beneath stone. There were graves that waited in the mouths of living men. There were graves made long before the body entered them, prepared by a signature, a seal, a spoken oath. He had stood beside enough of them to know that burial was rarely the end of a decision. More often, it was the decision’s first public form.
The stranger said, “Release him.”
“No.”
“He has copied what should not be copied.”
“Then you should have burned the source.”
“The source is not yours to burn.”
“Nor yours to read.”
A faint sound came from the corridor beyond the door. Not footsteps. Fabric brushing stone. Another presence, held back and waiting.
Halvard felt the room contract.
Ignatz heard it too. His breath turned shallow. “How many?”
The stranger looked at him. “Enough.”
“That is not a number.”
“It is not meant to be.”
Halvard almost smiled. The expression would have been a mistake. Instead, he leaned close to Ignatz’s ear.
“If they enter, you die first.”
Ignatz swallowed. “And if they do not?”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
“Then you may have time to explain why the record says Hollowvale.”
The stranger’s head tilted. “You have not read the whole page.”
“I have read the part you fear.”
“What do you think it means?”
“I think a place has been given a burden.”
“Hollowvale is a word.”
“So is a grave.”
The stranger moved with sudden violence.
Halvard shoved Ignatz aside and cut downward. The knife struck the stranger’s forearm, glancing from hidden metal beneath the sleeve. Sparks leapt and died. The stranger seized Halvard’s wrist. His grip was hard enough to numb the fingers.
Ignatz stumbled into the table. The lamp, unlit and cold, rolled against the wall.
For an instant the three of them were tangled in the dark: breath, cloth, the wet scrape of a boot searching for purchase. Halvard drove his shoulder into the stranger’s chest. They struck the door. The impact shook dust from the lintel.
The stranger’s other hand found Halvard’s throat.
Halvard did not struggle. He let his body slacken.
The grip tightened.
He brought his knee up.
The stranger grunted and released him. Halvard twisted free, caught the man’s cloak, and used its own weight to drag him sideways. The helm struck the stone jamb. Metal rang through the chamber.
Beyond the door, the waiting presence moved.
“Now,” the stranger called.
Ignatz snatched the fallen page.
Halvard turned on him. “Put it down.”
The scribe held the paper in both hands. His fingers trembled, but his voice did not. “You should have let me finish.”
“Finish what?”
“The correction.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
The stranger recovered, one hand braced against the wall. A dark line ran from beneath his sleeve. Not much blood. Enough to show the cut had reached flesh.
Ignatz raised the page toward the dead lamp.
“There is no Hollowvale,” the stranger said.
Ignatz looked at him. “There is always a Hollowvale.”
“That is not what the record says.”
“The record says what it is made to say.”
“And you made this?”
“I copied it.”
“From whom?”
Ignatz’s eyes found Halvard’s.
The question entered the room like a draft through a cracked window.
Halvard remembered the first page, the old ink, the pressure of a hand that had written too carefully. He remembered the way Ignatz had refused the question of service. Not a place. Not an office. The record.
A record does not bleed.
It does when men alter it.
Outside, someone struck the door.
The wood shuddered.
The stranger reached for his weapon.
Halvard stepped between him and Ignatz, knife raised. The choice came without ceremony. He had made worse choices in quieter rooms.
“Give me the page,” Halvard said.
Ignatz’s face tightened. “Why?”
“Because if they take it, they will not need to kill you.”
The second blow struck. A splinter burst inward and spun across the floor.
The stranger stared at Halvard. “You understand nothing.”
“Then correct me.”
“The Lantern was not housed in Hollowvale.”
Ignatz’s hands clenched around the paper.
The door groaned.
The stranger said, “The Lantern housed Hollowvale.”
For one breath, no one moved.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
The words were wrong in the mouth, wrong in the ear, wrong in every orderly column of the world. Halvard felt the meaning rise beneath them like something waking under ice.
Ignatz tore the page in half.
The sound was small.
The stranger lunged.
Halvard caught Ignatz by the collar and dragged him backward as the stranger’s blade came down. Steel struck the table, splitting the wood. The lamp leapt, rolled, and struck the wall hard enough to crack its casing.
A black wick showed inside.
Then it burned.
The flame was pale and narrow, bound by three dark rings that had not been there a moment before. They appeared one after another around the light, tightening without touch. The room filled with the smell of old ash and rain trapped beneath earth.
The stranger stopped.
Halvard felt Ignatz go still beside him.
On the floor, the torn halves of the page began to move.
Not by wind. Not by any hand.
The fragments drew together across the boards, ink crawling from one torn edge to the other. Letters unmade themselves. Lines shivered. The writing gathered into a single sentence beneath the wavering flame.
The Thrice-Bound Lantern housed in Hollowvale.
The door burst inward.
Cold air rushed through the chamber, carrying the weight of many bodies. Halvard lifted the knife, but the pale flame had already turned toward the threshold, and within its three bindings something struck once against the glass—
The glass trembled again.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Halvard did not look toward the door. The knife remained raised, its point fixed upon the stranger’s throat, while the dark beyond the threshold filled with the soft, wet sounds of men breathing through cloth.
Ignatz whispered, “How many?”
“Enough.”
“Ten?”
“Enough.”
A shape crossed the doorway. Then another. Their lanterns were hooded, their faces hidden beneath ash-colored wraps. No crest showed upon them. No blade rang against a scabbard. They entered with the quiet discipline of men who had learned that noise was a confession.
The stranger smiled.
It was not a smile of relief.
“You brought them,” Halvard said.
“I opened a door.”
“You opened this one.”
“And they were waiting outside it.”
The pale fire inside the Thrice-Bound Lantern bent toward the intruders. Its three bindings shone black against the glass, each strip carved with cramped old script. The thing within struck again.
This time, the sound came from the walls.
Dust sifted from the rafters.
Ignatz flinched. Halvard heard the movement and hated him for it—not because fear was a weakness, but because fear made men visible. The room had become a net of attention. Every breath tugged at it.
One of the masked figures raised a crossbow.
Halvard moved first.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
The knife left their hand and entered the figure beneath the jaw. The man’s bolt sprang wide, tearing through the stranger’s sleeve. Before the body finished falling, Halvard had crossed the room. Their shoulder struck the second intruder against the wall. Bone cracked. A gloved hand seized at Halvard’s throat, and Halvard drove two fingers into the soft place below the ear.
The man sagged.
Then the chamber broke open.
Steel flashed in the pale light. Ignatz swore and stumbled backward over the scattered page. Someone struck the table, spilling wax and oil across the boards. The flame rose blue. Shadows leapt up the walls, long-limbed and frantic.
Halvard caught a blade along their sleeve. The cloth parted. Cold kissed the skin beneath.
A hand seized their hair.
They drove their head backward.
The attacker grunted. Halvard turned within the grip, hooked an elbow beneath the man’s arm, and felt the joint give. He folded without a cry. Halvard took his sword before it struck the floor.
The sword was poor steel, narrow and hungry. It suited the room.
“Toward the Lantern!” Ignatz shouted.
Halvard saw him clutching a brass candlestick, his mouth bloodied, his eyes fixed on the ward. One of the masked figures had reached for it.
“Keep away from it!”
The command came from the stranger.
Not shouted. Not pleaded.
The intruder’s fingers hovered above the glass. The pale fire had lowered itself, gathered into a thin vertical flame. Within it, something moved like a man sinking beneath ice.
The masked figure drew back.
For the first time, their discipline failed.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Halvard cut him across the ribs.
The man fell against the table. The torn page slid beneath his knee. Ink crawled over the floorboards, black threads seeking one another. The sentence remained legible.
The Thrice-Bound Lantern housed in Hollowvale.
Halvard stared at it for one heartbeat too long.
A sword entered the space where their ribs had been.
They twisted aside. The blade scraped their coat, caught, and held. Halvard stepped close enough to smell tallow, old wool, and the sourness beneath the mask. They drove the stolen sword upward.
The attacker went slack.
More waited in the passage.
More than ten.
The room had no rear door. Its windows were too narrow for a grown body, and beyond them the night pressed against the glass like a blind sea. Halvard heard boots in the corridor, the restrained impatience of men ordered not to rush.
The stranger stood beside the Lantern with one hand upon the table.
“Why are they here?” Ignatz asked.
“Because the page spoke.”
“Pages do not speak.”
“Then you should be less afraid of them.”
The stranger turned toward Halvard. In the uncertain light, the face remained difficult to hold in memory. The features seemed to change whenever the flame shuddered—not truly changing, perhaps, but refusing the eye.
Halvard knew that sort of refusal.
They had worn it before the liege.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
They had bowed beneath banners, placed a hand over the heart, and spoken of loyalty while counting the men who would stand between the throne and the knife. The plot had required patience. It had required a grave expression, a steady voice, a talent for making treason resemble duty.
Halvard Vane the Grave-Sworn, born in 338 AS.
The old records had made a virtue of the name. The court had called them grave because they did not laugh, sworn because they kept their oaths. No record had preserved what mattered: that Halvard had plotted the death of their own liege, and that the liege had never understood how near the hand had come.
A masked man entered.
Halvard met him at the threshold.
The sword went low, then high. The man parried the first stroke and took the second across the throat. Blood sprayed the doorframe. Behind him, the others hesitated.
Not from the corpse.
From the Lantern.
Its three bindings had begun to glow.
The light was not bright. It was worse than brightness. It revealed the room without illuminating it, showing every crack in the boards, every stain in the mortar, every drop of blood hanging in the air before it fell. The faces beyond the doorway appeared beneath their masks as pale hollows.
A voice breathed from inside the glass.
Not words.
A counting.
The first binding split with a sound like a fingernail dragged across bone.
Ignatz dropped the candlestick. “That ward was forged in 72 AS.”
Halvard looked at him.
Ignatz’s expression had collapsed into naked terror. “The Thrice-Bound Lantern. It was forged in 72 AS. If one binding opens—”
“Then close it.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
“I don’t know how.”
“Then remember faster.”
The stranger seized Ignatz by the collar and pulled him away from the table. “It is not opening.”
The second binding shone.
“It is being answered,” the stranger said.
Outside, the men in the corridor began to chant.
The words were muffled by cloth and stone, but Halvard knew the cadence. They had heard it in old reports and sealed testimony, in accounts of drowned banners and villages that burned without flame.
The War of Drowned Light began in 225 AS and ended in 235 AS.
The war had taken 64617 casualties.
The Silent Choir was recorded as the victor.
Halvard remembered the official histories: the pale standards sinking beneath rain, the broken armies retreating through fields turned to black mud. Yet the victor’s silence had always been too complete. The war had collapsed into a decade of guerrilla reprisals, and every reprisal had carried the same patient shape—one village against another, one oath against another, grief made useful by unseen hands.
The spark had been secretly staged by The Silent Choir.
Everyone who mattered knew it.
No one who mattered admitted knowing.
The chant outside thickened. The third binding began to burn.
“Who are they?” Ignatz said.
Halvard listened to the voices.
“The Choir.”
The stranger’s head tilted. “No.”
The word struck Halvard harder than a denial should have.
“Then who?” Ignatz asked.
The stranger lifted a blood-wet finger and touched the glass.
The Lantern screamed.
Every masked figure in the corridor fell silent.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
A pressure seized the chamber. Halvard felt it behind the eyes, in the roots of the teeth. The air tasted of iron and ashes. Somewhere beneath the floor, something vast shifted in its sleep.
The stranger looked toward the page.
“Hollowvale is not a place,” they said.
Halvard’s hand tightened on the sword. “It is marked on the old roads.”
“Names are roads for those who cannot see the country.”
Ignatz stared at the stranger. “Then what is it?”
The third binding cracked.
The pale flame went out.
For an instant, there was only darkness.
Then a line of light appeared beneath the door.
It ran across the floor toward Halvard’s boots, thin as a drawn thread. Where it touched the blood, the blood turned white. The bodies began to twitch.
Halvard backed away.
The line reached the torn page.
The sentence vanished.
New writing rose in its place, each letter forming slowly, as if pressed upward from beneath the paper by a dead hand.
COME TO THE COAST.
Ignatz made a sound in his throat.
“Which coast?” Halvard asked.
The stranger did not answer.
Halvard already knew the only coast that mattered.
Gloamreach lay on the Pale Coast, a core location with a garrison of 2,483. Its status was quarantined. The old reports described its walls as sealed, its roads watched, its gates shut against all passage. A place set apart from the surrounding coast, guarded not merely against invasion but against whatever the surrounding world might carry inward.
The line of light turned toward the window.
Toward the sea.
“Gloamreach,” Halvard said.
The stranger’s silence confirmed nothing.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
That was confirmation enough.
Ignatz bent over the page, breathing hard. “We cannot go there.”
“Why?”
“Because it is quarantined.”
“Then we will be expected.”
“By whom?”
A fist struck the outer door.
The wood groaned.
Halvard glanced at the corpses. At the dark passage. At the Lantern, now black and still, its three bindings dull as dead wire.
“Not by friends.”
Another blow.
This one split the door.
The stranger reached beneath their coat and drew out a small iron seal. No emblem marked it. Its surface was blank except for a single depression shaped like a closed eye.
Halvard recognized the metal.
Not the seal itself. The workmanship.
The Iron-Ring Cartel used iron that way: objects without heraldry, authority stripped of ornament, commands made portable. But the seal bore no ring, and the Cartel did not deal in mysteries unless mystery could be weighed.
“The Iron-Ring Cartel?” Halvard asked.
“Not tonight.”
“House Morvain?”
“Not them.”
“The Ashen Vanguard?”
The stranger looked almost amused. “You ask as though the powers have only one face.”
The door shattered inward.
Men surged through the opening.
Halvard seized Ignatz and threw him toward the window. “Break it.”
Ignatz stared at the narrow panes.
“Now.”
He snatched up the fallen candlestick and smashed the glass. Wind poured through, wet and savage. Beyond lay a drop into darkness, though no ground could be seen.
“That is not a road,” Ignatz said.
“It is the only one.”
The stranger lifted the Lantern.
The instant their fingers closed around its frame, the three bindings flared.
Every man in the doorway froze.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
The pale fire returned behind the glass, but it no longer burned upright. It bent toward Halvard. Within it, a figure pressed both hands against the inner surface.
Halvard heard a voice.
Their own voice.
You plotted the death of your liege.
The sword nearly fell from their hand.
The words were not accusation. They were inventory.
You were born in 338 AS. You wore grief like armor. You called the knife duty.
Behind Halvard, Ignatz climbed through the broken window.
“Hurry!”
The masked men moved again.
Halvard turned toward the opening. The night waited beyond it, vast and blind. Somewhere below, water struck stone.
The stranger placed the Lantern against Halvard’s chest.
Cold entered them.
Not through skin. Through memory.
For one breath Halvard stood before the liege’s sealed chamber, hand upon the latch, listening to the slow breathing beyond. They felt again the weight of the poison hidden beneath their tongue. They remembered the final hesitation—not mercy, never mercy, but the terror of discovering that a life could be ended and still refuse to become simple.
Then the vision broke.
Halvard was falling through the window.
Ignatz caught their wrist.
The stranger followed, carrying the black Lantern.
Above them, the masked men crowded the ruined chamber. One raised a bow. Another shouted a command Halvard could not hear over the wind.
The arrow came.
The Lantern struck the stone ledge.
Its first binding split wide.
Pale fire poured downward—not flame, but a door.
Halvard saw a shoreline beneath it, white cliffs, sealed gates, and the distant watchfires of Gloamreach.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Then something on the other side looked back.
The stranger’s grip tightened around Halvard’s wrist.
“Do not let go,” they said.
Halvard looked down into the opening.
A second figure was falling upward toward them.
And it wore Halvard’s face.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
The bell beneath the floor rang once.
Sabelle Mournvale the Twice-Crowned lifted their head from the interrogation table. The sound had not come from the chapel above, where the bells were iron and cracked, nor from the watchtower, where the wind worried at the old bronze. It had risen through the stone beneath their boots: a low, submerged note, felt first in the teeth.
Across the table, Morwenna Ashgrove did not flinch.
That was the first lie.
The second was the smile she offered afterward.
“You hear many things in this place,” said Morwenna.
Her voice carried the disciplined calm of a Fleet Admiral. No tremor. No appeal. She sat with her wrists unbound upon the black wood, as though the room belonged to her and the inquisitorial lamps were merely poor weather glimpsed through a porthole.
Sabelle studied her in the dimness. The lamps burned with oil rendered from pale shore-moss, and their flames leaned toward the door despite the absence of a draft. Behind Morwenna, the wall was hung with the instruments of confession: hooks, wire, a silver basin gone green at the rim. The tools had been cleaned. Sabelle disliked cleanliness in an interrogation chamber. It suggested preparation, and preparation was a form of vanity.
“You heard nothing,” Sabelle said.
“Then why ask?”
“Because silence is sometimes an answer.”
Morwenna’s eyes moved to the crown upon the table.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
The Crown of Burned Names rested inside a circle of salt. Its blackened points rose like the fingers of a charred hand. Across its metal, names had been scored away until only pale scars remained. It was a ward forged in 266 AS, and attunement to it cost 60. Sabelle had worn it once. The memory still lived in their bones: the slow extinguishing of every private face, every unspoken tenderness, every name that had ever made the world seem less empty.
They had survived by becoming difficult to remember.
The other crown was not in the room. It never was when questions were being asked.
“The Crown of Burned Names does not protect liars,” Sabelle said.
“No,” Morwenna replied. “It protects the forgotten.”
“Those are often the same people.”
A little blood had dried beneath Morwenna’s left thumbnail. Not hers, Sabelle thought. Or not recently hers. The Fleet Admiral had come dressed for command, in a coat without ornament and gloves folded beside her chair. There was no sign of a struggle upon her. No visible mark, no loosened seam. Yet she had been summoned from the coast under seal, and the seal had not been broken by any hand in the room.
Sabelle had broken it themselves.
The five powers pressing their shadows across the Ashen Era had grown skilled at hiding knives beneath official wax. The Ashen Vanguard called its violence duty. House Morvain called its violence inheritance. The Silent Choir called its violence necessity. The Iron-Ring Cartel called its violence trade. The Bleeding Crown called its violence law.
Sabelle called it evidence.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
They drew a thin folio across the table. The parchment was gray from age and smelled of brine.
“Read the final line.”
Morwenna glanced down. “I can read.”
“Then do so.”
“The War of Drowned Light.”
The words seemed to darken the room.
That war began in 225 AS and ended in 235 AS. The record placed 64617 casualties beneath its final seal. The Silent Choir was recorded as the victor, though the conflict collapsed into a decade of guerrilla reprisals, and its spark had been secretly staged by them.
Every child of rank knew the first portion. The last portion was spoken only by people who wanted to die badly, or by people who had proof.
Morwenna’s gaze remained on the parchment.
“You possess naval reports from the war,” Sabelle said.
“I possess many reports.”
“You sell them.”
The Fleet Admiral’s mouth hardened. “To whom?”
“The Iron-Ring Cartel.”
For the first time, something alive moved behind her composure. Not fear. Calculation. It passed across her face like a fish beneath dark water and vanished before Sabelle could spear it.
The room gave another small shudder.
Below, in the cellar, the revenant turned against its bindings.
Sabelle felt the movement in the joints of their hands. The thing was awake. It had been awake for three nights, dragging its chains over the floorstones, whispering through a throat that had forgotten the shape of breath. Sabelle kept it because the dead remembered what the living had been paid to forget. They kept it because power did not always arrive wearing a crown. Sometimes it arrived wet with grave soil and waited for permission to speak.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Morwenna looked toward the floor.
“You have someone beneath us,” she said.
Sabelle allowed the silence to stretch until the lamps began to hiss.
“A poor choice of words,” Morwenna continued.
“Was it?”
“I serve aboard ships. I know the language of decks, holds, ballast. If something is moving beneath a floor, it is not my concern unless the floor gives way.”
“Your concern is what lies beneath every surface.”
“Then we share a profession.”
Sabelle’s hand closed over the edge of the table. They had been born in 263 AS, under a sky the old priests claimed was the color of drowned silver. The world had given them two crowns and the title High Inquisitor, though neither honor had ever felt like a gift. A crown was a promise made by someone who expected your head to remain still while they tightened it.
The cellar bell rang again.
Morwenna heard it this time.
Her eyes narrowed.
“Does the High Inquisitor invite the dead to witness interrogations?”
“The dead require no invitation.”
“Then perhaps you should ask it whether I betrayed you.”
Sabelle smiled without warmth. “You mistake accusation for trust.”
“I mistake nothing.”
They opened a second folio.
Inside lay a coastal survey, its ink blurred by salt. Gloamreach lay on the Pale Coast, sealed beneath quarantine. Its garrison was 2,483. The number had been written three times, each copy in a different hand. Around the mark for the harbor, someone had drawn a ring of black strokes, as though the place were an eye that must not be opened.
“Gloamreach is a core location,” Sabelle said. “The quarantine remains in force.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Morwenna said nothing.
“Your ships have approached its waters.”
“A fleet approaches many waters.”
“Your intelligence reached the Iron-Ring Cartel before it reached the proper authorities.”
“Your evidence is a suspicion wearing a uniform.”
“It is a uniform you recognize.”
The Fleet Admiral leaned back. The chair creaked beneath her, an old complaint.
Beyond the narrow window, the night pressed against the glass. Sabelle could see only a thin scatter of ash falling from the upper roofs. The Hold had been built high enough that weather sometimes passed below it. Somewhere beyond the walls, where the mountains broke the horizon, Cindermere Hold stood abandoned among the High Spires. It had been founded in 246 AS, and its garrison once numbered 8878. Now it was not a core holding. Its silhouette, blackened and remote, had become a lesson in what strength looked like after everyone worth killing had already been killed.
Morwenna watched Sabelle’s face.
“You want me to say Gloamreach is compromised,” she said.
“I want you to say what you know.”
“What I know is that sealed places breed profitable rumors.”
“And what you know of Cindermere Hold?”
Her expression did not change, but she looked again at the folio.
“Nothing worth saying.”
“Nothing worth saying is the Cartel’s favored currency.”
“Then you should arrest them.”
“The Iron-Ring Cartel does not sit in rooms.”
“It sits everywhere.”
A murmur rose from beneath the floor. This time it shaped itself almost into a word.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Sabelle felt the old pull in their chest, the revenant’s hunger pressing against the chain of its binding. Not hunger for flesh. That would have been simpler. It wanted recognition. The dead wanted to be told that their suffering had entered the world’s accounting.
The War of Drowned Light had 64617 casualties, the folio said.
The dead did not care whether the number was accurate. They cared that someone had written it down.
Sabelle set the parchment aside and brought out the reliquary.
The Diadem of Sorrowgate was small enough to rest in both hands. Its surface had the dull gleam of bone polished beneath deep water. It had been forged in 281 AS. Attunement to it cost 9. The cost was low, which made the artifact more dangerous; grief often entered cheaply and collected interest later.
Morwenna stared at it.
“Do you know what that is?”
“The Diadem of Sorrowgate.”
“Good.”
“Are you offering it?”
“I am showing you what remembers.”
The diadem’s inner rim glimmered. In its reflection, Morwenna’s face seemed older, then younger, then absent altogether. Sabelle saw a shoreline beneath a white sky. Ships without flags. Men and women kneeling in water that reached their throats. A radiance drowned beneath the waves, still shining where no sun could touch it.
The war’s appearance had been broken banners and drowned radiance. Its truth was treachery concealed beneath attrition, vengeance without an ending.
Sabelle withdrew their hand.
Morwenna’s breath had shortened.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
“You sell intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel,” Sabelle said. “The question is not whether. The question is what they intend to purchase.”
“And if I refuse to answer?”
“Then the cellar will answer for you.”
The lamps guttered.
Morwenna looked at the door.
Sabelle heard the chains below draw taut, one link after another. The revenant had risen. Its weight moved through the foundations. Dust sifted from the ceiling and settled upon the folios like gray snow.
“You are not what they say,” Morwenna whispered.
“They say many things.”
“They say the Twice-Crowned High Inquisitor has no private devotions.”
“Then they are wrong.”
A smile touched Morwenna’s mouth, but it was not the earlier smile. This one carried pity, and pity was an insult more intimate than hatred.
“You keep it bound beneath your cellar.”
Sabelle’s fingers tightened around the Diadem of Sorrowgate.
The revenant struck the underside of the floor.
Once.
The sound traveled through the table, through the salt circle, through the crown of blackened names. Morwenna rose as the room lurched, and for one breath the Fleet Admiral’s discipline broke entirely.
A voice came up through the stones.
Not a scream.
A name.
Sabelle turned toward the door, where the lock had begun to tremble, and Morwenna said, “You should have asked me what the Silent Choir found beneath Gloamreach,” and the dead below struck the floor again—
The dead below struck the floor again—
—and the lock burst inward.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
The door did not open so much as lose the argument. Iron teeth tore free of the wood. A breath of cellar-cold entered the chamber, carrying wet stone, old ashes, and the sweet corruption of something that had learned to wait without breathing.
Morwenna’s hand went to the weapon at her hip.
Sabelle noticed. They noticed everything when fear made a person precise.
“Do not,” Sabelle said.
The Fleet Admiral’s fingers remained where they were. Her face had regained its discipline, but discipline was only fear taught to stand upright. The lantern flame shivered between them. Across the table, the Crown of Burned Names lay within its salt circle, blackened points lowered toward the boards. Each scar upon it seemed to deepen as the voice beneath the room gathered itself.
Sabelle could feel the Diadem of Sorrowgate against their palm.
Not weight. Attention.
Its sorrow had teeth.
“You heard it,” Morwenna said.
“I heard the floor.”
“You heard your name.”
The third blow came.
The table split along its grain. Salt leapt from the circle and glittered in the air before settling over the Diadem like frost. The Crown of Burned Names did not move. It held the room as a nail holds flesh.
Sabelle looked at it.
“The Crown of Burned Names had an attunement cost of 60,” they said.
Morwenna stared.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Sabelle had spoken softly, yet the words seemed to descend through the chamber. The ward had exacted that cost from every hand that had ever reached for it, and Sabelle had never mistaken cost for proof of worth. Powerful things did not ask what a person could spare. They took what would leave a lasting absence.
“Why tell me that now?” Morwenna asked.
“Because you are looking at it as if it might protect you.”
“I am looking at it as if it might protect us.”
“There is no us in this room.”
The Fleet Admiral’s mouth tightened. “You invited me.”
“I permitted you to enter.”
“And now you regret the distinction.”
Sabelle turned from her. Beyond the broken door, darkness breathed beneath the steps. The cellar lay under the chamber, under the stone, under every sealed report and censored confession that had allowed this house to remain respectable. They had kept the revenant bound there because the alternatives had been worse. That was the phrase they had used when first they drew the chains. It had sounded like principle in the privacy of their own skull.
Now the thing below had spoken their name.
The sound came again, muffled through earth.
“Sabelle.”
Their fingers closed around the Diadem of Sorrowgate until its edges bit skin.
Morwenna took a step toward the door. “It knows you.”
“It knows a sound.”
“It called you.”
“So do beggars. So do judges.”
“It called you from beneath a ward that has held since before—”
“Do not finish that sentence.”
The Admiral stopped.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
The silence that followed was not empty. It had the crowded quality of a courtroom before the verdict, when every witness had already decided what truth would cost them.
Sabelle could hear water slipping somewhere below. A chain dragged across stone. Then another chain answered, not with metal, but with a low rasp that made the teeth ache.
Morwenna said, “The Silent Choir found it beneath Gloamreach.”
Sabelle’s gaze sharpened.
There it was. Not the secret itself, but the shape of its shadow.
“Found what?”
“You know what.”
“I know what they claimed to find.”
“They sent the report sealed.”
“You opened it.”
“I read it.”
“You sold it.”
Morwenna did not flinch. That was the trouble with trained liars. Their shame did not appear where shame belonged. It moved elsewhere, into the breathing, the posture, the careful refusal to touch the edge of the table.
“To whom?” Sabelle asked.
Morwenna’s eyes went to the black crown.
The answer did not need a voice.
“The Iron-Ring Cartel,” Sabelle said.
A faint sound escaped Morwenna—not denial, not agreement. Something smaller and more exhausted.
Sabelle felt the room contract around the name. The Cartel was not present, yet its hunger had a way of arriving ahead of its agents. Coin had no allegiance except to continuation. It entered a war through a purse, a harbor, a clerk’s sleeve. It left by every door.
“You gave them the report,” Sabelle said.
“I gave them a portion.”
“Which portion?”
“The portion that could be purchased.”
“Everything can be purchased.”
“Not everything.”
“Your intelligence can.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Morwenna’s gaze lifted. “You say that as though the Ashen Vanguard has ever paid in anything else.”
The floor shuddered beneath them.
Dust sifted from the ceiling. The lantern guttered, and the room filled with the copper smell of its dying wick. Sabelle placed the Diadem of Sorrowgate on the table beside the crown. The two relics did not touch. Grief required distance from erasure.
Under the boards, the revenant whispered.
“Sabelle.”
This time the voice carried an old cadence, a human shape worn thin by burial. It was not pleading. It had no need to plead. The bound were patient. Patience was the only dignity left to the dead.
Morwenna’s hand withdrew from her weapon.
“What did you bind down there?”
Sabelle faced her.
The question had been waiting between them since the Admiral crossed the threshold. It had merely lacked the courage to become audible.
“You came for the answer,” Sabelle said.
“I came for what the Silent Choir found.”
“No. You came to learn whether I had already found it.”
Morwenna’s expression hardened. “If you knew, you would have told no one.”
“Correct.”
“That is not a defense.”
“It is not meant to be.”
Another blow struck beneath the floor, but the revenant did not speak afterward. The quiet was worse. Sabelle felt the pressure of the chains through the soles of their boots, a tugging beneath bone. The binding held. It had held through years of prayer, threat, and the long, humiliating labor of keeping something powerful enough to hate from remembering how to die.
Morwenna said, “The Pale Coast is sealed.”
“You know that.”
“Gloamreach is quarantined.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
“You know that as well.”
“I know its garrison is 2,483.”
“Then you know enough to understand what would happen if panic reached them.”
The admission hung in the chamber. Morwenna heard it. Sabelle saw the calculation enter her eyes, crossing from one side of the ledger to the other.
“Is it under Gloamreach?” Morwenna asked.
Sabelle said nothing.
“Is that what the Choir found?”
“Ask the Choir.”
“They are not here.”
“They prefer it that way.”
A smile touched Morwenna’s lips and vanished. “You speak of them as if you admire their methods.”
“I speak of them as if I have survived them.”
“The War of Drowned Light ended with their victory.”
Sabelle’s thumb moved over the Diadem’s rim. “Victories are often what the survivor calls the last cruelty.”
“And the deaths?”
“Do not use dead bodies as currency with me.”
“I am trying to prevent more.”
“No. You are trying to keep the Iron-Ring Cartel from learning that the Silent Choir’s report has value.”
Morwenna’s silence confessed more cleanly than words.
The revenant stirred beneath them. A slow scrape. Then the boards bowed upward.
Sabelle moved before thought could interfere. They seized the Crown of Burned Names and pressed it against the floor.
The ward answered with heat.
Not fire. Recognition.
Blackened metal flared beneath their hands. The scars cut into its surface filled with a dull, ember-red light, and the air thickened until Morwenna gasped. Beneath the crown, something struck the boards and recoiled. The entire house seemed to draw a breath through its foundations.
Sabelle held the ward down.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Pain opened along their palms. It was not the cost of attunement; that price had been paid elsewhere, in chambers where witnesses had gone blind and names had been burned from records still warm with ink. This was only resistance. This was the crown reminding its keeper that protection and mutilation had always shared a root.
“Do not make me release it,” Sabelle said.
Morwenna’s eyes fixed on their bleeding hands. “You cannot control it.”
“I control the chains.”
“For now.”
The words slipped through Sabelle’s guard.
For now.
Below, the revenant laughed. The sound was delicate, almost courteous.
Morwenna heard it and went pale.
Sabelle pressed harder. “What did you sell?”
“The Choir’s route.”
“Whose route?”
“Their route to the chamber.”
“What chamber?”
Morwenna’s gaze shifted toward the cellar door, toward the darkness that had no right to be listening.
“The chamber beneath Gloamreach.”
Sabelle felt the crown pulse beneath their hands.
“You sold the Cartel a way into the quarantine.”
“I sold them a warning.”
“You sold them access.”
“I sold them the knowledge that access existed.”
“Do not decorate treason.”
Morwenna’s discipline broke then—not entirely, but enough. Her breath came shallow. Her shoulders lowered as if an invisible weight had been set upon them.
