The silence that followed was not empty. It had the crowded quality of a courtroom before the verdict,
when every witness had already decided what truth would cost them.
Sabelle could hear water slipping somewhere below. A chain dragged across stone. Then another chain
answered, not with metal, but with a low rasp that made the teeth ache.
Morwenna said, “The Silent Choir found it beneath Gloamreach.”
Sabelle’s gaze sharpened.
There it was. Not the secret itself, but the shape of its shadow.
“Found what?”
“You know what.”
“I know what they claimed to find.”
“They sent the report sealed.”
“You opened it.”
“I read it.”
“You sold it.”
Morwenna did not flinch. That was the trouble with trained liars. Their shame did not appear where shame
belonged. It moved elsewhere, into the breathing, the posture, the careful refusal to touch the edge of the
table.
“To whom?” Sabelle asked.
Morwenna’s eyes went to the black crown.
The answer did not need a voice.
“The Iron-Ring Cartel,” Sabelle said.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
A faint sound escaped Morwenna—not denial, not agreement. Something smaller and more exhausted.
Sabelle felt the room contract around the name. The Cartel was not present, yet its hunger had a way of
arriving ahead of its agents. Coin had no allegiance except to continuation. It entered a war through a
purse, a harbor, a clerk’s sleeve. It left by every door.
“You gave them the report,” Sabelle said.
“I gave them a portion.”
“Which portion?”
“The portion that could be purchased.”
“Everything can be purchased.”
“Not everything.”
“Your intelligence can.”
Morwenna’s gaze lifted. “You say that as though the Ashen Vanguard has ever paid in anything else.”
The floor shuddered beneath them.
Dust sifted from the ceiling. The lantern guttered, and the room filled with the copper smell of its dying
wick. Sabelle placed the Diadem of Sorrowgate on the table beside the crown. The two relics did not
touch. Grief required distance from erasure.
Under the boards, the revenant whispered.
“Sabelle.”
This time the voice carried an old cadence, a human shape worn thin by burial. It was not pleading. It had
no need to plead. The bound were patient. Patience was the only dignity left to the dead.
Morwenna’s hand withdrew from her weapon.
“What did you bind down there?”
Sabelle faced her.
The question had been waiting between them since the Admiral crossed the threshold. It had merely
lacked the courage to become audible.
“You came for the answer,” Sabelle said.
“I came for what the Silent Choir found.”
“No. You came to learn whether I had already found it.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Morwenna’s expression hardened. “If you knew, you would have told no one.”
“Correct.”
“That is not a defense.”
“It is not meant to be.”
Another blow struck beneath the floor, but the revenant did not speak afterward. The quiet was worse.
Sabelle felt the pressure of the chains through the soles of their boots, a tugging beneath bone. The binding

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
held. It had held through years of prayer, threat, and the long, humiliating labor of keeping something
powerful enough to hate from remembering how to die.
Morwenna said, “The Pale Coast is sealed.”
“You know that.”
“Gloamreach is quarantined.”
“You know that as well.”
“I know its garrison is 2,483.”
“Then you know enough to understand what would happen if panic reached them.”
The admission hung in the chamber. Morwenna heard it. Sabelle saw the calculation enter her eyes,
crossing from one side of the ledger to the other.
“Is it under Gloamreach?” Morwenna asked.
Sabelle said nothing.
“Is that what the Choir found?”
“Ask the Choir.”
“They are not here.”
“They prefer it that way.”
A smile touched Morwenna’s lips and vanished. “You speak of them as if you admire their methods.”
“I speak of them as if I have survived them.”
“The War of Drowned Light ended with their victory.”
Sabelle’s thumb moved over the Diadem’s rim. “Victories are often what the survivor calls the last
cruelty.”
“And the deaths?”
“Do not use dead bodies as currency with me.”
“I am trying to prevent more.”
“No. You are trying to keep the Iron-Ring Cartel from learning that the Silent Choir’s report has value.”
Morwenna’s silence confessed more cleanly than words.
The revenant stirred beneath them. A slow scrape. Then the boards bowed upward.
Sabelle moved before thought could interfere. They seized the Crown of Burned Names and pressed it
against the floor.
The ward answered with heat.
Not fire. Recognition.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Blackened metal flared beneath their hands. The scars cut into its surface filled with a dull, ember-red
light, and the air thickened until Morwenna gasped. Beneath the crown, something struck the boards and

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
recoiled. The entire house seemed to draw a breath through its foundations.
Sabelle held the ward down.
Pain opened along their palms. It was not the cost of attunement; that price had been paid elsewhere, in
chambers where witnesses had gone blind and names had been burned from records still warm with ink.
This was only resistance. This was the crown reminding its keeper that protection and mutilation had
always shared a root.
“Do not make me release it,” Sabelle said.
Morwenna’s eyes fixed on their bleeding hands. “You cannot control it.”
“I control the chains.”
“For now.”
The words slipped through Sabelle’s guard.
For now.
Below, the revenant laughed. The sound was delicate, almost courteous.
Morwenna heard it and went pale.
Sabelle pressed harder. “What did you sell?”
“The Choir’s route.”
“Whose route?”
“Their route to the chamber.”
“What chamber?”
Morwenna’s gaze shifted toward the cellar door, toward the darkness that had no right to be listening.
“The chamber beneath Gloamreach.”
Sabelle felt the crown pulse beneath their hands.
“You sold the Cartel a way into the quarantine.”
“I sold them a warning.”
“You sold them access.”
“I sold them the knowledge that access existed.”
“Do not decorate treason.”
Morwenna’s discipline broke then—not entirely, but enough. Her breath came shallow. Her shoulders
lowered as if an invisible weight had been set upon them.
“They already knew,” she said. “The Iron-Ring Cartel already knew there was something beneath
Gloamreach. They were buying confirmation. If I refused, someone else would have given it.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
“Then you might have allowed someone else to be damned.”
“I have allowed worse.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
“Have you?”
A long pause.
The revenant spoke from under the floor.
“Morwenna.”
The Fleet Admiral turned toward the cellar.
Sabelle watched the change in her. Recognition moved through her face like a blade through cloth.
“You know that voice,” Sabelle said.
Morwenna did not answer.
“You have heard it before.”
The boards cracked beneath the crown.
Morwenna whispered, “No.”
The revenant said her name again, and this time the chains below began to ring.
The chains rang again.
Not in panic. Not in pain.
In recognition.
Sabelle felt the sound pass through the soles of their boots and climb the bones of their legs. The cellar
was below them, behind the sealed door and the iron locks, beneath the chamber where the Fleet Admiral
had come to bargain with a High Inquisitor. Beneath the house, beneath the frost-stiffened earth, the
revenant waited in its dark.
Morwenna’s hand had gone to the hilt at her side.
“You said it was bound,” she murmured.
“It is.”
“That is not what I asked.”
“No.” Sabelle turned from the cellar door. “It is not.”
The crown upon their head seemed suddenly too heavy. The Crown of Burned Names pressed its scorched
rim into their brow, every blackened mark along it drinking the candlelight. It had been forged in 266 AS,
when remembrance was still considered a kind of mercy. The makers had believed a ward could protect a
name by consuming it.
They had been wrong.
Or perhaps they had understood protection better than anyone living.
The revenant dragged its chains across stone.
Morwenna looked toward the floor. “How long?”
Sabelle said nothing.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
“How long has it been under this house?”
“Long enough.”
“That is not an answer.”
“It is the only one you are owed.”
The Fleet Admiral’s mouth tightened. Discipline held her face together. It did not hold the fear beneath it.
Fear was a tide; Sabelle had spent years learning how it moved through people before it broke the surface.
The voice came again.
“Morwenna.”
The candle flames bent toward the cellar door.
Morwenna flinched.
There. The truth, unarmored for half a breath.
Sabelle had been born in 263 AS, in a city whose bells had been melted down for weapons before they
learned the shape of their own name. By the time they took the office of High Inquisitor, they had ceased
believing that truth made anything cleaner. Truth was merely another instrument. It could cauterize. It
could open a wound. It could be sold.
Morwenna had sold it.
Not all of it. Not yet.
“The Iron-Ring Cartel knew there was something beneath Gloamreach,” Morwenna said. “They paid for
certainty.”
“And you gave it to them.”
“I gave them suspicion.”
“You gave them a map.”
“I gave them enough to keep their ships from sailing blind.”
“Ships do not need maps to find graves.”
Something struck the underside of the floor.
Dust sifted from the beams.
Morwenna’s gaze sharpened. “You have kept it here without reporting it.”
“Yes.”
“You are the High Inquisitor.”
“I am aware.”
“You were appointed to uncover abominations.”
“I have uncovered one.”
“And concealed it.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Sabelle stepped closer to the cellar door. The wood had been sealed with salt, black wax, and a thin line of
blood that had dried brown in the grain. “The Silent Choir would have destroyed it.”
“Perhaps that would have been merciful.”
“Perhaps.” Sabelle placed two fingers against the crown. “The Silent Choir has never confused mercy with
restraint.”
The old records called the War of Drowned Light a victory for the Silent Choir. The record was correct. It
was also incomplete.
The war began in 225 AS and ended in 235 AS. Its ledgers carried the same number wherever they had
survived: 64617 casualties. Not rounded. Not corrected. A number too precise to mourn and too large to
comprehend. The conflict collapsed into a decade of guerrilla reprisals after the banners came down, and
the Silent Choir remained recorded as the victor. Its spark had been secretly staged by them.
Sabelle had read the sealed testimony.
The first light had been drowned on purpose.
Morwenna watched them. “You speak as though you know what it is.”
“I know what it remembers.”
“What does it remember?”
The chain below the floor went taut.
A voice scraped upward through the boards.
“The light.”
Morwenna’s face emptied.
Sabelle heard the answer before she understood the question. A cold pressure gathered behind their eyes.
The revenant had never spoken of the war. It had resisted every command that required language. It had
torn through three binding circles rather than name the dead.
Now it had chosen to speak.
“What light?” Morwenna asked.
The revenant laughed.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
The sound was wet and small, as though something had drowned while trying to breathe.
Morwenna stepped backward. “You knew it was here.”
“I knew something was here.”
“You knew.”
“I suspected.”
“You brought me to this house.”
“I summoned you to this house.”
“Why?”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Sabelle looked at her then, truly looked. “Because the Iron-Ring Cartel has been buying pieces of
Gloamreach from you, and I wanted to know whether you understood what you were selling.”
Morwenna’s eyes hardened. “You already knew.”
“I knew you were selling intelligence.”
The silence that followed had a blade’s edge.
The Fleet Admiral’s expression did not change. It did not need to. Confession had entered the room
without being spoken.
Outside, wind worried at the shutters. Beyond them lay the Pale Coast, all salt glare and dead water, and
Gloamreach sealed behind its quarantine lines. The town was a core location despite the silence around it,
guarded by a garrison of 2,483. No vessel was meant to approach its shore without sanction. No
messenger was meant to leave it. Yet the Iron-Ring Cartel had found ways to send questions through
walls.
Morwenna had answered.
“How much?” Sabelle asked.
“Enough to keep men alive.”
“Whose men?”
“The men under my command.”
“Your command does not extend to the Cartel.”
“It extends to whatever prevents a slaughter.”
“Does it?”
Morwenna’s hand slipped from her sword. “You think this is about coin.”
“I think coin is the cleanest part of it.”
Beneath them, the revenant began to whisper.
The words were too low to make out, but the rhythm carried through the boards. A litany, perhaps. Or a
list. Sabelle had learned that the dead did not always distinguish between prayer and indictment.
Morwenna heard it too.
“What have you done to it?”
“Bound it.”
“With what?”
“Law.”
“That is not what binds the dead.”
“No,” Sabelle said. “Names do.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
They drew the Diadem of Sorrowgate from beneath their coat. It lay in their palm like a piece of winter: a
reliquary, narrow and pale, its metal filigree shaped around a dark inner hollow. The Diadem of

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Sorrowgate had been forged in 281 AS. Its attunement cost was 9. Sabelle had paid it willingly, though the
payment had left them unable to dream for a season.
The diadem trembled.
Below, the revenant answered.
Morwenna stared at the artifact. “You used that on it?”
“I used what was required.”
“And the Crown?”
“The Crown of Burned Names holds the boundary.”
“The diadem holds the name.”
Sabelle closed their fingers around it. “The diadem holds what remains of one.”
A crack opened along the floorboard between them.
Black vapor leaked through.
Morwenna drew her blade.
Sabelle did not.
The thing below pulled once against the chains. The house groaned around them. Somewhere in the walls,
old nails shifted. A smell rose from the seam: brine, wet ash, and the sweet rot of flowers left too long in a
sealed room.
“Tell me,” Morwenna said, “what did you bring into Gloamreach?”
“You brought something into Gloamreach.”
“I brought orders.”
“You carried them.”
“For the Ashen Vanguard.”
“For House Morvain.”
“For the Silent Choir.”
Morwenna’s gaze flicked toward the crown. “And for the Bleeding Crown?”
Sabelle said nothing.
The five powers had learned to speak of the Pale Coast as though it were a border between them. The
Ashen Vanguard claimed the roads. House Morvain claimed the old blood. The Silent Choir claimed the
dead, whenever the dead could be made useful. The Iron-Ring Cartel claimed whatever could be moved.
The Bleeding Crown claimed the right to punish anyone who disputed the claim.
Gloamreach belonged to none of them.
That was why all of them wanted it.
The board split.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
A pale hand rose through the gap.
Its fingers were corded with black veins. Salt crusted the nails. A ring of iron had been driven through the
little finger, and a chain ran from it into the dark.
Morwenna’s blade flashed down.
Sabelle caught her wrist.
“Do not.”
The revenant’s hand remained between them.
“Morwenna,” it said.
The Fleet Admiral strained against Sabelle’s grip. “Let me go.”
“No.”
“It knows me.”
“Yes.”
“It should not.”
“No.”
Morwenna’s voice broke for the first time. “Then what is it?”
Sabelle released her.
The hand withdrew. The chain clattered down into silence.
For several breaths, neither of them moved.
Then something beneath the floor began to scratch.
One stroke.
A pause.
Another stroke.
Morwenna looked at the boards. “It is writing.”
Sabelle knelt.
The Crown of Burned Names warmed against their skull. Its wards stirred, not in warning but in
recognition. Sabelle pressed their palm to the floor and felt the revenant’s will move beneath it like a
drowned body turning in deep water.
Letters appeared in the dust.
Not carved. Remembered.
MORWENNA.
Then another line formed beneath it.
NOT THE FIRST.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Morwenna made a sound that might have been anger or grief.
Sabelle stared at the words until the candlelight blurred.
The cellar door opened by itself.
Below, chains began to ring in every corner of the dark.
Morwenna stood at the foot of the stairs.
The dark beyond the open door had changed. It no longer waited like an absence. It breathed, slow and
patient, drawing the candle flame toward itself. Each chain answered the breath with a small metallic
shiver.
Sabelle rose. “You know this place.”
“I know what was buried beneath it.”
“That is not the same thing.”
“No.” Morwenna’s face had gone pale beneath the soot. “It is worse.”
The letters in the dust stirred. MORWENNA broke apart, its grains crawling into new shapes.
BORN: 288 AS
Sabelle read it aloud.
Morwenna closed her eyes.
“I was born in 288 AS,” she said. “In the ash winter, when the old king’s pyres burned for thirteen days.
My mother swore the smoke entered the house before I did. She said I came into the world already
choking.”
A chain snapped somewhere below.
The sound travelled up through the foundations.
Sabelle looked at the black stairwell. “What was buried?”
“Names.”
“Whose?”
Morwenna descended one step. “Everyone the Crown required forgotten.”
The Crown of Burned Names tightened around Sabelle’s skull. Behind their eyes, dead voices began to
murmur. They heard fragments: a miller’s daughter, a deserter, a saint with a butcher’s hands. Names
without bodies. Crimes without graves.
At the bottom of the stairs, a second candle burned on a stone ledge.
Its flame was green.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Around it stood twelve iron chairs, each occupied by a figure wrapped in funeral cloth. Their heads hung
low. Their chains ran from throat to throat, binding them into a circle.
The thirteenth chair was empty.
Morwenna entered the circle.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Every corpse lifted its head.
“Do not,” Sabelle whispered.
“If I do not sit,” Morwenna said, “the house will choose someone else.”
The cloth over the nearest corpse split. Beneath it was a woman’s face, shrivelled and blackened, with
Morwenna’s eyes.
“Not the first,” the dead woman rasped.
Morwenna lowered herself into the empty chair.
The chains surged.
They pierced her wrists, her ribs, the hollow beneath her tongue. No blood came. Only smoke, pouring
from her wounds and filling the cellar with the stink of burnt roses.
Sabelle reached for her, but the Crown dragged their hand away.
Letters appeared across Morwenna’s brow.
MORWENNA ASHGROVE BORN: 288 AS REMEMBERED: NEVER
Morwenna looked at Sabelle through the smoke.
“Now,” she said, “you know where the first name is buried.”
The cellar door slammed shut above them.
In the darkness, something began to climb.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Chapter 14
The dead of Blackport had never learned to keep quiet.
They whispered through wet stone, through the iron grates beneath the floor, through the black water that
gathered in the old cisterns and breathed up the stink of salt, ash, and old blood. Isolde Fellgard the
Unforgiven heard them whenever the night drew close enough to the walls.
Not voices. Never voices.
A pressure behind the eyes. A pulse in the teeth. The remembered weight of a blade entering flesh and
finding, beneath skin, the warm resistance of a life that had not yet agreed to end.
They stood alone in the records chamber with one gloved hand resting on the table. Their other hand held
a narrow silver knife.
The knife had not been drawn for murder. Not yet.
Its point touched the map before them, where the coast had been reduced to a crooked line of ink. Pale
Coast. Gloamreach. Cindermere Hold. The names had been written and rewritten by hands that believed
ink could command the world to remain legible.
Beyond the slit windows, rain moved across the darkness like a curtain being drawn by an unseen servant.
Isolde closed their eyes.
They were back in Blackport.
The walls had been red with reflected fire. Broken banners dragged along the mud. Men cried out beneath
the hooves of frightened horses, and the sea, close beyond the streets, hammered the harbor pilings with
the patience of a thing waiting to be fed.
They had fought in The Purge of Blackport, fighting for House Morvain.
The words were written in the record before them. The clerk had given the sentence its own line, as though

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
that distinction mattered. As though the dead cared which banner had been held above the hand that killed
them.
Isolde remembered the banner. They remembered the taste of soot. They remembered kneeling in the
flooded street with blood running from their palm into the black water—not their own blood, though they
had been cut badly enough to feel it.
Blood-Mage, the old records called them.
The name had once been a warning. Later it became a title. Now it was spoken as if it were a sentence
from which no appeal could be made.
Their reflection trembled in the shallow water pooled atop the table. The face that looked back was pale
and severe, its eyes dark beneath the hood. The face of an Unforgiven Blood-Mage. The face of someone
who had learned to make grievance useful.
A latch clicked behind them.
Isolde did not turn. “You are late.”
“I was not told there would be a clock.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Ossric Ashgrove entered carrying three ledgers against his chest. He moved with the careful discomfort of
a man accustomed to balancing weight but not to being watched while he did it. He was a quartermaster,
and his hands bore the evidence: ink beneath the nails, grease along the knuckles, a small white scar where
a crate-hook had bitten him.
Ossric Ashgrove had been born in 333 AS. The date sat in a column among other dates, neat and
bloodless. Isolde had seen it earlier that evening and wondered whether he knew how many people had
died before he took his first breath.
He set the ledgers down.
“Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched asked for the casualty rolls.”
“Then Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched should have come for them.”
“The Arch-Prelate does not come to records chambers.”
“An Arch-Prelate who forged their own lineage papers should be less particular about where they stand.”
Ossric’s mouth tightened. He had no canonical temperament, the records would have said, if records were
honest enough to admit ignorance. He only looked tired.
“Lower your voice.”
“Why? Are the stones loyal to Malchior?”
“The stones are loyal to whoever owns the blood in the mortar.”
Isolde looked at him then.
Ossric lowered his gaze first.
A second figure waited beyond the doorway, broad in the shoulders, wrapped in a dark mantle damp with
rain. No physical features had been recorded for Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless, though his authority
entered every room before he did. He was a Warden-Commander, and command clung to him like frost.
Born in 258 AS, the record said.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
The Oathless. The name had been given to him by mouths that feared him, or by his own enemies, or
perhaps by the hand that first set it down. Names were weapons with handles hidden inside them.
Ignatz stepped into the chamber.
“Leave us,” he told Ossric.
Ossric remained beside the table. “I was ordered to deliver the ledgers.”
“You have delivered them.”
“That is not the same as being dismissed.”
Ignatz’s gaze shifted to him. “You have become precise.”
“I have always been precise.”
“Then you have become brave.”
The quartermaster said nothing. Isolde watched the silence pass between them. It had the brittle quality of
ice over deep water.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Ignatz moved to the table. His gloved finger rested on the map, near the Pale Coast.
“Gloamreach,” he said.
The word seemed to draw the room inward.
Gloamreach lay on the Pale Coast, quarantined behind its own silence. Its garrison numbered 2,483. The
number had been written in red, then circled twice, as if arithmetic could serve as a ward. No ships were to
make harbor there. No message was to leave without inspection. No dead were to be carried beyond its
sealed roads.
“Gloamreach is still closed,” Isolde said.
“It is a core location.”
“So the ledgers claim.”
“The ledgers claim many things.”
Ignatz looked at them. Beneath the calm of his face, something moved and vanished. A thought. A
calculation. Isolde could smell wet wool and the faint metallic tang of chain beneath his mantle.
He secretly sold intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel.
The knowledge had come to Isolde in pieces: a missing dispatch, a convoy diverted before its orders were
issued, a seal broken and pressed shut again with wax too smooth to trust. Ignatz had made a career of
guarding thresholds. It was almost elegant that he had learned to profit from opening them.
“Why bring me here?” Isolde asked.
“Because you fought at Blackport.”
“I did more than fight.”
“That is what the record says.”
“The record is shy.”
Ossric glanced at the ledgers. “The record says Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven fought in The Purge of
Blackport, fighting for House Morvain.”
The exactness of it struck harder than accusation.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
For an instant, Isolde saw the face of their liege as it had been in the last chamber: astonished, not afraid.
That had been the worst of it. Fear could have been forgiven. Surprise had no such mercy.
They had plotted the death of their own liege.
The secret had lived beneath every oath they spoke afterward, warm as a buried coal.
Isolde pressed the silver knife into the map until its point pierced the parchment.
“Read the rest,” they said.
Ossric hesitated.
Ignatz did not. “The War of Drowned Light began in 225 AS and ended in 235 AS, with 64617 casualties.
The conflict collapsed into a decade of guerrilla reprisals. The Silent Choir is recorded as the victor.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
“The spark was secretly staged by The Silent Choir,” Isolde said.
Rain tapped the windows.
The old war entered the room without opening the door: drowned radiance, broken banners, triumph
stripped of all triumph. The Silent Choir had won, according to the record. The dead had not received the
victory. They had received reprisals, then more reprisals, until every surviving account sounded like a
confession spoken through a mouthful of mud.
Ignatz studied the map. “You know the figures.”
“I know what they buried under them.”
“64617.”
“Numbers are coffins with no bodies inside.”
Ossric’s fingers moved over the nearest ledger. “Cindermere Hold appears in the old garrison rolls.”
“Cindermere Hold was founded in 246 AS among The High Spires,” Ignatz said. “Its garrison once
numbered 8878.”
“Now it is abandoned,” Isolde said.
“And not a core holding,” Ossric added.
The quartermaster spoke as though reciting inventory. Isolde wondered what it meant to carry ruin in
columns: eight thousand eight hundred and seventy-eight absent from a fortress; two thousand four
hundred and eighty-three sealed behind quarantine; sixty-four thousand six hundred and seventeen
reduced to a line no clerk would dare smudge.
“Why show me this?” Isolde asked.
Ignatz unfolded a narrow strip of parchment. It bore no seal.
“Because someone has altered the Blackport account.”
Isolde felt the room grow colder.
“Altered how?”
“A name removed. A command reassigned. A company moved from one street to another.”
“Companies do not move on paper.”
“People do. Then paper follows.”
“Whose name?”
Ignatz did not answer.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Beyond him, Ossric’s face had gone still. The quartermaster knew something, or feared that he did. His
eyes remained fixed on the parchment.
Isolde reached for it.
Ignatz’s hand closed over the strip first.
The motion was fast enough to be an insult.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Blood stirred beneath Isolde’s skin. It rose in their veins with the familiar eager pressure, answering the
sudden heat in their anger. A drop welled at the base of their thumb where the glove seam had split. It
hung there, dark and shining.
Ignatz noticed.
“Do not,” he said.
“I have done worse.”
“Yes.”
The word carried no accusation. That made it worse.
The lamp flame bent toward Isolde. Shadows climbed the walls. In the wavering light, the maps seemed to
breathe: coastlines flexing, mountain ranges opening and closing like ribs.
Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched would want the rolls because lineage was a kind of battlefield,
and forged blood could be defended only by making every other bloodline look uncertain. Born in 289 AS,
Malchior wore sanctity like a garment tailored by a liar. The Arch-Prelate had forged their own lineage
papers. Isolde had seen the old seals. They had seen where the ink had been made to imitate age.
The five powers watched one another through the cracks of the realm: the Ashen Vanguard, House
Morvain, the Silent Choir, the Iron-Ring Cartel, and the Bleeding Crown. Each claimed to be holding back
the dark. Each kept one hand inside it.
Ignatz released the parchment.
“Read it,” he said.
Isolde took the strip.
The writing was cramped. The ink had bled at the edges, but one line remained clear.
Their name.
Not their title. Not Unforgiven.
Isolde Fellgard.
A mark followed it, shaped like a hook driven through a circle.
They knew that mark.
The blood in their glove began to move.
Ossric whispered, “What does it mean?”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Isolde held the parchment closer to the lamp. The hook seemed to twist, becoming almost a letter, almost a
wound.
Behind the walls, something knocked once.
Then again.
Ignatz reached for his sword.
Isolde did not move. They were listening to the blood, to the old cisterns, to Blackport calling across the
years with the drowned patience of the dead. The mark on the parchment opened like an eye, and from

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
somewhere beneath the floor came a voice that was not a voice—
“Your liege,” it said, and the lamp went out.
The darkness did not fall. It thickened.
Isolde felt it gather against their face, warm as breath. Ignatz’s sword came free with a dry whisper, and
Ossric made a small sound behind them—the involuntary noise of a man discovering that his body had
betrayed him before his mind could choose courage.
“Hold,” Isolde said.
Their voice returned from beneath the floor.
Hold.
The blood in their glove tightened. It crawled along the seams, seeking the pulse in their wrist. Every drop
remembered the mark. Every drop had become an ear.
Ignatz shifted. “What is below us?”
“A question,” said Isolde.
“No.”
The word came from the dark at their feet.
Not the voice beneath the floor. Ignatz’s voice.
Isolde turned toward him. They could not see his face, but they felt the scrape of his breath, controlled and
shallow. A Warden-Commander did not fear darkness. A Warden-Commander feared what darkness
might reveal.
“Put away the sword,” Isolde said.
“You heard it.”
“I heard you.”
“I did not speak.”
“Not with your mouth.”
Something moved below them. The flagstones groaned in their sockets. Ossric stumbled against the table,
and glass shattered under his heel.
“I was born in 333 AS,” he said, too quickly, as if reciting an inventory might preserve him. “I have no
part in this. I am a quartermaster. I keep stores. I count grain. I do not open—”
The floor knocked once.
Ossric swallowed the rest.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Isolde knelt. Cold seeped through their trousers. Beneath the stone, water whispered through old channels.
They remembered the cisterns under Blackport: drowned masonry, silted steps, the pale hands that had
risen where no living bodies remained. Their blood remembered more than they did. That was the curse of
it. Blood kept every door it had ever touched.
A thin red thread slipped from their glove and crept between the stones.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
The voice beneath them spoke again.
“Your liege.”
Isolde laid two fingers against the crack.
The answer came as pain.
They saw a chamber lit by six candles, though none burned with flame. They saw a hand signing a decree.
They saw the ring on that hand, dull with old blood. They saw their own fingers close around the throat
beneath it.
No face. No name.
Only the pressure.
The memory was not theirs. Or it was theirs, and the darkness had stripped away the mercy of recognition.
Ignatz caught their shoulder. “What did you see?”
Isolde rose slowly. “A door.”
“To where?”
“To the part of you that you sell.”
His grip tightened.
Ossric breathed, “Commander?”
Ignatz let Isolde go. “You are speaking madness.”
“Am I?”
The darkness seemed to lean toward him.
Isolde could smell iron now—not blood, not exactly, but the mineral scent of wet chains. Somewhere far
beneath the hold, a lock turned. The sound traveled through the stone with patient intimacy.
They remembered the first time Ignatz had come to them with a sealed packet and a warning not to ask
who had paid for its contents. He had called it necessity. Men with command called every betrayal by that
name. They built their honor around the wound and asked everyone else to admire the scar.
“Tell me,” Isolde said, “what does the Iron-Ring Cartel buy from you?”
Ossric went still.
Ignatz did not.
A blade of darkness seemed to pass between them.
“You have mistaken me for someone who can be threatened.”
“No,” Isolde said. “I have mistaken you for someone who still believes threats are necessary.”
The flagstones shuddered.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
This time the voice did not come from beneath them. It breathed directly against Isolde’s ear.
Your liege.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
The blood in their glove burst through the leather.
It spilled in a red crescent across the parchment. The hook-and-circle mark drank it. For a moment, the
symbol became bright enough to see. The parchment curled inward, not burning but folding around an
absence.
A face emerged in the black.
Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched.
Isolde knew the image though they had never trusted the person. The Arch-Prelate’s sanctified authority
had always seemed to strain against the shape of its own lie. The face blurred at the edges. Beneath it,
letters surfaced and dissolved.
Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched, born in 289 AS.
Then the image changed.
A hand lifted a document toward candlelight. The seal was perfect. The ink was old. The lineage was
false.
“He forged his own lineage papers,” Isolde whispered.
Ignatz’s sword lowered by a fraction. “What?”
The parchment showed another hand writing over the first. The letters crawled like insects.
Forged.
Then the face vanished.
Ossric pressed himself against the wall. “Who is your liege?”
Isolde looked at him. “You heard the voice.”
“I heard a word.”
“A word can be a chain.”
The floor opened.
Not wide. Not enough for a body. A seam appeared between the stones, and from it rose a breath of
drowned air. The chamber filled with the smell of black water and old ash. Isolde’s stomach clenched.
Their blood-thread vanished into the crack.
Below, something scraped upward.
Ignatz stepped in front of Ossric.
It was almost noble.
That was what made it obscene.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Isolde watched him take the stance of a guardian, watched the old reflex settle across his body like armor.
Yet beneath the coat, beneath the insignia, beneath every oath he had worn until it frayed, the Iron-Ring
Cartel waited with its open hand. Intelligence was a kind of blood. Once sold, it did not return to the vein.
“How much?” Isolde asked.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Ignatz’s face remained invisible.
“How much what?”
“For the names. The routes. The positions of men who believed your office meant safety.”
The scraping stopped.
He said, “You know nothing.”
“I know you secretly sell intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel.”
Ossric gasped.
The sound was swallowed by the crack.
Ignatz’s sword came up.
Isolde did not move. Their blood slid from the torn glove and hung in the air between them, a dark red
filament trembling toward the blade.
“Put it away,” they said.
“You should not have said that name.”
“Which name? The Cartel’s? Or yours?”
The darkness behind Ignatz stirred. A second figure took shape there—not seen, only inferred from the
way the air bent around it. The voice spoke through his shadow.
“Your liege.”
Ignatz turned.
For the first time, command abandoned him.
Isolde saw the opening and understood that all betrayals were made of such openings: a breath withheld, a
hand unguarded, a man facing the wrong direction.
They had plotted the death of their own liege.
The knowledge rose in them without shame and without pardon. It had not been an impulse, nor an
accident born of war. It had been plotted. Considered. Nurtured in silence until the deed became inevitable
enough to resemble fate.
Their liege had been a door, too.
Perhaps every throne was.
“Isolde,” Ignatz said.
Their name sounded like an accusation in his mouth.
“No,” they answered. “Not tonight.”
The seam widened. Black water pushed through, carrying scraps of parchment and pale threads that
caught on the stones. One fragment struck Isolde’s boot. They bent and lifted it.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text: A map.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
The coast had been drawn in faded ink. Along the margin, a single notation remained legible.
Gloamreach.
The name was followed by three words: Pale Coast. Quarantined. Core.
Then, beneath them:
Garrison: 2,483.
Ossric leaned closer despite himself. “Gloamreach.”
“Do not touch it,” Isolde said.
“I have not.”
“You are thinking about it.”
“I am a quartermaster.”
“As you keep reminding us.”
The map darkened where Isolde’s blood touched it. A second location appeared farther inland, elevated
above a jagged line of peaks.
Cindermere Hold.
Founded in 246 AS among The High Spires.
Garrison once numbered 8878.
Abandoned. Not a core holding.
The ink bled down the parchment like tears. The hold’s silhouette rose in the center of the map: blackened
towers, empty embrasures, a ruin lifted beyond reach. Immense strength hollowed into stone.
Ignatz stared at it. “Why show us this?”
“Because it wants to be remembered,” Isolde said.
“What does?”
“Everything.”
For an instant, another image came: banners drowned in pale radiance, fields split by old trenches, soldiers
moving beneath a light that had no sun behind it. The vision bore a name, etched across the dark in letters
of salt.
The War of Drowned Light.
It began in 225 AS.
It ended in 235 AS.
64617 casualties.
The Silent Choir was recorded as the victor.
But behind the banners, behind the drowned radiance and broken standards, veiled hands arranged the first
spark. The war’s spark had been secretly staged by The Silent Choir. The victory was only the cleanest lie

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
left standing after the reprisals.
Isolde tasted ash.
“The Silent Choir,” Ignatz said, reading the name as it formed.
“Their war,” said Isolde. “Their victory. Their spark.”
Ossric’s eyes shone in the dark. “How can a dead war speak?”
“It never died.”
The vision collapsed.
The five powers seemed to gather at the edge of thought: The Ashen Vanguard, House Morvain, The
Silent Choir, The Iron-Ring Cartel, and The Bleeding Crown. Their names did not appear on the
parchment, yet the blood made room for them. They pressed against one another in the darkness,
contending over ruins that had outlived the hands that first claimed them.
A drop fell from above.
It struck Isolde’s cheek.
They wiped it away and smelled iron.
Ignatz’s sword arm began to tremble.
“Commander,” Ossric whispered.
“I know.”
“No,” Isolde said. “You do not.”
From the open seam, a hand emerged.
It was not flesh. It was a shape made of wet shadow, fingers long and jointed, the nails packed with silt. It
reached toward Isolde’s glove.
The blood leapt to meet it.
Pain went through them so violently their knees struck the floor. Their mouth filled with copper. Beneath
their skin, every vein opened like a red road.
The hand touched their wrist.
And the voice, no longer beneath the floor, no longer inside the walls, spoke from within their own chest.
“Name your liege.”
Isolde saw Ignatz lift his sword.
They saw Ossric reach for the broken glass.
They saw the darkness turn its faceless attention toward the door.
Beyond it, footsteps approached—measured, unhurried, and familiar enough to make the blood in Isolde’s

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
glove begin to kneel.
The latch lifted.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Isolde’s blood tightened around their bones. The hand at their wrist withdrew, leaving a numbness that
was almost tenderness. Ignatz’s sword hung between them and the door, its edge trembling. Ossric
crouched beside the hearth with a shard of glass pinched in his fist, his breath coming in small, wet
catches.
The door opened inward.
Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched entered without haste.
The candlelight found the pale planes of their face and the dark fall of their vestments. Ash clung to the
hem as if the road had tried to bury them and failed. An Arch-Prelate should have carried the scent of oil,
incense, and clean stone. Malchior carried smoke. It threaded the chamber behind them.
The darkness beneath the floor went still.
“Name your liege,” it whispered from Isolde’s chest.
Malchior’s gaze settled on the glove, on the blood kneeling beneath its leather, and then on Isolde’s face.
“Do not,” Ignatz said.
It was not an order to Malchior. It was a plea addressed to whatever had entered with them.
Isolde rose slowly. Their knees had gone weak, but weakness was merely another form of exposure, and
they had survived too long by concealing both. The handprint on their wrist darkened. Five bruises
emerged beneath the skin, each one shaped like a narrow mouth.
“Your sword is drawn,” Malchior said.
Ignatz did not lower it. “Your presence was unannounced.”
“Doors are for those who believe themselves separate from what waits beyond them.”
Ossric swallowed. The glass trembled in his hand. He was a quartermaster; he knew the value of every

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
hinge, nail, ration, and blade in a room. He knew what could be counted. The thing below the floor had
made a ruin of counting.
Isolde looked at him and saw the fear he had tried to pack away like winter grain.
Then the voice spoke again.
“Name your liege.”
The word liege opened something behind their eyes.
They saw a table slick with wine. A seal broken under their thumb. A blade held not in anger but in
patience. The chamber where they had planned the death of their own liege had been colder than this one,
though no wind had touched it. They remembered the silence afterward—not grief, not triumph, but the
terrible relief of a door unbarred.
The secret had lived in them longer than any confession could survive.
Their blood knew it.
“Isolde,” Ignatz said.
There was warning in the name. Or recognition. With Ignatz, the two had become difficult to separate.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
The blood under Isolde’s glove surged toward the sound.
Ignatz flinched.
A folded packet slipped from inside his coat and struck the floor.
The wax seal split.
Thin sheets slid across the stone. One came to rest against Isolde’s boot. The ink had been written in
several hands, neat as spear wounds. Cargo routes. Watch rotations. Names of stores and movements
reduced to marks. At the bottom of one page, the insignia of the Iron-Ring Cartel gleamed in black wax.
The chamber seemed to contract around it.
Ossric stared. “Warden-Commander.”
Ignatz’s sword lowered by a finger’s breadth.
“Do not mistake paper for treason.”
“Paper is how treason travels,” Isolde said.
His eyes found theirs. For the first time, command left his face. Beneath it was calculation, and beneath
calculation, the exhausted terror of a man who had sold pieces of the world and discovered that the world
kept receipts.
The darkness laughed softly inside Isolde’s ribs.
Malchior stepped over the papers. “The Iron-Ring Cartel buys information because information is cheaper
than armies.”
“You know their prices?” Isolde asked.
“I know the price of everything that claims to be sacred.”
There it was: the faint abrasion beneath the sanctity. The lineage papers. The forged ancestry hidden
beneath the Arch-Prelate’s robes, ink and seal fashioned into a bloodline where none could be proven.
Isolde had seen the uncertainty in Malchior’s gaze whenever old records were opened, the way their
fingers pressed flat against the pages as though touch might force falsehood to become inheritance.
The thing below knew it too.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
“Name your liege,” it murmured.
Malchior’s mouth tightened.
“You are not the first priest to arrive carrying a counterfeit bloodline,” Isolde said.
Ossric made a sound like a cough.
Ignatz turned on them. “Enough.”
“No.” Isolde lifted the page with the toe of their boot. “We have all brought our hidden ledgers into this
room.”
Malchior’s eyes sharpened. “You speak as though yours is empty.”
Their wrist burned.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
The blood on the glove pushed against the seams, eager to escape. In its red sheen, Isolde saw the old
campaign roads and the drowned banners. They saw The War of Drowned Light, which began in 225 AS
and ended in 235 AS, leaving 64617 casualties behind it. The Silent Choir was recorded as the victor. The
spark had been secretly staged by The Silent Choir, though the songs afterward had called it providence,
necessity, fate—any word that could wash blood from the hands of the living.
The war had not ended when the banners fell. It had collapsed into a decade of guerrilla reprisals, each
killing remembered as an answer to another killing.
The thing beneath the floor stirred at the memory.
“Names,” it breathed. “All debts require names.”
A tremor ran through the stones.
Far below, something scraped its fingers along the underside of the world.
Isolde stepped toward the scattered papers. Their blood followed, a dark line moving through the cracks in
the floor.
“Why bring us here?” they asked.
Malchior did not look at the floor. “I did not.”
“Then why come?”
“Because the seal was broken.”
They meant the packet. Or perhaps something older.
Isolde bent to pick up another sheet. The ink blurred, then steadied. A location had been entered in the
margin: Cindermere Hold. Founded in 246 AS among The High Spires. Once its garrison had numbered
8878. Now abandoned, no longer a core holding. The figures stood together like a gravestone and an
accusation.
“Cindermere,” Ossric whispered.
Malchior looked at him.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
He dropped the glass. It shattered across the floor, and the sound woke every shadow in the chamber.
“I have never been there,” Ossric said.
“No one asked,” Ignatz replied.
The quartermaster’s face had gone gray. “It is not a supply concern.”
“Everything is a supply concern,” Isolde said. “Even a ruin.”
Beneath them, the thing gave a slow, pleased pulse.
The page in Isolde’s hand warmed. Another entry surfaced beneath the first, as though the ink had been
waiting under the ink.
Gloamreach. Pale Coast. Quarantined. Garrison: 2,483.
The number was exact. The place felt exact too: sealed gates, pallid surf, watchfires kept behind walls,
every breath measured against what might enter with the tide.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Malchior’s hand moved toward the page.
Isolde burned it before they could touch it.
The parchment blackened without flame. Its ash climbed upward in a thin spiral and hung between them.
Malchior watched it rise.
“Blood-Mage,” they said.
The title was not accusation or praise. It was a door being tested.
“I have never hidden what I am.”
“No,” Malchior said. “Only why.”
Their words struck more deeply than they should have.
Isolde had been born in 286 AS. The fact had once been written in a registry beside a mark that meant
living, legitimate, and claimed. Now it felt like another piece of evidence against them. They had carried
grievance as others carried a family sword. Ambition had sharpened it. Betrayal had given it a handle.
Ignatz’s gaze flicked toward them. “You knew this place was awake.”
“I suspected.”
“And you brought us anyway.”
“I brought no one.”
The floor cracked.
A line opened from the hearth to the door. Red light shone inside it—not fire, not reflection, but the color
of blood held up to the sun. Ossric stumbled backward. Ignatz seized his collar and dragged him clear.
The voice rose through Isolde.
“Name your liege.”
Their teeth clicked together. The question had become a hook. It pulled at the place where obedience had
once lived.
House Morvain came to mind—not as liege, not as refuge, but as a banner beneath which they had fought
in The Purge of Blackport. The memory carried soot, iron, and the taste of men praying through broken
teeth. They had served a cause without surrendering the whole of themselves. That distinction had
mattered then.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
It mattered less now.
Malchior came close enough for Isolde to smell the ash on their clothes.
“Say nothing,” the Arch-Prelate whispered.
“Why?”
“Because it is not asking you for allegiance.”
The red seam widened.
From somewhere beneath, a multitude drew breath.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Malchior’s expression changed. The sanctified mask slipped, revealing the person beneath it: not a fraud
exactly, but someone who had forged their own lineage papers and then lived long enough to fear the day
the forgery would acquire a voice.
“It is asking who owns the death you carry,” they said.
Isolde’s heart stopped.
The chamber vanished.
They were back at the table. Their hand was steady. The blade waited beneath the cloth. Their liege stood
on the other side, speaking of loyalty as though loyalty were a chain that grew stronger each time it cut the
skin.
Isolde had plotted the death. Not dreamed it. Not wished it in the privacy of hatred. Plotted it. Measured
the hour, the witnesses, the distance between mercy and suspicion.
The blood at their wrist opened its mouths.
“I own it,” Isolde said.
The darkness recoiled.
Every candle went out.
In the black, Ignatz swore. Ossric struck the wall. Malchior seized Isolde’s arm, but the touch sent a vision
through them: forged seals, a false descent, papers hidden beneath a vestment; a name built from ash and
forced into the shape of inheritance.
Then something below spoke with a voice that was no longer a whisper.
“Then kneel.”
The floor gave way beneath Isolde.
They fell only an inch before the blood caught them—every drop spilled in the chamber, every dark thread
beneath the stones, every buried memory with a pulse. Their body hung above the opening, suspended in a
red web.
Below waited a stair descending into absolute dark.
At its foot, far beneath the ruined hold, someone struck a bell.
Once.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Malchior’s grip tightened. Ignatz raised his sword. Ossric began to pray to a power he did not name.
Isolde looked into the darkness and understood that the footsteps beyond the door had never been
approaching them.
They had been ascending.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Chapter 15
The rain came down as ash.
It whispered against the shutters of the upper chamber, sifted through the cracks, and gathered in the
grooves of the table where the candles had burned low. Corvus Hollowmere the Pale watched the grey
flakes melt upon their glove. They became water, then vanished into the black leather.
The chamber had no windows large enough for a person to pass through. That was considered a comfort
by those who had built it. Corvus had never trusted comforts.
A single lamp burned beside the table. Its flame bent whenever the wind pressed against the walls.
Beneath it lay five seals impressed in wax: the Ashen Vanguard, House Morvain, the Silent Choir, the
Iron-Ring Cartel, and the Bleeding Crown. Five powers contending over what remained of the realm, each
calling its appetite by a different name.
A sixth seal lay broken.
Corvus touched the ragged wax with one finger.
“Who opened it?”
The door remained shut. Beyond it, footsteps paused, then resumed. Whoever had come had been taught
patience. That narrowed nothing. Patience was the first lesson of every court, every army, every
conspiracy that expected to survive its maker.
The latch lifted.
Hesper Wrenfield entered without haste, rain darkening the edges of their clothing. No insignia marked
them. No sword drew the eye. They carried only a leather tube beneath one arm.
“Outrider,” Corvus said.
“Hesper Wrenfield.” The reply was neither proud nor deferential. “You sent for me.”
“I sent for a report.”
“Then you sent for me.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Corvus studied the young face before them and found no expression worth stealing. Hesper Wrenfield had
been born in 404 AS. The fact had been written in three ledgers, copied by three hands, and contradicted
by none. Their service as an Outrider had taken them through roads where men learned to lie with their
mouths closed.
“Put it down.”
Hesper placed the tube on the table.
It rolled through the ash and stopped against the broken seal.
Corvus did not open it. “You came from Gloamreach?”
“Yes.”
The word seemed to lower the temperature of the chamber.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Gloamreach lay on the Pale Coast, a core location sealed beneath quarantine. Its garrison numbered 2,483.
The number had been repeated so often that it had acquired the flat, bloodless sound of prayer. Two
thousand four hundred and eighty-three souls behind the barriers, while the coast watched them from
beyond the cordons and pretended not to listen for screaming.
“What did you see?”
“Nothing.”
“That is not a report.”
“It is the report.” Hesper’s gaze shifted to the lamp. “The gates remained closed. The quarantine remained
in force. No vessel left the shore. No messenger entered.”
“And yet you returned.”
“I was allowed to return.”
Corvus leaned back. The chair gave a dry complaint.
There were truths that arrived loudly, with horns and banners. They were rarely the dangerous ones. The
dangerous truths slipped beneath doors and waited for someone to notice that the room had begun to smell
of earth.
“Who allowed you?”
Hesper looked at the sealed tube. “The guard at the western gate.”
“Name?”
“I did not ask.”
For the first time, something moved in Hesper’s expression. Not fear. Perhaps the memory of a mistake.
Corvus opened the tube.
The parchment inside was narrow, folded twice, and stained at one corner with a dark residue. No script
marked the outer face. Inside, a sketch had been made in charcoal: a tower without a roof, a circle beneath
it, and seven lines descending into blackness.
Cindermere Hold.
The hold had been founded in 246 AS among The High Spires. Its garrison had once numbered 8878.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Now it stood abandoned, no longer a core holding, its blackened silhouette lifted above the stone like the
corpse of some immense beast that had died upright.
Corvus placed the parchment flat.
“Where did you find this?”
“Gloamreach.”
“That was not my question.”
“It was under a floorstone in a guardroom.”
“Whose guardroom?”
“The western gate.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
The lamp flame shuddered.
Hesper continued. “The marks were fresh.”
“Fresh enough to be made by whom?”
“I saw no one.”
“No one is not a person.”
“No,” said Hesper. “It is what remained.”
Corvus let the silence thicken between them.
Under the floorstone, then. Beneath a gatehouse in a quarantined place. A drawing of Cindermere Hold,
though the abandoned hold was far from the Pale Coast, if distance still meant anything in the Ashen Era.
Roads had been broken by war, by flood, by old magic sleeping beneath the soil. Messages crossed the
realm by hands, by birds, by rumor, and sometimes by methods that left no corpse a priest could identify.
Corvus had been born in 351 AS. They remembered none of the world before their birth, but memory was
not required to inherit a wound. The old wars had entered every house like smoke.
“The War of Drowned Light began in 225 AS,” Corvus said.
Hesper did not answer.
“It ended in 235 AS. The records list 64617 casualties. Then the conflict collapsed into a decade of
guerrilla reprisals.” Corvus traced the charcoal circle. “The Silent Choir is recorded as the victor.”
“Recorded by whom?”
“By those who survived to write.”
“And the truth?”
Corvus looked at the broken seal bearing the Choir’s mark.
“The war’s spark was secretly staged by them.”
The words passed into the chamber and did not return.
Beneath their shirt, against the skin, the hidden oath tightened.
It had no metal clasp, no scar, no priestly witness. It lived in the architecture of silence: what Corvus did

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
not say, what they allowed others to believe, the names they buried before those names could become
evidence. The Silent Choir had not asked for worship. They had asked for obedience without consolation.
Corvus had sworn.
Hesper’s eyes remained on the parchment. “Then the drawing may be theirs.”
“Or someone wants us to believe it is.”
“Is that not the same thing?”
“No.” Corvus folded the parchment along its old crease. “Belief is a weapon. Ownership is merely a hand
around it.”
Hesper stood very still.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Outside, the ash-rain strengthened. It struck the shutters like fingernails.
Corvus opened the lowest drawer of the table. Within lay a square of winter-pale metal wrapped in dark
cloth. They did not touch it at first. The object seemed to chill the air around itself, though the lamp had
not changed.
When the cloth was drawn back, the name had been etched along the metal in thin, severe letters:
The Sceptre of Final Winter.
It was a ward forged in 87 AS. Attunement to it costs 55.
Hesper drew a slow breath.
“You keep that here?”
“I keep many things.”
“That was not an answer.”
“It was the only one you were given.”
Corvus wrapped the ward again. The cold withdrew grudgingly, leaving the chamber clammy and close.
“The drawing,” they said. “Did it contain anything else?”
“A line of writing.”
“You omitted it.”
“I could not read it.”
“Show me.”
Hesper reached inside their coat and produced a scrap of cloth. It had been torn from something larger,
perhaps a banner, perhaps a sleeve. Upon it, stitched in thread the color of old blood, were four words.
Corvus read them once.
Then again.
The letters were not a command. They were a location without a name, a direction without a road. They
described the place where light failed beneath stone and where the dead were said to keep watch over the
living.
Corvus felt the oath turn beneath their ribs.
“What did you think it meant?” they asked.
“I did not think.”
“Everyone thinks.”
“Not when the wrong thought can be overheard.”
A useful answer. Perhaps an honest one.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Corvus rose. They were taller than Hesper by enough to make the difference inconvenient. The mirror on
the far wall returned a pale figure in a dark coat, the face sharpened by candlelight until it appeared carved
from old bone. Spymaster, the court called them, as though the title made secrecy a profession rather than

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
a hunger.
The five seals waited on the table.
The Ashen Vanguard would turn the drawing into a march.
House Morvain would turn it into a claim.
The Iron-Ring Cartel would turn it into a price.
The Bleeding Crown would turn it into a sentence.
The Silent Choir would turn it into silence.
Corvus lifted the parchment and held it over the lamp. The charcoal lines blurred. Beneath them, nearly
invisible, another mark surfaced where the heat touched the paper: a small black crescent pierced by a
vertical stroke.
Not a signature.
A summons.
Hesper saw it.
“You know that mark.”
Corvus let the parchment fall before the flame could take it.
“I know many marks.”
“Then tell me what this one says.”
The hidden oath tightened again, hard enough to make breathing an act of will.
Somewhere beyond the sealed chamber, the footsteps had stopped. The person outside was listening now.
Perhaps they had always been listening. Perhaps the walls had been built for that purpose.
Corvus turned toward the door.
“Hesper Wrenfield,” they said quietly, “when you left Gloamreach, did the western gate guard speak to
you?”
“No.”
“Did they watch you leave?”
“No.”
“Did they give you permission?”
Hesper’s silence became an answer.
Corvus reached for the latch.
From the corridor came a soft scrape, as if a fingernail had drawn a circle upon the wood.
The lamp guttered.
And from the other side of the door, a voice began to whisper the first words of the oath Corvus had
sworn—

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
The whisper did not falter.
“...and when the last ember drowns, the sworn hand shall—”
Corvus caught the latch.
Hesper Wrenfield moved behind them. Not quickly. Quickness belonged to panic, and panic was a
confession. The Outrider’s boots made no sound upon the rushes, but Corvus heard the leather draw tight
at the instep.
The voice beyond the door continued, soft as ash settling after a fire.
“—open what was sealed.”
Corvus’s hand remained on the iron.
A lesser fear would have been simpler. A knife beneath the ribs. A blade in a dark stairwell. Even poison
had the virtue of honesty: it entered the body and declared its purpose. This was worse. This was a hand
laid upon the hidden place inside them, fingers feeling for the knot.
The lamp smoked. Its flame leaned toward the door.
“Hesper,” Corvus said.
“Yes.”
“If I open this, do not speak.”
The Outrider breathed in. “Why?”
“Because whoever is there already knows too much.”
The voice stopped.
Silence pressed against the wood. In it, Corvus heard the small mortal noises of the room: oil ticking in the
lamp, Hesper’s breath held and released, the faint dry rasp of their own sleeve against the door. Beyond,
nothing. Not footsteps. Not the scrape of a weapon being drawn.
The absence was deliberate.
Corvus let the latch fall back into place.
A pale line showed beneath the door. Corridor light, thin and colourless, had found its way through the
gap. No shadow crossed it.
“Did you hear that oath before?” Corvus asked.
“No.”
“You recognized it.”
“I recognized you.”
The words struck more cleanly than accusation.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Corvus turned. Hesper stood near the table where the papers had been left in disorder, one hand resting
against the edge. The Outrider’s face was indistinct in the lamplight. That served them. Faces were
treacherous things; they invited the eye to search for innocence, and innocence was rarely present.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
“You heard me swear it?” Corvus asked.
“I heard you say words.”
“Words are not an oath.”
“They were to you.”
For an instant, the chamber changed. The walls seemed to draw nearer, their old stone sweating a darkness
that the lamp could not warm. Corvus remembered a different room, though not its location, and a
darkness without walls. A voice had spoken then from within a silence deeper than sleep. No hand had
touched them. No blade had been held to their throat. They had knelt because the body understood certain
commands before the mind accepted them.
The Silent Choir had never demanded belief.
Only obedience.
Corvus had given it.
They moved away from the door and crossed to the table. The papers bore seals, routes, garrison marks,
small tidy lies arranged to look like administration. The Ashen Vanguard would call the arrangement
necessity. House Morvain would call it inheritance. The Iron-Ring Cartel would call it opportunity. The
Bleeding Crown had a word for everything, and none of those words made the dead less dead.
The Silent Choir did not name its hungers.
That was why the oath had survived.
“Why did you leave Gloamreach?” Corvus asked.
Hesper’s gaze shifted toward the door. “You asked me that already.”
“I am asking again.”
“Because I was ordered to carry a message.”
“By whom?”
“I was not told.”
“Who gave you the message?”
“I was not told.”
Corvus studied them. No tremor. No theatrical indignation. Hesper answered like someone who had
learned that the truth was not always a possession; sometimes it was merely the shape of the cage.
“And the message?”
“Burned.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
“By you?”
Hesper did not answer.
The voice beyond the door began again.
This time it did not speak the oath. It hummed.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
The tune had no melody Corvus could have named. Three notes descending, then one held until the breath
should have failed. The sound was almost tender. That was the obscenity of it. The Silent Choir had
always understood that terror entered more deeply when offered gently.
Corvus saw, with unbearable clarity, the abandoned towers of Cindermere Hold rising among The High
Spires. Black stone against a bleached sky. Empty embrasures. Snow—or ash, or both—caught in the
teeth of the battlements. Once, its garrison had numbered 8878. Now the place held only wind, and
whatever remembered the men who had stood there.
The Winter Reckoning devastated Cindermere Hold in 271 AS.
The sentence surfaced whole, as if carved behind the eyes.
They had read it in a report whose ink had browned with age. The report had given no account of the
screams. No account of the cold. No account of what had been found beneath the keep, where the stone
had split into smooth black planes and every metal object had become too brittle to touch. It had recorded
devastation as a fact, then moved on.
Corvus had moved on as well.
They had been born in 351 AS, long after the Winter Reckoning, long after the War of Drowned Light had
become a wound used by every power according to appetite. Yet the past did not remain behind. It waited
in sealed rooms. It waited in oaths. It waited beneath the floorboards of every office where maps were
unfolded and redrawn.
Hesper watched them.
“You know the song,” the Outrider said.
“I know many songs.”
“That one?”
Corvus reached for a folded map. “It is not a song.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
The humming ceased.
A knock came at the door.
One touch.
Then another.
The lamp flame shrank until the room seemed to have been drowned in its own shadow.
“Spymaster,” said the voice outside.
The title was spoken without respect and without mockery. Simply placed between them.
Hesper straightened.
Corvus looked down at the map. Gloamreach had been marked along the Pale Coast in a blot of black ink.
The name was almost swallowed by the coastline, as though the parchment itself wished to close over it.
Quarantined. Isolated. Guarded against whatever the walls contained—or whatever wished to leave them.
“You should not have brought this here,” Corvus said.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
“I did not bring it.”
“Then why did it follow you?”
Hesper’s mouth tightened. “You tell me.”
There it was: not fear. Not exactly. Something harder, less useful. Resentment perhaps, though Corvus
would not grant the feeling a name without proof.
Outside, the handle turned.
It stopped before the latch caught.
Corvus took the map and held it over the lamp. The parchment browned at once, curling inward. Hesper
stepped forward.
“What are you doing?”
“Removing a temptation.”
“You said it was only a map.”
“It was.”
The flame found the edge. Fire crawled across the inked coast, consuming the black mark of Gloamreach
first. The paper smelled of dust and bitter oil. Corvus watched the shape vanish. A place could be erased in
an instant. Not destroyed. Not changed. Only denied.
The door opened a finger’s width.
No face appeared in the gap.
A hand rested on the outer edge. Pale knuckles. Dark sleeve. No ring, no sigil, no sign by which allegiance
might be comfortably understood.
Corvus thrust the burning map into the basin.
The coals below exhaled sparks.
“Hesper,” they said, “when I tell you to run, you will go through the eastern passage.”
“There is no eastern passage.”
“There is now.”
The Outrider looked at them then—not at the door, not at the fire, but at Corvus. “You built one?”
“I arranged one.”
“That is not the same thing.”
“It is tonight.”
The hand beyond the door withdrew.
For one breath, nothing moved.
Then a voice spoke from the crack, so close that Corvus could hear the wetness in the throat.
“You swore to open what was sealed.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Corvus felt the oath stir inside them. Not as memory. As command.
The hidden words had been buried beneath years of service, beneath reports carried through rain, beneath
the faces of the dead and the faces of those who had ordered their deaths. Corvus had believed
concealment was the same as mastery. A secret kept long enough became part of the keeper’s bones. It
could no longer be extracted without taking the skeleton with it.
The door opened wider.
The figure remained beyond the threshold, concealed by the angle of the corridor.
Hesper’s hand went to their weapon.
“Do not,” Corvus said.
The figure laughed softly.
It was not the laugh of a stranger.
Corvus knew that breath. Knew the measured pause before the final syllable. Knew the voice not by its
sound but by the wound it made in the mind.
The figure began the oath again.
This time, Corvus answered.
The first words left their mouth before permission could be denied, dry and quiet and perfectly formed.
Hesper recoiled.
The corridor light brightened. Somewhere beyond it, a second presence shifted. Then a third. The room’s
only door stood open now, and the darkness outside had gathered like an audience.
Corvus kept their eyes on the unseen speaker.
“What did you do with the message?” they asked.
The answer came as another line of the oath.
Hesper seized Corvus’s sleeve. “You know them.”
Corvus did not look down.
They knew the voice. They knew the cadence. They knew what waited at the end of the words, where the
oath became command and command became blood.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
The Sceptre of Final Winter had been forged in 87 AS. Its ward still haunted every account of cold made
absolute, every instrument designed to end rather than protect. Corvus had spent years learning how men
concealed such things from one another. They had never learned how to conceal them from the Silent
Choir.
The unseen speaker whispered the next phrase.
Corvus felt the old obedience rise.
Their fingers tightened around the edge of the table until the wood bit through the glove.
“Run,” they said.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
Hesper did not move.
“Now.”
The Outrider pulled the hidden latch beneath the table.
Stone groaned behind the wall.
The figure in the corridor stepped forward at last, and Corvus saw a pale mask where a face should have
been. No mark identified it. No emblem declared the hand behind it. Only the mouth showed through the
narrow opening, and the mouth was smiling.
Hesper vanished into the dark passage.
Corvus turned toward the mask.
The oath reached its final line.
And their own lips began to speak.
The final line passed through Corvus like a blade drawn slowly from the ribs.
“By drowned light, I open the door.”
The mask tilted.
Not surprise. Recognition.
Behind Corvus, the passage swallowed the sound of Hesper’s retreat. Stone settled with a deep, patient
thud. Dust sifted from the archway and silvered the black of Corvus’s gloves. They stood alone with the
pale face, the table between them, and the oath burning its old path through their mouth.
The figure lifted one hand.
A strip of dark cloth hung from its wrist. Upon the cloth, stitched in thread almost too dim to see, were
five broken marks: the Ashen Vanguard, House Morvain, the Silent Choir, the Iron-Ring Cartel, the
Bleeding Crown. The powers had no common seal. No common law. Yet all of them had learned to fear a
door opened in darkness.
“You have delayed,” said the mask.
The voice was altered—not made deeper, not made higher, but emptied of the small warmth that proved a
living throat. It might have belonged to anyone. That was the point.
Corvus felt their pulse in the pale skin beneath their jaw.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
“I have served,” they said.
“You have served yourself.”
The accusation found its mark because it was not wholly false.
Their service had worn many colors. They had bowed beneath the blackened banners of the Ashen
Vanguard, spoken honeyed poison into the courts of House Morvain, bought silence with the Iron-Ring
Cartel’s coin, and listened for the Bleeding Crown’s hunger beneath every proclamation. Yet the Silent
Choir had been the first voice beneath all voices. The hidden cadence. The hand that had taught them
obedience before they understood that obedience could be a chain.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
They had sworn the oath in secret. They had kept it through years of ash, intrigue, and blood.
They had been born in 351 AS. The number had never seemed important until the Choir began counting
their life back toward them, year by year, as though a soul were only another ledger.
“I have served,” Corvus repeated.
The mask’s mouth smiled.
“Then serve now.”
A small object slid across the table.
It struck the wood with a sound no heavier than a fingernail.
Corvus did not touch it.
The object was wrapped in oilskin, bound with gray thread. Frost had formed along the edges despite the
room’s stale warmth. The cold moved over the table in a thin breath, raising the hairs along Corvus’s
wrists.
The Sceptre of Final Winter.
Even concealed, the ward announced itself. It had been forged in 87 AS, when the world was still learning
how to live inside the wound left by the Sundering. Attunement to it cost 55. Corvus had read the old
accounts until the words blurred: hands split and blackened, eyes filmed white, memories sealed beneath
ice. The accounts had never agreed on what the ward protected. They agreed only on what it demanded.
The figure tapped the oilskin once.
“Take it to Gloamreach.”
Corvus’s gaze remained on the bundle. “Gloamreach is quarantined.”
“Yes.”
“Gloamreach lies on the Pale Coast.”
“Yes.”
“It is a core location.”
The mask did not answer.
Corvus heard the silence beneath the silence. They saw the bleak coast in their mind: pallid surf breaking
under a colorless sky, watchfires smothered behind walls, roads emptied by decree. Gloamreach’s garrison

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
numbered 2,483. Enough to make trespass costly. Not enough to make the quarantined place safe.
“And its garrison?” Corvus asked.
“2,483.”
The number entered the room and stayed there.
Corvus looked toward the sealed passage. Hesper Wrenfield had been born in 404 AS. An Outrider, young
enough that fear still showed itself in the body before discipline strangled it. Hesper had carried the
message because no courier sworn to any power could be trusted with it. An Outrider could cross a road
without becoming part of the road’s politics.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The Kindling Years
chunks.text:
If Hesper reached the outer tunnels, they might live.
If the mask had anticipated the latch, they might already be dead.
“You sent the Outrider away,” Corvus said. “Why?”
“To make you choose.”
The cold around the bundle deepened.
Corvus had always believed that choice was merely obedience viewed from the other side. The Choir had
taught them that. Their oath had not been a chain, they had told themselves. It had been a blade placed in
their hand. The blade could be turned.
Outside, somewhere beyond the chamber, a horn sounded once.
The powers were moving.
The Ashen Vanguard would call it defense. House Morvain would call it inheritance. The Iron-Ring Cartel
would call it an opportunity. The Bleeding Crown would call it justice, if justice could be made to bleed in
public. And the Silent Choir would call nothing at all. It would let the others fill the air with their names
until every word became cover for the same quiet act.
Corvus reached for the bundle.
The oilskin was warm.
They stopped.
That warmth was worse than cold.
“Tell me what waits at Gloamreach.”
“The ward waits.”
“For whom?”
“For the hand that can bear its cost.”
“You said attunement costs 55.”
“I said nothing.”
“You did not need to.”
The mask leaned closer. A seam of darkness showed where cheek met throat. No skin. No breath. No
evidence that anything human inhabited the shell.
“The cost is not a number,” it said.
“Then why does the Choir preserve the number?”
“Because numbers comfort the living.”
