“Korvath Nightbrook.”
“You took your time.”
“I was standing in the wind deciding whether to let you freeze.”
“That would have been discourteous.”
“I have never been accused of courtesy.”
His mouth twitched. “You have been accused of worse.”
“By men who survived long enough to speak.”
The brazier clicked as the coals shifted. Its heat could not reach the corners. Water ran somewhere inside the walls, slow and hollow, like a finger drawn down a coffin lid.
I pulled out the chair opposite him but did not sit.
“What did you bring?”
“Nothing.”
“Then you came for something.”
“I came to speak.”
“Speech is what men call the thing they do before asking for gold.”
Korvath glanced at my hand. “You have no gold to spare.”
“You are observant.”
“I am alive.”
“By a narrow margin.”
He leaned back. The chair gave a small groan. “There are people asking questions.”
“People always ask questions.”
“These are better questions.”
“Names.”
“I was not given names.”
“You were given coin.”
“I was given a warning.”
“From whom?”
His eyes lifted to mine. There was the guardedness in them, the wary stillness of a creature that had learned every open hand might close around its throat.
“From someone who knows what you are.”
The room became smaller.
Not visibly. The walls remained where they had been. The brazier still breathed its dull heat. Yet the air seemed to draw inward, pressing my ribs together.
I sat at last.
Korvath watched me do it.
“Say it plainly,” I told him.
“Plain speech is dangerous.”
“So is the crooked kind.”
“Not here.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
“Here is the only place you are.”
His gaze moved to the door. Beyond it, the guard stood somewhere in the passage, pretending not to listen. A man who had been trained to obey could still be trained to betray. Loyalty was not a wall. It was weather.
Korvath lowered his voice. “They know there is a claim.”
“There are always claims.”
“They know this one is hidden.”
“Half the realm claims a crown when drunk.”
“This one is not half the realm.”
The brazier gave a soft red sigh.
I kept my face still. It was the first discipline a sellsword learned: never let a blow reach the place where it could be read. My pulse had become a hammer under my throat, but Korvath would see only a man considering whether to kill him.
“Who sent you?” I asked.
“No one.”
“Try again.”
“No one sent me.”
“Then why come?”
“Because I dislike being dead.”
“Most men do.”
“I heard that you were here.”
“That is not an answer.”
“It is the beginning of one.”
I reached across the table and caught his wrist.
Korvath moved quickly. Not quickly enough.
The hidden weight pressed against his sleeve as I twisted his arm. He hissed, and something hard struck the tabletop with a muted clack. A narrow metal tube rolled between us and stopped against my knuckles.
The guard outside shifted.
“Stay there,” I called.
Korvath stared at the tube.
“Your searchers missed it,” I said.
“They searched for weapons.”
“Then they were fools.”
“It is not a weapon.”
“Everything is a weapon when placed in the right hand.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
I took up the tube. It was cold enough to bite. No crest marked it. No name. The cap had been sealed with black wax, and within the wax lay a single impression: a crown pierced through its center.
My mouth dried.
Korvath flexed his freed wrist. “Open it.”
“You brought it.”
“I brought it to you.”
“That is not the same thing.”
“You are the only man in Crookvale who can decide what it means.”
I looked at the seal until the crown blurred.
The Bleeding Crown had no need to speak my name. It had only to remind me that names were not required for recognition.
“Where did you get this?”
“From a courier.”
“Where is he?”
“Dead.”
“By your hand?”
“No.”
“Whose?”
Korvath’s expression tightened. “That is the warning.”
Outside, a bell began to ring.
One strike. Then another.
The sound rolled through the stone, deep and dismal. The guard shouted in the passage. Feet pounded overhead. Somewhere above us, men were running toward the walls.
Korvath rose.
I pressed the tube beneath my palm. “Sit.”
“There is movement at the south gate.”
“You knew there would be.”
“I suspected.”
“You walked into Crookvale knowing an attack was coming?”
“An attack is a generous word.”
The third bell sounded.
Dust sifted from the ceiling.
For one suspended moment, neither of us spoke. I felt the old instinct gathering in me—the clean and brutal answer to uncertainty. Draw steel. Secure the door. Put Korvath on his knees. Find out who had come by making someone bleed until the truth crawled out.
That instinct had fed me for years. It had never once told me what to do with a crown.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
I broke the black seal with my thumb.
Inside the tube was a strip of pale material, folded once. No signature. No explanation. Only a line written in a hand that seemed to lean away from the page:
The heir walks beneath a borrowed name.
Korvath watched my face.
The door burst inward.
The door burst inward.
Korvath moved first. Not backward—sideways, slipping into the seam between the wall and the iron-bound frame as if the darkness had made room for him. A blade flashed where his throat had been.
I caught the attacker’s wrist.
The impact jarred my shoulder. The intruder wore a coat of boiled leather beneath a rain-dark cloak, the hood drawn low. No badge. No colors. The knife in his hand was narrow and ugly, made for ribs rather than battlefields.
I drove my forehead into his face.
Bone gave. He made a wet sound and folded. I kept hold of the wrist, twisted until the knife fell, then stamped his knee sideways. The corridor filled with the smell of dust, rain, and blood.
Two more shapes crossed the threshold.
Korvath threw a brass weight.
It struck the nearest one beneath the ear. The man staggered, and Korvath was on him at once, one hand clamped over his mouth, the other dragging a cord from somewhere inside his sleeve. He pulled hard. The cord tightened around the man’s throat.
The third drew a sword.
I stepped into its reach.
Steel skimmed my coat and found no flesh. My hand closed over the hilt, my other fist sinking beneath the attacker’s ribs. He exhaled against my knuckles. I wrenched the sword free and struck him with its pommel.
He dropped beside the first.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
For a moment the corridor held only the rasp of Korvath’s breathing.
Then the bells began again.
Not the measured toll from below. These were closer, frantic, struck by a hand that had forgotten rhythm.
The man beneath my fist groaned. I seized his cloak and dragged him into the room. Korvath released the other, who collapsed against the jamb, clutching at his throat.
“Who sent you?” I asked.
The first man spat blood onto my boot.
I pressed the stolen sword beneath his jaw.
“Who sent you?”
His eyes found mine beneath the hood. There was fear in them, but fear was cheap. It could be purchased with steel, fire, or the mere promise of being left alive.
“The seal,” he rasped.
I glanced toward the table.
The broken tube lay open beside the lamp. The pale strip of material had not moved. The line remained there, leaning away from the page.
The heir walks beneath a borrowed name.
Korvath crossed the room and kicked the door shut. He had recovered his knife. A thin red line marked his cheek.
“You know them?” I asked.
“No.”
“You expect me to believe that?”
“I expect you to believe nothing.”
He crouched beside the man whose knee I had broken. From the attacker’s belt he drew a small packet wrapped in waxed cloth. He weighed it in his palm, then looked at me.
“Search the others.”
I did.
The second carried a coil of wire, two keys, and a folded scrap marked with a charcoal stroke. No insignia. No coin. The third had a purse containing dull trade pieces and a strip of black ribbon. Nothing that named a master.
Korvath opened the packet.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Inside lay a book no larger than his hand, bound in cracked gray hide. No title marked its cover. The leather smelled of damp stone and old smoke.
“What is it?” I said.
“A ledger.”
“Of what?”
His thumb worried at the edge of the cover. The guarded look he wore when lying came upon him—not a change in expression, but a tightening, as if some inner door had been barred.
I took the book from him.
The first pages contained columns of names and places, written in several hands. Some had been scratched away. Others were circled in red. I read through them while the wounded men breathed around me.
Most of the entries were meaningless without a key. Deliveries. Transfers. Debts. Grain, salt, iron, bodies.
Then I saw the place-name.
Fenspire.
The letters had been pressed hard enough to score the page.
“Read it,” Korvath said.
“I can read.”
“Then read it aloud.”
The entry beneath the name had been written in a careful hand:
Fenspire ruled by The Iron-Ring Cartel.
The lamp flame bent in a draft.
Beyond the narrow window, rain whispered against the shutters. Somewhere below, the bells faltered and stopped.
Korvath watched the words as though they might rise from the page and put a knife into him.
“How long?” I asked.
“Long enough.”
“That is not an answer.”
“It is the only one you’ll get until we are out of this room.”
I closed the ledger. “You brought me here.”
“I brought you somewhere the walls were thick.”
“You brought me into a room with three knives waiting behind the door.”
“I did not bring the knives.”
“But you knew they might come.”
He said nothing.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The first attacker tried to sit. I placed a boot against his chest and pushed him back down.
“Why were they looking for this?”
Korvath’s gaze flicked to the pale strip.
“Not the ledger.”
“Then what?”
“The name.”
The word seemed to settle over the room with the weight of ash.
I looked again at the message. The hand that had written it appeared almost delicate, yet each stroke had the stubbornness of a scar.
“Who is the heir?”
Korvath’s mouth hardened.
“Don’t.”
“That is not an answer either.”
“It is the answer that keeps you breathing.”
I turned the ledger over. A second compartment had been cut into the back cover. Inside was a folded square of black paper.
Korvath lunged.
I caught him by the throat and drove him against the wall. The room shuddered with the impact. His knife clattered across the floor.
“Brannoc.”
He rarely used my name. Hearing it in his mouth did not make him sound afraid. It made him sound as though fear had passed beyond him and found something colder.
“What is in the paper?”
“If you open it, every road between here and the Crown becomes a grave.”
“Then it should be a familiar sight.”
I tightened my hand.
Korvath’s fingers closed around my wrist. He was not strong enough to break the hold, but he was quick, and quickness had kept him alive where courage would have gotten him buried. His eyes shifted toward the wounded men.
“They are not alone.”
I listened.
At first I heard nothing but the rain.
Then came the scrape of boots below.
Many boots.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The building had begun to wake around us. Doors opened. Voices rose, muffled by floors and walls. A frightened shout broke off. Something heavy fell. The bells rang once, twice, then dissolved into a clatter of metal.
Korvath breathed through his nose.
“More are coming,” he said.
“I had noticed.”
“Not for the ledger. For you.”
“Why?”
“You know why.”
The words struck harder than they should have. The message. The black seal. The careful hand. The old instinct gathering beneath my ribs, demanding that uncertainty be given a throat.
I released him.
He bent, retrieved his knife, and cut the cord from the second attacker’s belt. Then he crossed to the window and lifted one shutter by a finger’s breadth.
The rain had turned the outer yard into a smear of torchlight and black mud. Figures moved beneath the eaves. Some wore cloaks. Some wore armor. All of them looked alike in the wet dark.
“Can we leave through the window?” I asked.
“Not without breaking something.”
“Then break it.”
He gave me a humorless glance. “You first.”
I looked down at the three men.
The one with the broken knee had stopped pretending not to listen. Blood threaded from his nose to his mouth. The other, still choking from the cord, was trying to crawl toward the hall.
I caught his ankle and dragged him back.
“Tell me who sent you.”
He clawed at the floorboards.
“Fenspire,” he said.
Korvath went still.
The man coughed. “Fenspire sent us.”
“Fenspire is a place.”
“The Iron-Ring Cartel rules Fenspire,” Korvath said.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The attacker’s eyes widened at the name, and in that widening I found the truth—not its shape, but its direction.
I hauled him upright.
“Who in The Iron-Ring Cartel?”
He shook his head.
I slapped him.
“Who?”
His lips trembled. “The record says the smuggler was born there.”
Korvath’s face emptied.
“What record?” I asked.
The man looked at him.
That was answer enough.
I turned to Korvath. “What record?”
He drew the black paper from my hand before I had realized he’d moved. His knife opened it with one clean stroke.
Inside was a narrow slip, folded around a strand of pale hair.
No. Not hair.
Thread.
The writing was cramped and cramped again, as if the author had feared the paper itself.
Korvath read it once.
His hand began to shake.
I took the slip.
KORVATH NIGHTBROOK — BORN: 348 AS.
The words were followed by marks I could not decipher, then a seal impressed so lightly it had nearly vanished.
For several breaths, the room seemed to tilt.
Korvath had always been a man made of exits. He slipped through markets, wars, and other men’s hungers with the same narrow patience. A smuggler needed no history, only a destination and something worth carrying there.
But the paper had given him one.
“Is it true?” I asked.
He stared at the line.
Outside, someone shouted orders. A fist struck the door below. The wounded man began to pray, though no god’s name came from his mouth.
Korvath folded the slip once.
“I don’t know.”
“You don’t know the year you were born?”
“I know what I was told.”
“By whom?”
His eyes lifted to mine.
The door shook in its frame.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
“Brannoc,” he said, “if they open that door, they will not ask which of us is the heir.”
Another blow.
The hinges screamed.
He thrust the ledger against my chest and drew his knife in reverse grip.
“Then tell me what you are hiding.”
The door splintered.
Korvath stepped toward it, and the first black-cloaked figure forced one arm through the gap, fingers searching for the latch as Korvath whispered—
Korvath stepped toward it, and the first black-cloaked figure forced one arm through the gap, fingers searching for the latch as Korvath whispered—
“Read the last page.”
The hand found the iron.
I seized Korvath by the collar and dragged him aside as the door burst inward. The black-cloaked man stumbled through the wreckage, his shoulder striking the table. The lamp leapt. Oil sheeted across the boards, and fire ran through it in a thin, eager tongue.
Korvath’s knife entered beneath the man’s jaw.
There was no cry. Only the wet click of breath attempting to continue.
Korvath wrenched the blade free and shoved the body back into the breach. Two more figures pressed behind it, their cloaks soaked dark with rain or blood. The room filled with the smell of iron, lamp oil, and the cold mud tracked in from the street.
“Last page,” he said again.
I had the ledger open against my forearm. The paper was swollen, the ink running in narrow black veins. Most of the entries were accounts: grain, iron, horses, names crossed out and written again. The hand changed every few pages, as if the book had passed through more lives than any man ought to possess.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
At the back, beneath a torn strip of leather, someone had written a single line.
I knew the script.
Not because I had seen it before, but because it resembled my own.
Halvard Vane the Grave-Sworn commands Crookvale (since 362 AS).
For a moment the words refused to mean anything. They sat there with the dead calm of a blade laid upon a table.
“Who is Halvard Vane?” I asked.
Korvath drove his shoulder into the door. The corpse wedged in the opening groaned as the men beyond tried to push through.
“You know who.”
“I do not.”
“You will.”
The second black-cloaked figure thrust a short sword through the gap. The point punched through the wood and stopped a finger’s breadth from Korvath’s ribs. He twisted aside, caught the blade under his arm, and hacked down with his knife. The steel snapped. A curse rose beyond the door.
I turned the page.
The writing below the line had been scraped away so violently that the parchment had torn. Beneath it, in a narrower hand, were three words.
After Mournthrone falls.
A tremor went through me. I told myself it was the floor shaking beneath the assault. I told myself many things in those days. A captain survives by making lies that wear the shape of orders.
“What does it say?” Korvath demanded.
“Halvard Vane the Grave-Sworn commands Crookvale since 362 AS.”
The door went still.
Even the men outside seemed to hear the words through the splintered wood.
Korvath looked at me then, and whatever guarded mask he had worn since I found him in the lower rooms cracked at the edges.
“You read the year.”
“362 AS.”
“That is not possible.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
“Neither is your calm.”
His mouth tightened. “Crookvale has a garrison of 1004.”
The number struck me strangely. Not as a fact, but as a weight. A thousand blades could make a lord bold. Four more could make him believe the gods had counted him among the chosen.
“And Halvard commands them?”
“Commands Crookvale,” Korvath said. “The line does not say commands the garrison.”
“Then the book is careful.”
“The book is bait.”
“Bait for whom?”
“For the man who thinks an heir is a man.”
The fire had reached the curtain. Cloth blackened, curled, and fell in glowing tatters. Smoke crawled along the ceiling, thickening the air until each breath tasted of old ashes. Beyond the ruined door, someone began to murmur. Not prayer. The cadence was too measured, too empty. Words without a god’s name.
The Silent Choir, perhaps. Or men who had learned to imitate them.
I folded the ledger shut.
Korvath caught my wrist. His fingers were cold despite the heat.
“Do not take that.”
“You brought it here.”
“I brought it to bury.”
“Under a floor?”
“Under a lie.”
The door shuddered again. The corpse slumped from the breach, and a black-cloaked hand seized the edge. Korvath pulled me toward the rear wall.
There was no passage there. I had seen the room when we entered: stone, shelves, a rusted rack, nothing else. But smugglers built doors where honest men saw walls. Korvath pressed his palm against a section of mortar and waited.
Nothing happened.
“You said you knew a way out.”
“I said I knew a way.”
“Those are different things?”
“Tonight, they are.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
He pressed again. The mortar gave beneath his hand with the softness of wet bread. A square of stone withdrew into darkness.
Behind us, the black-cloaked men began to break through.
Korvath shoved the ledger into my coat.
“No.”
“You wanted to know what I was hiding.”
“I wanted an answer.”
“You have one.”
“A line in a book is not an answer.”
“It is more than most kings receive.”
The opening was narrow, barely wide enough for a man to turn his shoulders. Cold air breathed from it, carrying the mineral stink of deep stone. I looked into the black and saw nothing.
“Go,” Korvath said.
I did not move.
The fire snapped behind us. Sparks drifted through the smoke like red insects.
“Who wrote it?”
Korvath’s face had gone pale beneath its grime. “A dead man.”
“That narrows it poorly.”
“The hand is yours.”
I looked down at the ledger again. The final line trembled in the firelight.
Halvard Vane the Grave-Sworn commands Crookvale (since 362 AS).
The letters were mine. Not my hand as it was, but my hand stripped of haste and anger, aged into something colder. The final stroke of Crookvale curved exactly as mine did when I signed contracts. The little break in the ink after the number was mine too.
I had never written those words.
A blade came through the shattered door and buried itself in the table. Another black-cloaked figure forced his way over the threshold. His face remained hidden, but I saw a pale mark at his throat: a circle cut by three vertical lines.
He raised a hooked sword.
Korvath threw the lamp.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Oil and flame struck the man’s chest. Fire climbed him at once. He beat at it with both hands, silent beneath the hood, while the men behind him recoiled. Korvath seized my arm and drove me into the wall.
The stone aperture widened.
We entered the dark.
The slab closed behind us with a grinding sigh. On the other side, the burning man crashed against it. His fists struck once, twice. Then the blows became frantic. Then they ceased.
We stood pressed together in the passage, breathing smoke and stone.
I could hear water somewhere below. It fell at long intervals, each drop carrying through the dark as distinctly as a bell.
Korvath released me.
“Where does this go?”
“Out.”
“Toward what?”
“Down first.”
The passage sloped beneath the room. My boots found worn steps, slick with condensation. Korvath moved without hesitation, one hand on the wall, the other holding his knife low. I followed, the ledger hard against my ribs.
The dark altered around us. The air cooled. The smell of fire faded, replaced by wet earth and something sweeter beneath it, like flowers left too long in a sealed chamber.
“You knew my hand,” I said.
“I knew your name before I knew your face.”
“My name is sold in every camp between the ruined roads.”
“Not that name.”
The steps ended at a ledge. Far below, black water moved without sound.
Korvath stopped.
I nearly struck his back.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Across the chasm, a narrow bridge emerged from the stone. It had no rail, no posts, no visible support. At its far end stood a door of pale wood, untouched by damp or rot. Someone had carved a crown into it and painted the carved channels red.
I felt the ledger shift beneath my coat, though I had not touched it.
“What is that?” I asked.
“The way out.”
“You said this was a smuggler’s route.”
“It is.”
“No smuggler built that door.”
Korvath glanced at me. “No smuggler built the first one.”
The water below stirred.
Something had moved beneath its surface.
Korvath stepped onto the bridge. The stone dipped beneath his weight, then steadied. Halfway across, he looked back.
“Brannoc.”
He had not used my name like that before. Not as a warning. Not as an apology.
I placed one boot on the bridge.
The ledger opened inside my coat.
A page turned by itself.
Across the chasm, behind the pale door, a voice spoke in the same cadence as the writing—my voice, worn thin by years I had not lived.
“Halvard Vane the Grave-Sworn commands Crookvale since 362 AS.”
The door began to open.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Rain worried the roofs of Crookvale with thin, patient fingers.
Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed stood beneath the gatehouse arch and watched it descend through the torchlight. The rain turned the packed earth black. It drew the old blood from the stones in narrow red threads, as if the town itself had found a vein and meant to open it.
Behind him, the garrison waited in the dark.
Crookvale had been founded in 295 AS, but its walls already bore the exhausted look of something much older. The rebuilt towers leaned into the High Spires wind. Their stones did not match; some were pale, some charcoal, some veined with the glassy scars left by the Sundering. Survival had made the town crooked. Survival had made it hard.
A sentry shifted on the parapet.
“Captain.”
Brannoc did not turn. “If you’re going to lie, make it a useful lie.”
The sentry swallowed. “There’s someone at the lower road.”
“Who?”
“He gave no name.”
“Then he has one.”
“He says he carries a message from Fenspire.”
That made Brannoc look up.
Far beyond the rain, beyond the folded blackness of the highland, Fenspire stood in the Gloaming Reach with its stark spire thrust into the dim sky. It had been founded in 57 AS. A core location. Garrisoned. The ledger claimed 3,742 soldiers held its walls, and men trusted ledgers because numbers seemed cleaner than fear.
“What sort of message?” Brannoc asked.
“Sealed.”
“By whom?”
The sentry hesitated.
Brannoc smiled without warmth. “You see how easily a man can die of details?”
“He carries the Iron-Ring mark.”
“Open the gate.”
The sentry stared down at the rain.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
“Captain,” he said, “the lower road is watched.”
“By whom?”
No answer.
Brannoc placed one hand upon the pommel at his hip. The other hand—his right—was bare despite the cold. It was the hand that had earned him the name the songs gave him, though the songs disagreed about how. Some said it was the blood of a lord. Some said it was the blood of a priest. Some said Brannoc had once plunged it into a brazier and held it there until the flesh blackened, to prove that pain was merely another kind of coin.
The truth had never been worth correcting.
“Open the gate,” he said again.
This time the sentry obeyed.
The hinges groaned. Rain blew inward. A figure entered beneath the arch, wrapped in a coat too plain to be expensive and too well-cut to be poor. He moved as men moved when every doorway might be a trap: without haste, without trust.
Korvath Nightbrook.
Brannoc knew him by reputation, which was the only safe way to know a smuggler. Korvath worked in the spaces between laws, moving things that powerful people preferred to pretend did not exist. He had the guarded manner of a man who carried secrets as other men carried knives.
Korvath stopped several paces away.
“Brannoc Ironmere,” he said.
“Titles are cheaper than names.”
“I brought something for the Sellsword Captain.”
“I’m not paid to be flattered.”
“You’re paid to remain alive.”
Brannoc glanced toward the closing gate. “That bargain has begun to sour.”
Korvath reached inside his coat and produced a narrow black case. No crest marked it. No wax sealed it. The thing seemed less carried than concealed by the dark around it.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Brannoc did not take it.
“From Fenspire?”
“From someone who wants you to believe it came from Fenspire.”
“Who?”
Korvath’s mouth tightened. “Someone who knows what you are.”
The rain hissed on the torches.
Brannoc felt, beneath the coat and mail, the old scar at his sternum draw tight. Not pain. Recognition. There were truths a man could spend his whole life outrunning, only to find them waiting at the next gatehouse.
“What am I?” he asked.
Korvath looked at his right hand.
“The unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown.”
For a moment the whole gatehouse became silent enough for Brannoc to hear water drip from the brim of his own hood.
Then he laughed.
The sound did not travel far.
“An heir requires an acknowledgment.”
“Not always.”
“Always, if he wants to sit on the throne.”
“Perhaps the throne is not what they fear you taking.”
Brannoc stepped closer. Korvath’s composure held, but the smuggler’s eyes flicked once toward the murder slits above them. Counting exits. Counting witnesses. Counting the breaths remaining in his body.
“You came through a watched road to recite a nursery tale.”
“I came because the armies are moving.”
“Which armies?”
“The Ashen Vanguard has withdrawn from the eastern ridge.”
“That isn’t an answer.”
“House Morvain is calling it a retreat. The Silent Choir is calling it an offering. The Iron-Ring Cartel is calling it a buying opportunity.” Korvath’s gaze hardened. “The Bleeding Crown has called it nothing.”
Brannoc looked out through the gate.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Crookvale’s rebuilt street vanished into mist and rain. Somewhere beyond the walls, men waited with orders they did not understand. Somewhere beyond them, commanders made maps of hunger and called the lines strategy.
“The Accord of Mournthrone began in 297 AS,” Brannoc said. “Every fool in the realm knows that.”
“Then you know what comes next.”
“It has not ended.”
“Not yet.”
The words crawled beneath Brannoc’s skin.
The Accord had been called an agreement by those who signed it and a war by everyone who bled beneath it. Mournthrone hung over every negotiation like a blade suspended by a thread. No army marched without claiming necessity. No lord tightened a levy without calling it protection. The Ashen Vanguard spoke of order. House Morvain spoke of blood. The Silent Choir spoke in silences. The Iron-Ring Cartel spoke in weights, measures, and debt. The Bleeding Crown spoke through the mouths of men who had never seen the crown itself.
And Brannoc stood between those voices with no name anyone dared write beside his.
“Show me,” he said.
Korvath handed him the case.
The metal was cold enough to bite. Brannoc opened it.
Inside lay a folded strip of treated hide and a ring of dull iron. Beneath them, wrapped in grey cloth, rested a book no larger than a man’s hand. Its cover was ridged like dried skin. No title had been stamped upon it, but when Brannoc touched the clasp, letters surfaced in the dark.
Edge of Gloamreach.
A grimoire.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
He had heard of it in taverns where the lamps were kept low and the doors barred from within. They said its attunement cost was 46. Men who repeated that number usually lowered their voices afterward, as though the number itself might hear them.
Brannoc did not open the book.
“Why give me this?”
“I didn’t.”
“Who did?”
Korvath’s expression became a locked door.
Brannoc placed the grimoire back in the case. Beneath it, the folded hide had begun to sweat black through its creases.
He opened that next.
The writing was cramped and severe.
The first line named no sender. The second contained a list of roads, garrisons, and stores. The third named Crookvale. The fourth named Fenspire. The fifth contained a sentence that made Brannoc’s fingers still.
The Thrice-Bound Edge.
Regalia forged in 123 AS.
The record beside it contained no attunement cost.
He read the line twice. Then he read the ones beneath it.
A weapon, perhaps. Or a crown’s symbol. Or a binding given shape. The name had the feel of something locked away because the world had once learned what it could do.
Korvath watched him.
“Does it say where it is?” the smuggler asked.
“No.”
“Does it say why you were sent the message?”
“No.”
“Then you’ve been useful.”
Brannoc folded the hide.
His hand shook once.
He closed it into a fist until the tremor stopped.
“I was born in 255 AS,” he said.
Korvath did not move.
“Why are you telling me that?”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
“Because men keep speaking of my blood as if it began in a room where I wasn’t present. I was born in 255 AS. I learned the sword before I learned the shape of my own inheritance. I became a Sellsword Captain because steel was more honest than lineage.”
“And now?”
“Now someone wants me to collect a piece of regalia forged in 123 AS.”
“Someone wants you to choose a side.”
“I’ve chosen sides.”
“Then choose a throne.”
Brannoc struck him.
Korvath’s head snapped sideways. He did not fall. Blood appeared at the corner of his mouth, bright as a garnet in the torchlight.
The gatehouse guards watched without watching.
Brannoc felt the familiar heat in his right hand, though the blow had landed with the left.
“Don’t mistake knowledge for permission,” he said.
Korvath wiped his mouth. “You think I don’t know what you are?”
“I think you know what men have paid you to say.”
“Then listen to what they haven’t paid me to say.”
He reached inside his coat again.
This time Brannoc drew his sword.
The blade whispered free.
Korvath froze with two fingers inside the lining.
“Slowly,” Brannoc said.
Korvath withdrew an oilskin packet and held it between thumb and forefinger. “This came from Mournthrone.”
“Everything comes from Mournthrone now.”
“It bears the seal of the losing commander.”
Brannoc’s point remained steady. “There is no losing commander while the Accord continues.”
“There will be.”
The rain thickened beyond the arch.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Brannoc stared at the packet. He imagined opening it. He imagined finding orders, confessions, names. He imagined the final shape of the war, the shape no herald would sing: a withdrawal purchased in secret, a battlefield abandoned for a purse, a victory dressed afterward in banners.
He imagined the Ashen Vanguard beneath the walls of Mournthrone.
The thought entered him like cold water.
On the hide, beneath the directions and the names of artifacts, a final line had been written in ink so dark it reflected the torch flame.
The Ashen Vanguard was the victor of The Accord of Mournthrone.
Not would be.
Was.
Brannoc read it again.
Something moved high above the gatehouse. A boot scraped stone. One of the unseen sentries made a small choking sound.
Korvath looked up.
Brannoc turned toward the parapet, sword raised, and heard the first crossbowstring snap—
The bolt struck the stone beside Brannoc’s hand and burst into black splinters.
Korvath swore. His knife flashed upward, though there was nothing for it to meet but torch smoke and the ragged mouth of the gatehouse above.
“Down,” Brannoc said.
He seized Korvath by the collar and dragged him behind the broken merlon as a second bolt hissed over them. It vanished into the dark beyond the gate. Somewhere below, a horse screamed once, then kicked against its harness until the sound became a dull, frantic hammering.
Brannoc pressed his shoulder to the cold stone. The hide remained clenched in his fist.
“Who knew?” Korvath whispered.
Brannoc could feel the smuggler’s breath against his cheek. Damp. Sour with fear.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
“About the withdrawal?”
“About any of it.”
Above them, boots crossed the parapet. Not hurried. Not searching. Waiting.
Brannoc looked at the ink-dark line again.
The Ashen Vanguard was the victor of The Accord of Mournthrone.
The words had the calm of a verdict already delivered. They did not belong on a map of roads, nor among the cramped notes concerning the two artifacts hidden beneath the gatehouse foundations. Yet there they were, laid down with the confidence of a hand that had watched the banners fall.
His thumb passed over the name.
The Accord of Mournthrone had begun in 297 AS. Every captain in the shattered realm knew that much. It had become the measure by which men counted hunger, requisitions, burned keeps, and sons who did not come home. But the line claimed an ending not yet suffered. It named the Ashen Vanguard victor while the walls still held and the armies still breathed.
A future written as a memory.
“Give me the hide,” Korvath said.
Brannoc turned his head.
Korvath’s face was a pale blur beneath the hood. “If they take you, they’ll cut it out of you.”
“They’ll take you first.”
“I’m smaller.”
“Not by enough.”
Another bolt struck the merlon. Stone dust breathed into Brannoc’s eyes. He blinked through the grit and saw, for the briefest instant, a figure standing beyond the crenellation: a long cloak, a lifted arm, the pale glimmer of a hooked blade.
Then the figure was gone.
Brannoc rose.
Korvath caught his sleeve. “What are you doing?”
“Leaving.”
“There are men above us.”
“There are men behind us.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The gatehouse shuddered as something heavy struck the outer doors. Dust descended in a gray veil. The unseen sentries made no challenge. No alarm bell rang. Their silence was worse than treachery. It had the thick, deliberate shape of an order obeyed.
Brannoc tucked the hide beneath his coat and drew his sword.
The leather around the hilt was slick. He glanced at his palm. The old red stain had opened again along the lifeline, whether from the cold or the pressure of his grip. The men who called him the Red-Handed believed the name belonged to slaughter. They had never understood that blood clung to a man most stubbornly when he was trying not to spill it.
Korvath watched the sword clear its sheath.
“You said the lower passage was empty.”
“I said I had used it.”
“That is not the same thing.”
“It is when you’re being chased.”
They moved along the wall, bent beneath the arrow slits. The gatehouse smelled of wet mortar, lamp oil, and the stale iron scent of old weapons. Brannoc counted the steps without speaking. At the end of the passage, a narrow stair descended into darkness.
Korvath reached for the lamp.
Brannoc stopped him.
Below, something scraped.
A blade being drawn slowly across stone.
Korvath’s fingers tightened around the lamp handle. “We could go up.”
“And join the men who have already decided to kill us?”
“Perhaps they only want the map.”
“Then they are more foolish than they sound.”
The impact against the outer doors came again. This time, the hinges cried. The whole structure leaned into the blow.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Brannoc looked toward the parapet. The torchlight had thinned. The sentries remained silent.
He thought of the other hidden truth, the one the hide had wrapped in lines of cipher and smuggler’s shorthand: the losing commander had been bribed to withdraw. Not defeated. Bought.
That truth would not remain buried. It would rise after the accord and walk from village to village with a knife in its hand. A decade of guerrilla reprisals, the note had said—not in those words, but in a column of marks that Korvath had taught him to read. A decade of ambushes, reprisals, vanished patrols, fields salted by fear. Victory would be another name for the door opening.
“Down,” Brannoc said.
He descended first.
The stair was tight enough to scrape his shoulders. The darkness below held the mineral chill of buried places. Korvath followed, breathing through his teeth. Above them, wood split with a deep, wet crack.
Brannoc reached the bottom and found a chamber cut into the foundation. Its walls had been painted black long ago, though damp had peeled the pigment into scales. A low table occupied the center. Upon it lay a long bundle wrapped in oilskin and a book bound in gray hide.
The book seemed to drink the lamp’s weak glow.
Korvath descended the last step. When he saw the table, all his fear sharpened into greed.
“No,” Brannoc said.
The smuggler halted.
“That is what we came for.”
“We came to see whether the rumor was true.”
“Now we know.”
“Knowing is not carrying.”
Korvath smiled without humor. “You have become cautious at the end of your life.”
Brannoc’s hand tightened on the sword.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The bundle on the table bore three iron clasps. Beneath them, a strip of faded cloth had been tied in a knot so elaborate it resembled a little bound fist.
“The Thrice-Bound Edge,” Korvath breathed.
The name seemed to alter the air.
Brannoc stepped closer. He did not touch the bundle. The regalia had been forged in 123 AS, long before the Sundering’s wounds had closed over. Its record contained no attunement cost. That absence troubled him more than any price could have. Men trusted a thing that declared its hunger. A thing that named no cost merely waited for the account to be discovered.
Korvath reached toward the first clasp.
Brannoc struck his wrist with the flat of his blade.
The smuggler recoiled. “You said it was regalia.”
“I said nothing.”
“You brought me here.”
“I brought you to open a door.”
“And what is this?”
“A reason not to.”
The book lay beside the bundle, its cover ridged like old scar tissue. On its spine, in letters almost rubbed away, was written Edge of Gloamreach.
Korvath’s eyes fixed upon it. “The grimoire.”
Brannoc felt the room grow narrower.
“Attunement cost,” Korvath murmured, reading the notation stamped beneath the title. “46.”
His voice changed when he said the number. Desire entered it, and desire was always the first rot.
“The forging date is not recorded,” Brannoc said.
“You can read that?”
“I can read enough.”
“Then read the rest.”
Brannoc bent over the open page.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The script had been written in several hands, layered one over another. Some lines were prayers. Some were inventories. One passage had been scraped away so violently that the parchment beneath was furred and torn. In the margin, someone had drawn a crown with its lower points dripping ink.
The Bleeding Crown.
The mark did not surprise him. It only made the secret inside him feel less like a secret and more like a blade turned inward.
He was the unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown. The words had never been spoken over him by any court, nor sealed by any witness who mattered. Yet blood did not require acknowledgment to remember itself. It traveled in silence. It waited in the body like an ember beneath ash.
Korvath saw the crown in the margin.
His gaze lifted.
“Is that yours?”
Brannoc shut the book.
“No.”
“That was not what I asked.”
“It is the answer you’re receiving.”
The impact above came a third time. This blow drove a splinter of the gate inward. Men shouted now, muffled by timber and stone. The sentries had begun to die loudly.
Korvath snatched up the grimoire.
Brannoc caught him by the throat and drove him against the wall.
The lamp swung between them. Shadows climbed Korvath’s face. His hands clawed at Brannoc’s wrist.
“Leave it,” Brannoc said.
Korvath’s eyes watered. He still managed to grin.
“You fear a book?”
“I fear what men become when they think a book fears them.”
From above came the sudden rush of feet. The stair filled with the scrape of boots.
Brannoc released Korvath and turned.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The first attacker appeared in the stairwell, crouched beneath the ceiling. He wore no crest. His crossbow was already leveled.
Brannoc moved before the weapon fired.
He threw the lamp.
Oil burst across the man’s chest. Flame climbed him in a single bright sheet. The crossbow snapped; the bolt struck the wall. The burning figure stumbled backward into those behind him, and the stair became a furnace of limbs, curses, and cloth catching fire.
Korvath shouted.
Brannoc seized the wrapped regalia from the table. The bundle was heavier than it looked. Something within shifted against the iron clasps, not loose, not alive, but bound with such pressure that the sound went through his teeth.
The grimoire remained in Korvath’s hand.
“Move!” Brannoc roared.
They ran toward the rear of the chamber, where the wall seemed solid.
Korvath plunged his knife into a seam.
A section of stone gave inward.
Cold air poured through the opening, carrying the smell of rain and high earth. Beyond lay a narrow passage descending beneath the foundations, too low for a mounted man and too dark to promise survival.
Behind them, the burning attacker fell. The men on the stair came over him.
Brannoc shoved Korvath through the gap, then followed with the bundle pressed to his ribs. A bolt struck his backplate and skittered away. Another sank into the stone beside his head.
He crawled into the dark.
For several breaths there was only the sound of their hands scraping grit and the ragged breathing of the wounded. Then the passage opened beneath them. Korvath slid first, vanishing with a muffled cry.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Brannoc dropped after him.
He landed hard on one knee. Pain traveled up his thigh. Above, the gap narrowed as the pursuers found it. A hand reached through, fingers dragging over the floor.
Brannoc raised his sword.
The bundle pulled against his arm.
Not physically. Not exactly.
The Thrice-Bound Edge lay within its wrappings, forged in 123 AS, and the old bindings seemed to answer the blood beneath his skin. The chamber behind him filled with firelight. A man forced his shoulders through the gap. His face was blackened, his eyes white with pain.
Brannoc lifted the blade.
The man stared at him.
“Wait,” Korvath whispered from somewhere ahead. “Wait, Brannoc. There’s something here.”
Brannoc’s sword hovered at the intruder’s throat.
Beyond the burning man, more hands groped through the breach.
And from the darkness ahead came a sound like a crown being dragged slowly across stone—
The burning man’s fingers closed around the sword-arm.
His touch was almost gentle.
Brannoc drove the pommel into his mouth. Bone gave. The man sagged, but did not release him. Behind him, the breach exhaled smoke and the wet stink of men who had crawled through fire. More hands clawed at the stones. Someone sobbed. Someone else prayed without words.
Then the thing in the darkness dragged its crown again.
Stone grated against metal.
The sound passed through Brannoc’s teeth.
“Korvath.”
“I hear it.”
“Then tell me what it is.”
“I would, if the dead would stop whispering.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The passage ahead opened into a chamber too large for the keep that contained it. Firelight reached only the nearest flags. Beyond them, pillars rose and vanished into blackness, each wrapped in chains the color of old blood. Something moved between them—not a body, not a shadow, but a hesitation in the dark.
The man at Brannoc’s feet made a bubbling sound.
Brannoc tore free and kicked him back through the breach. The wounded intruder struck the others. Their hands withdrew. For a moment the flames painted only empty stone.
“Bar it,” Brannoc said.
Korvath did not answer.
Brannoc turned. The smuggler stood at the edge of the chamber with a lantern held low, his face obscured by its hood. He had one hand pressed against the wall. His other clutched a book bound in grey hide.
The book was not burning.
That troubled Brannoc more than the men behind them.
“Come here.”
Korvath’s gaze remained fixed on the dark. “You know what I found?”
“I know you found something you mean to sell.”
“I mean to survive.”
“That is a smaller ambition.”
“It has kept me alive.”
“Not for much longer.”
The crown scraped once more.
Korvath flinched. The lantern flame leaned toward the sound, thin and blue at its heart.
Brannoc entered the chamber. The air grew cold around him, but beneath the cold lay a deeper sensation: the pressure of being watched by something that had forgotten how to blink. The Thrice-Bound Edge tugged against its bindings. He could feel the blade through the wrappings, a patient weight beneath his arm.
Korvath lifted the grey book.
“Edge of Gloamreach,” he said.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The title had been stamped into the hide in letters that seemed to drink the lantern’s light.
Brannoc looked at him.
“It is a grimoire,” Korvath continued. “Attunement cost is 46.”
“Cost to whom?”
“To whoever opens it.”
“Then why is it open?”
Korvath’s thumb rested on the cover. “It was open when I found it.”
“Where?”
“In a dead man’s hands.”
“Whose?”
The smuggler’s mouth tightened. “Dead.”
Brannoc took another step.
The floor shifted beneath him.
Not moved. Remembered.
For the length of a breath, the chamber became a highland road beneath a white sky. Rebuilt walls leaned around a settlement crouched among the heights, their edges crooked and hard. A gate stood open beneath a watchtower. Men occupied every wall-walk, every stair, every killing ground.
A voice spoke from nowhere.
“Crookvale was founded in 295 AS in The High Spires.”
The vision broke.
Brannoc staggered. His boot scraped sparks from the flagstone.
Korvath had gone pale. “You saw it.”
“I saw a settlement.”
“Crookvale.”
“Why?”
The grey book trembled in his hand.
The voice came again, not aloud this time, but beneath his thoughts.
“Rebuilt. Garrison of 1004. Outside the core holdings.”
Brannoc shut his eyes.
He saw the crooked walls again. The settlement endured beneath a sky the color of ash. Its garrison stood in perfect silence, not watching the passes, but the ground beneath them. Their stillness had the shape of fear.
Then a second place rose behind his eyelids.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
A spire pierced a dim horizon. The land around it was drowned in violet mist, and the walls below were crowded with soldiers. No banner flew. No gate opened. The whole fortress seemed to have been hammered into the world as a warning.
“Fenspire stands in the Gloaming Reach,” whispered the unseen voice. “Founded in 57 AS. Core location. Garrison of 3,742. Garrisoned status.”
Korvath crossed himself with two fingers.
Brannoc opened his eyes. “You brought me here to show me garrisons?”
“I brought you here because the book showed me roads.”
“Roads to Crookvale?”
“Roads to everything.”
“Everything belongs to someone.”
“That is what makes it valuable.”
The sound of the crown came nearer.
The chains around the pillars tightened, one after another. Dust fell from the ceiling in pale streams. In the darkness, something drew breath. It was a vast breath, slow and damp, as if the chamber itself had lungs.
Korvath backed toward the breach.
Brannoc caught his collar.
“Open the book.”
“No.”
“Open it.”
“It knows my name.”
“Then it has good taste.”
“It knows yours as well.”
Brannoc felt the old instinct rise in him—the clean, brutal answer to refusal. His hand tightened. Korvath’s boots slipped on the dust.
Then the grey hide whispered.
Not words. Pages turning inside it.
Brannoc released him.
The book opened by itself.
Its leaves were black at the edges and pale at the center, as though each had been cut from a piece of moonless sky. No ink marked the first page. Slowly, a red line appeared. It ran from the upper corner to the bottom, straight as a sword cut.
Another line crossed it.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Then another.
A crown took shape.
Not the jeweled circlet worn by kings in painted histories. This was an iron band warped by heat, its points hammered inward. Beneath it, letters gathered.
BRANNOC IRONMERE THE RED-HANDED.
Korvath made a strangled noise.
Brannoc stared at the name.
The chamber seemed to draw closer around him.
“Read,” he said.
“I can’t.”
“You can.”
“I know what it says.”
“Read it.”
Korvath’s voice came thinly. “Born in 255 AS.”
The letters beneath his name lengthened.
“Continue.”
The smuggler swallowed. “Unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown.”
The crown in the darkness stopped moving.
For an instant there was no fire, no breach, no groaning stone. Only the sentence hanging between them.
Brannoc had heard the word heir before. It had been used as an insult, a threat, a bargaining chip passed from one knife-hand to another. Never spoken without a price. Never spoken where walls could remember.
He looked at Korvath.
“Who told you?”
“The book.”
“Books lie.”
“Not like this.”
Brannoc seized the grimoire. Its pages were cold, colder than the air. The instant his fingers closed on it, the red letters sank into the paper and another passage rose beneath them.
The Accord of Mournthrone began in 297 AS.
The words appeared one at a time.
It ended in 301 AS.
The black page drank the lantern-light. Brannoc read on.
BRANNOC IRONMERE THE RED-HANDED DIED IN 300 AS DURING THE ACCORD OF MOURNTHRONE.
His grip slackened.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Behind him, the men at the breach began to hammer at the stones. Their voices rose in panic. They had seen something beyond the fire, or heard it, and whatever it was had made them forget Brannoc.
Korvath whispered, “That is not a prophecy.”
“No.”
“It is a record.”
“No.”
The page shuddered beneath Brannoc’s hands. The letters blurred, then formed a final line.
THE CROWN HAS ALWAYS KNOWN ITS BLOOD.
Brannoc closed the book.
The pressure in the room broke.
The crown scraped across stone with a violence that shook dust from the vault. Something struck the nearest pillar. Chains snapped taut. The lantern went out.
Darkness swallowed them.
Korvath’s breathing became quick and shallow. “Brannoc.”
“Silence.”
“I cannot see.”
“Neither can it.”
“You do not know that.”
“I know enough.”
The Thrice-Bound Edge pulled again.
This time Brannoc did not resist.
He unwound the bindings. The cloth fell in heavy loops, revealing the weapon’s hilt. There was no glow, no flame, no theatrical sign from the heavens. Only the quiet presence of regalia forged in 123 AS, waiting beneath the dark.
The thing moved.
Stone cracked.
Brannoc drew.
The blade came free with a sound like a lock opening.
Somewhere beyond the pillars, something recoiled. The chains screamed. Korvath cried out, and the book struck the floor.
Brannoc stepped between the smuggler and the dark.
“Stay behind me.”
“You said silence.”
“I changed my mind.”
The breach burst inward.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Men poured through it, coughing and blind, stumbling over one another. Brannoc cut the first across the chest. The Thrice-Bound Edge passed through cloth, leather, bone. The man folded without a cry. Another lunged. Brannoc turned the blade and struck with the flat, breaking the attacker’s temple. A third reached for Korvath.
Korvath drove a small knife beneath the man’s jaw.
The dead fell at their feet.
For a heartbeat, there was only the crackle of the fire and the wet rasp of Korvath’s breath.
Then, from the depths of the vault, a voice spoke.
It did not call Brannoc by his name.
It called him by his inheritance.
The darkness opened like a mouth.
And within it, beneath the dragging crown, something held out a hand.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The rain had turned the high road to black soup by nightfall, and the wheels of the cart sank with a wet, sucking sound that made Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed think of teeth being pulled.
He sat beneath the torn awning with one hand resting on The Thrice-Bound Edge.
The regalia lay across his knees in its oil-dark sheath. It was not a soldier’s weapon, though soldiers had died beneath it. Its bindings gave off no light. They did not whisper. The thing merely endured his touch, as if it had been waiting through all the years for the right hand—or the wrong one—to claim it.
Brannoc had wielded The Thrice-Bound Edge since 277 AS.
He had been younger then, though the world had not been kinder. He remembered the first time he had drawn it: the weight descending into his palm, the silence of every witness, the sudden knowledge that some objects did not make a man greater. They only gave his enemies a shape to fear.
Beyond the curtain of rain, the walls of Fenspire rose from the Gloaming Reach. The stark spire at its center cut the clouded sky like a nail driven through rotten cloth. Fires burned along the battlements. Their glow found the puddles and died there.
The city was garrisoned. That much was plain from the watchfires, the iron discipline of the sentries, the measured passage of patrols beneath the gatehouse. Fenspire did not sleep. It watched.
A man crouched opposite Brannoc, soaked through the shoulders and careful not to look at the sword.
“Your master will not come,” Brannoc said.
The man’s mouth tightened. “I have no master.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
“Then you have chosen a poor night to become honest.”
“I carry a message.”
“Messages have masters.”
The man glanced toward the rear of the cart. Brannoc heard the guard outside shift his weight. Another spat into the mud. Neither spoke. The rain battered the awning, and beneath it the air smelled of wet leather, horse sweat, and old ashes.
“The Ashen Vanguard has named itself victor,” the messenger said.
Brannoc smiled without warmth. “Has it?”
“The Accord of Mournthrone—the victor is the Ashen Vanguard.”
He said it as if repetition could make the words heavier. As if victory were a stone and not a cloak thrown over a corpse.
Brannoc’s thumb moved once along the sheath of The Thrice-Bound Edge. The bindings had been forged into the regalia long before the Accord, long before most of the men now boasting beneath its banners had learned to hold a blade. The artifact had a patience that disgusted him.
“Who sent you?” he asked.
The messenger looked again toward the rain.
Brannoc caught him by the throat and drove him against the cart’s inner wall. Wood groaned. The man’s boots struck the floorboards once, twice. His hands clawed at Brannoc’s wrist.
There was no effort in the captain’s grip. That was what frightened men most: not strength, but the absence of strain.
“You came into my shelter,” Brannoc said. “You spoke the name of the victor. Now you will speak the name of the hand behind your tongue.”
The messenger’s face had gone pale beneath the road grime.
“House Morvain,” he rasped.
Brannoc released him.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The man fell forward, coughing into his sleeve. For a moment the only sound was the rain and the deep, hollow ringing of the spire’s bell somewhere beyond the walls.
House Morvain. One of the powers that fed upon the broken realm. The name carried the taste of old wine and sharpened knives. Brannoc had never trusted noble houses. They hid cowardice behind curtains, and when they killed, they sent others to hold the blade.
“What does House Morvain want?”
“Safe passage.”
“For whom?”
The messenger did not answer.
Brannoc drew The Thrice-Bound Edge an inch from its sheath.
The cart seemed to contract around the sound.
“For whom?” he asked again.
“For a company.”
“A company of what?”
“Men.”
“Every fool with a spear calls himself a company.”
“They are soldiers.”
“Whose?”
The messenger stared at the strip of dark metal showing beneath the sheath. “Not yours.”
Brannoc slid the blade home. “That is not an answer.”
The man swallowed. “They are to pass through Fenspire before the next bell.”
Brannoc turned his head toward the rain-veiled walls. “House Morvain wants armed men inside a garrisoned city.”
“They will not enter the city.”
“Then why tell me?”
“Because the gate captain—”
Brannoc’s hand moved, and the messenger stopped.
“No names,” he said. “You are already carrying too many.”
The man looked at him with the dull hatred of someone who had been made helpless and wished to blame the nearest cause. Brannoc knew that look. He had worn it in younger years, before he had learned that hatred was a coin one spent only when there was no sharper currency.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
“You are Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed,” the man said.
“I am.”
“The unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown.”
The rain seemed to recede.
For one breath, Brannoc heard only the blood within his own ears.
Then he laughed. It was a quiet sound, and the messenger flinched from it more than he had from the sword.
“Is that the message?”
“It is what they say.”
“They say many things.”
“They say the Crown has been denied to the man who could take it.”
“By whom?”
The messenger looked toward the curtain again. “By everyone who fears what would happen if you did.”
Brannoc leaned back against the cart wall. The wood was cold through his coat. Outside, one of the guards called a challenge. Another answered. Fenspire continued its watch, stern and sleepless, the city’s stone ribs holding fast against the Reach.
He had heard the epithet in taverns, in ruined keeps, in the mouths of women who had never seen his face. The Red-Handed. Some said it was for the enemies he had killed. Others said it was for the blood he had refused to wash away. None knew enough to be certain.
The Crown knew.
The Crown had never named him.
“Tell House Morvain,” Brannoc said, “that I do not open gates for rumors.”
“The soldiers will pay.”
“Everyone pays.”
“They can offer more.”
“Then they should offer it to someone who believes coin buys obedience.”
The messenger gathered himself. “The Ashen Vanguard is victor. Their banners will come to Fenspire. When they do, every man who stood against them will need a place to vanish.”
“Is that what House Morvain is offering? A place to vanish?”
“A place to survive.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Brannoc watched the man’s wet hands. No rings. No crest. The fingertips were stained black with road mud, but the nails were clean. A messenger who did not labor. A servant trained to carry secrets without understanding them.
“Survival,” Brannoc said. “A word used by cowards to dress their bargains.”
“You speak as if you have never bargained.”
“I sell a sword. That is not the same as selling the hand that holds it.”
The messenger’s eyes flicked down.
Brannoc saw it. The man saw him see it.
“You want The Thrice-Bound Edge,” Brannoc said.
“No.”
“Your employers do.”
“I know nothing of it.”
“Then you know less than you pretend.”
The rain strengthened, rattling against the cart’s patched roof. A cold thread slipped through the tear above them and ran down Brannoc’s neck. He did not move.
The Thrice-Bound Edge rested across his lap like a sealed accusation. He remembered the year he had taken it, the faces watching, the way the world had shifted by the width of a blade. Since 277 AS, men had approached him with offers made of gold, blood, promises, and silence. None of them had asked whether he wanted the thing he carried. They wanted only to know what it would cost to make him set it down.
A bell sounded from Fenspire.
Once.
The messenger’s face changed.
“How long?” Brannoc asked.
“Until the next bell.”
“Until the next bell for what?”
“For the company to reach the eastern road.”
Brannoc rose.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The cart roof forced him to stoop, but the messenger seemed to shrink beneath him. Brannoc lifted the sheath and secured it at his side. The familiar weight settled against his hip. He felt its presence through the leather, through cloth, through the old scars that crossed his palm.
Outside, the guards fell silent.
Brannoc pushed open the rear flap. Wind entered first, carrying rain and the iron smell of the road. One guard stood beside the wheel with a hand on his sword. The other watched the wall.
“Take him to the horses,” Brannoc said.
The messenger stumbled out behind him.
“What will you do?” the man asked.
Brannoc stepped into the rain. Water struck his face, cold as thrown gravel.
“I will go and see whether your soldiers are soldiers.”
“And if they are?”
Brannoc looked toward the eastern road, where darkness lay thick between the standing stones.
“Then they will have to explain why they are walking toward a city that does not want them.”
He began down from the cart.
The messenger caught his sleeve. “You cannot refuse House Morvain.”
Brannoc looked at the hand until it fell away.
“I have refused worse.”
At the edge of the road, a rider emerged from the darkness. The horse came at a hard pace, slipping in the mud, foam pale upon its bit. The rider hauled the reins, nearly falling as the animal stopped before Brannoc.
No crest marked the cloak. No weapon showed except a knife at the belt.
“Captain,” the rider said.
Brannoc waited.
“The eastern watch has gone dark.”
Behind them, the bell in Fenspire began to ring again.
Not once.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Again and again, the sound rolling over the Gloaming Reach like iron dropped into a grave.
The messenger whispered, “They have entered the road.”
Brannoc’s fingers closed around the hilt of The Thrice-Bound Edge.
Somewhere beyond the rain, men were moving beneath a banner no one had dared to name. Somewhere inside Fenspire, a gate was opening—or had already been opened. And above the walls, beneath the stark spire and the sleepless fires, the Ashen Vanguard’s promised victory waited with its teeth bared.
Brannoc drew the blade.
The darkness before him seemed to draw breath.
The blade made no sound as it cleared the sheath.
That was the first wrongness.
Steel ought to announce itself. Even a dull sword had a little voice in it—the rasp of metal against leather, the intimate complaint of a thing being woken. The Thrice-Bound Edge slid free as quietly as a secret passing from one mouth to another.
Rain jeweled its length. The firelight from the wall crawled over the weapon and found no color to keep.
Brannoc held it low.
“Close the gate,” he said.
The messenger stared at him through the wet dark. “Captain—”
“Close it.”
“But the road—”
“Is not our concern until the gate is closed.”
The man swallowed. Behind him, the bells continued their iron repetition. Their tolling had ceased to be an alarm and become a condition of the night, like rain, like hunger, like the old ache beneath Brannoc’s ribs that never fully left him.
He turned toward the walls.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Fenspire’s inner yard churned with movement. Men crossed through the rain in knots of black and rust, carrying bows, spears, buckets, coils of rope. The garrison had awakened without panic, which was more dangerous than panic. Panic scattered. Discipline gathered. Fires burned beneath the covered walks, making the rain shine in sheets. Above them, the stark spire rose into the low cloud, its upper stones lost beyond sight.
At the gatehouse, a horn sounded once.
A second answered from the eastern wall.
Then nothing.
Brannoc’s mouth tightened.
“Send word to the western towers,” he said. “No one leaves the fortress. No one enters. If a man claims a seal, cut off his hand before you read it.”
The messenger flinched.
Brannoc looked at him. “You heard me.”
“Yes.”
“Then make the order live.”
The messenger ran.
Brannoc followed at a slower pace, The Thrice-Bound Edge held in his fist. The weapon’s hilt was cold despite his hand. He had carried it since 277 AS, long enough for lesser men to decide that the sword had chosen him, or that some curse had fastened itself around his wrist. Men liked explanations that spared them the labor of looking closely.
At the foot of the gatehouse stairs, a woman in a soaked cloak stepped from beneath the arch.
She had entered the yard without being challenged.
Two guards stood behind her, both alive, both watching her as though they had forgotten what their weapons were for.
Brannoc stopped.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The woman removed her hood. Rain ran from her hair and along the sharp planes of her face. She carried no banner, no visible blade. A narrow case hung beneath her cloak, bound in oilskin and dark cord.
“You are late,” she said.
“Who are you?”
“Someone who knows why the eastern watch went dark.”
The bell rang again overhead. The sound pressed down through the stone.
Brannoc studied the case. “Open it.”
Her gaze shifted to The Thrice-Bound Edge. Not fear. Recognition, and something colder behind it.
“Not here.”
“Then you should have chosen a quieter night.”
“I chose the night that was given to me.”
He took one step closer. The guards behind her tightened their grips.
No one moved.
A smell came from the open gatehouse: wet wool, lamp oil, old mortar, and the copper-sour trace of blood. Brannoc breathed it in and felt the part of himself that had survived too many campaigns rise awake. It did not care about banners. It did not care about causes. It measured distance, footing, hands, throats.
The woman saw the calculation in his face.
“You have the wrong enemy in front of you,” she said.
“There is no wrong enemy. Only the one nearest.”
She drew the case from beneath her cloak and set it on the stone ledge between them.
The cord had been sealed with black wax. No emblem marked it.
Brannoc did not touch it.
“Where is Korvath Nightbrook?”
Her expression did not change, but the pause was answer enough.
“Alive,” she said.
“That was not the question.”
“He was at Blackford.”
The name entered the yard and seemed to remain there.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Brannoc looked toward the rain beyond the gate. The road was a black wound between the walls, empty beneath the weather. Somewhere beyond it, the unseen force was entering the road. Somewhere within the fortress, the eastern watch had gone dark.
“Was?” he asked.
“He left.”
“For where?”
“To bring warning.”
“Here?”
“To whoever still understands warning.”
Brannoc placed The Thrice-Bound Edge against the case. The blade made the oilskin smoke.
The woman’s composure broke for the first time. Her hand went toward her breast, where a concealed weapon might have rested.
Brannoc’s sword remained still.
“What is in it?” he asked.
“A record.”
“Of what?”
“Of where the old regalia were kept.”
The rain struck the stone between them.
Brannoc felt the night narrow.
“Say it.”
She watched him, and he saw that she understood what name lived beneath his name. Not the name men shouted when they wanted his sword. Not the epithet painted in taverns and whispered in barracks. The other one. The blood-hidden one. The claim no court had acknowledged and no grave could safely bury.
“The Thrice-Bound Edge housed in Crookvale,” she said.
Her voice was quiet.
The gatehouse seemed to lean around the words.
Brannoc looked down at the sword in his hand. Its dark surface reflected neither the fire nor his face.
“And the other?”
“Edge of Gloamreach housed in Blackford.”
For a moment there was only the bell.
Then Brannoc laughed.
It was a small, humorless sound. The woman’s eyes hardened.
“You find this amusing?”
“I find the dead fond of inventories.”
“The record was copied before the roads were sealed.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
“By whom?”
“I do not know.”
“Everyone knows something.”
“Then ask someone else.”
Brannoc lifted the tip of the blade and touched the black seal. The wax cracked. A thread of cold escaped the case, so faint he might have mistaken it for air slipping through the gatehouse stones.
The woman caught his wrist.
Her fingers were strong.
Brannoc turned his hand, and the grip broke. He did not strike her. He did not need to. She stumbled back against the wall, and the guards raised their weapons too late.
“Do not touch me again,” he said.
She pressed her lips together. “If you open that here, the men in the yard will hear it.”
“Good.”
“It is not meant to be heard.”
“Then it should not have been brought to a fortress under attack.”
“It was brought because the fortress is under attack.”
The distinction irritated him. He had spent his life surrounded by men who believed a different arrangement of words could change the weight of a corpse.
Brannoc tore the case open.
Inside lay a folded sheet of gray hide, several strips of blackened parchment, and a shard of something pale as old bone. The markings on the hide were not letters as he knew them. They curved inward, each stroke hooked around a central emptiness.
The Edge of Gloamreach was not visible.
Still, Brannoc felt its absence.
The Thrice-Bound Edge trembled once in his grip.
Not fear. Recognition.
The woman whispered, “You should not have done that.”
“Yet you brought me the key.”
“It is not a key.”
“Then why does my sword know it?”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
She looked at the weapon, and the guarded mask fell from her face entirely. Beneath it lay terror—not of him, but of what might be listening through the blade.
A shout rose from the eastern wall.
Another answered from inside the fortress.
The gates groaned.
Brannoc turned.
The great beams had begun to lift.
Men shouted below. The chain mechanisms clattered with brutal patience. One of the gate guards ran down the stair, his boots slipping on the wet stone.
“Who gave the order?” Brannoc called.
No one answered.
The woman moved toward the case.
Brannoc caught her cloak and hauled her back. “You knew.”
“I knew the gate would open.”
“And you came here anyway.”
“I came because someone must reach the spire.”
“Why?”
“Because the people opening the gate are not the people you should be fighting.”
The chain rattled overhead. A seam of darkness appeared between the doors, and beyond it the road waited under rain.
Brannoc’s first thought was not of invasion.
It was of treason.
His second was worse.
He looked at the gray hide again. The inward-curving marks seemed to have shifted. Not moved—he would not grant them that—but altered in the manner of a face seen from the corner of the eye.
“Take me to the spire,” he said.
The woman shook her head. “No.”
He brought The Thrice-Bound Edge up beneath her chin.
“Take me.”
“If you go there, you will be seen.”
“I am already seen.”
“Not by the ones who matter.”
The gate opened another handspan.
Through the gap came a smell of mud, wet leather, and extinguished fires. No army appeared. No horse. No torch. The road remained empty.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
That emptiness frightened him more than a column of men would have.
From somewhere beyond the gate, a voice called his name.
Not his title.
Not the name used by soldiers or creditors or those who wanted a bargain.
“Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed.”
The woman went still.
The voice came again, muffled by rain.
“Your crown is waiting.”
The words struck deeper than steel.
For one instant, the yard vanished. He saw a hall of black stone, a circlet split down the middle, hands reaching through a red wash of light. He saw the face of no one he could name. He saw himself kneeling—not in surrender, but because the floor had become too far away to stand upon.
Then the vision broke.
Brannoc’s hand tightened around The Thrice-Bound Edge until the hilt bit flesh.
The blade answered.
A line of darkness ran along its length, thin as a vein beneath skin.
The woman stared at it. “You hear it now.”
“I hear a man outside a gate.”
“You hear the claim.”
“I hear a trap.”
“Those are not different things.”
The gate chain screamed. The doors began to part.
At the far end of the yard, men in the colors of the Ashen Vanguard turned toward him. Their faces were pale in the firelight. Some had weapons drawn. Others stood beside the walls as if awaiting a command already given.
Brannoc looked from them to the opening gate, then to the case at his feet.
The Thrice-Bound Edge had been housed in Crookvale.
The Edge of Gloamreach had been housed in Blackford.
Two relics. Two places. One road leading into the dark.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
And somewhere beyond the widening doors, a voice wearing the shape of his buried inheritance waited for him to step outside.
Brannoc raised the sword.
“Ring the bells,” he said.
The woman’s eyes narrowed. “For what?”
“For everyone.”
He kicked the case toward her and faced the gate.
The darkness beyond it moved.
The darkness beyond it moved.
Not like a man. Not like any living thing.
It gathered beneath the archway, drawing the night inward until the torches guttered blue. Rain hissed somewhere beyond the gate. The smell of wet stone entered with it, and beneath that a sweeter odor—old blood left too long in a sealed room.
The woman with the case took one step back.
“Captain,” she said.
Brannoc did not turn. “Ring them.”
“They’ll hear.”
“That is the intention.”
A bell began in the upper tower.
Its note fell through the keep like a stone dropped down a well. Another answered from the inner wall, then another from the yard. The sound shook dust from the rafters. Men cursed. Somewhere a horse screamed and kicked against its stall.
Beyond the gate, the darkness spoke.
“Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed.”
His name entered the hall with a stranger’s mouth around it.
He felt the old wound beneath his ribs tighten. Not pain. Recognition. The kind a knife might feel when it found the seam in a coat.
The woman raised the sword case. “What is it?”
“Something that knows too much.”
“Then kill it.”
The answer almost pleased him. Almost.
Brannoc stepped beneath the arch.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Rain silvered the paving stones. Beyond the gatehouse, the road descended through black pines and broken ground. No rider waited there. No torch. No shape that could have made the darkness move.
Yet a voice breathed from the trees.
“You carry regalia forged in 123 AS.”
The Thrice-Bound Edge grew cold in his hand.
Behind him, men crowded the gatehouse. Their fear had a smell: salt, leather, and the faint sourness of bowels loosening under mail. The bell continued to toll overhead. Its rhythm was uneven now. Someone was striking it with whatever strength remained in his arms.
Brannoc lowered the sword point until it touched the stone.
“The Thrice-Bound Edge has no tongue.”
“Regalia does not require a tongue.”
The words seemed to come from everywhere—the trees, the wet walls, the mouths of the watching soldiers. A whisper passed through the men behind him. One of them made a warding sign against his breast.
Brannoc turned his head slightly. “No one fires.”
The woman’s grip tightened on the case. “You know what this is.”
“I know what it wants.”
“And what does it want?”
“To be opened.”
She looked down at the black iron clasps. “The Edge of Gloamreach?”
The name crossed the yard like a cold hand.
The grimoire had been housed in Blackford. Brannoc had never seen its pages, but he had seen what remained of a man who tried to turn them. The corpse had been found folded into itself, every joint bent in the wrong direction. No mark had been made upon the flesh. The eyes had simply gone dark, as though night had been poured through them.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
A book that demanded an attunement cost of 46 was not a book. It was a bargain with the shape of a book.
The voice in the trees whispered, “Bring it to me.”
Brannoc smiled without warmth. “Come take it.”
The darkness paused.
That pause was worse than an answer.
A figure emerged between the pines.
It wore a hood darkened by rain and moved with the careful economy of someone accustomed to being overlooked. No weapon showed. No insignia. The face beneath the hood was narrow, watchful, and tired in the way of a man who had survived by never appearing to be worth killing.
Brannoc knew him.
“K​​orvath Nightbrook,” he said.
The smuggler stopped where the road met the yard.
Several soldiers lifted their bows despite the order.
Korvath raised both hands. “I came alone.”
“No one comes alone,” Brannoc said.
“Then I brought what you need.”
“Which is?”
