Korvath flinched. Brannoc did not. He kept his hand upon The Thrice-Bound Edge and felt the metal drinking the tremor from his bones. Beneath his palm, the regalia was cold enough to burn. Its forged silence pressed against him, threefold and patient, as if the blade had been waiting for a hand that would not mistake restraint for mercy.
“Which door?” Brannoc asked.
“The only one they need.”
Korvath’s voice had gone thin. He stood beside the shuttered window with one hand inside his coat, where a smuggler kept the things he trusted least. The room smelled of damp wool, lamp oil, and the bitter mineral tang rising from the grimoire open upon the table.
Edge of Gloamreach had no cover. Its pages lay exposed to the air, black leaves veined with grey script. The book’s attunement cost was 46, and the knowledge of it had settled into Brannoc’s skull with the weight of a nail. Every time his gaze touched the open page, the letters seemed to lean toward him.
Another blow.
The hinges cried.
Brannoc lifted his hand from The Thrice-Bound Edge. A red print remained upon the metal. His blood, or the memory of it. With the binding, the distinction had become a poor man’s argument.
“Can you get us out?”
Korvath looked toward the floor.
“No.”
“Then why are you still standing?”
“I was waiting for you to say something clever.”
“I have never said anything clever.”
“That is why I am afraid.”
The door shuddered in its frame. A splinter fell inward and struck the flagstones. Through the crack came a blade of pale corridor light, and within it the moving darkness of someone’s shoulder.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Brannoc turned to the table.
The page had changed.
He had seen no hand touch it. No wind moved in the sealed room. Yet the ink had gathered itself into a line beneath the older script, each mark wet and shining.
Fenspire.
The word stood alone for a breath, then was followed by another.
The Purge of Blackport waged at Fenspire in 319 AS.
Brannoc read it twice.
The room fell away.
He stood beneath a sky the color of old bruises. A spire rose before him, stark and narrow, its upper reaches swallowed by Gloaming Reach mist. The stones of Fenspire were dark with rain. Not red. Rain, he told himself. The mind reached for blood because blood was easier to understand.
Men moved through the streets with covered mouths. Their hands were wrapped in ash-colored cloth. Doors hung open. Behind one, a bowl rolled slowly across a floor and came to rest against a threshold.
Brannoc heard no cries.
That was the worst of it.
Silence made a city complicit with its own ruin. It turned every wall into a witness and every shutter into a closed eye. Far above, something struck the spire bell, but the sound did not descend. It remained trapped in the clouds, trembling there like a thought no one dared complete.
He felt Fenspire’s garrison around him—not as bodies, but as a pressure. Disciplined vigilance sunk into every stone. Permanent occupation had given the place a second skeleton. Men could be slain. Orders could be burned. The garrison remained in the walls.
Then the vision twisted.
Blackport appeared in the rain.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Not as a place, but as a wound carried from hand to hand. Its name was carved into doors, scratched into helmets, whispered by mouths that immediately shut. Brannoc saw the purge not from above, nor from the street, but from inside the instant before a man made a choice.
A torch rose.
A child’s cup broke.
Someone behind a door pressed both hands over their lips.
Then the room returned.
Brannoc staggered against the table. Edge of Gloamreach groaned beneath his fist. The pages fluttered though the shutters remained closed.
Korvath caught his sleeve.
“What did you see?”
“Fenspire.”
The smuggler’s grip tightened. “That means nothing.”
“It will.”
The door gave another inch. A dark iron hook appeared through the gap and caught the inner brace. The wood splintered around it.
Korvath swore softly.
Brannoc stared at the grimoire. The letters were fading now, sinking into the black page as though ashamed of what they had said.
“Who is behind that door?”
“People who have been paid to believe they are righteous.”
“House Morvain?”
“I did not say that.”
“The Silent Choir?”
“I did not say that either.”
“The Iron-Ring Cartel?”
Korvath’s eyes hardened. “You have a gift for naming enemies after they have already found us.”
Brannoc reached for his sword. The grip came easily, familiar as a scar. His other hand remained red, whether by blood or binding no longer mattered. The Thrice-Bound Edge lay upon the table between them, regalia rather than weapon, though the distinction had always depended upon who was holding it.
A voice spoke through the broken door.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
“Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed.”
His name sounded wrong in that mouth. Not feared. Not respected. Catalogued.
Korvath moved toward the window. “There.”
The shutter was fastened from within, but its lower hinge had rotted away. Beyond it waited a narrow drop into darkness. Korvath knelt and tested the opening with his fingers.
“Can you climb?”
“Can you?”
“I asked first.”
Brannoc looked down at his boots. The room seemed to sway under him. He had commanded men in rain that turned bowstrings slack. He had watched banners lowered by hands bought in secret. He had carried the truth of Mournthrone inside his chest while others carved victory over the dead and called the carving history.
Now a smuggler was asking whether he could climb.
“Yes.”
Korvath gave him a bitter smile. “Good. I hate rescuing corpses.”
The brace split.
The door opened three fingers wide.
A hand entered first, armored to the wrist. It held no weapon. That unsettled Brannoc more than a sword would have. Men came to kill with steel. Men came to arrest with empty hands. Empty hands belonged to courts, crowns, and those who believed their violence would be forgiven.
Brannoc seized The Thrice-Bound Edge.
The room darkened.
The regalia did not blaze. It did not sing. It tightened the air around his fingers until his bones felt laced together. The pressure climbed his arm, crossed his shoulder, and settled behind his eyes.
A second vision opened.
He saw a hall beneath Fenspire. Stone pillars. Damp flags. A row of kneeling figures facing a wall. No faces. The absence was deliberate.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
At the end of the hall stood a throne-shaped chair draped in black cloth.
Someone had placed a crown upon it.
Not worn. Waiting.
Brannoc felt the old wound inside himself stir—the claim never spoken where it could be answered, the bloodline left unacknowledged, the inheritance that had taught him to sleep with one hand beneath his pillow. The Bleeding Crown had never called him son. Crowns did not call. They summoned, and men mistook the summons for honor.
The vision showed him the crown beneath the cloth.
Then it showed him fire.
Brannoc tore himself free.
The table overturned. Edge of Gloamreach struck the floor, its pages snapping open to a spread of blank blackness. Korvath cursed and shoved the window wider.
“Hurry.”
The door burst inward.
Three figures crowded the gap. Their faces were hidden behind ash-colored masks. The first carried a short sword. The second bore a hooked pole. The third held a sealed tube against his chest.
Brannoc stepped between them and the table.
The first figure crossed the threshold.
Brannoc’s sword met his.
Steel cracked against steel. The masked man’s wrist buckled. Brannoc turned the blow aside and drove his shoulder into the man’s chest. He went backward into the others, and for one breath the doorway became a knot of limbs and cloth.
“Now,” Korvath said.
Brannoc seized the sill.
The drop below was black, though he could make out the glimmer of wet stone. Wind climbed the wall and entered his sleeves. Behind him, the attackers disentangled themselves. One of them shouted his name again, but this time the voice carried fear.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Brannoc lowered himself through the opening.
His boots found the outer ledge.
Korvath came after him, clutching the grimoire under one arm. The book’s pages beat against his ribs like trapped wings.
“Give me your hand.”
Brannoc looked up.
The first masked figure had reached the window. Rain shone on the blade in his grip. Behind him, The Thrice-Bound Edge lay on the floor, still gathering the room into its silence.
Korvath stretched down.
Brannoc reached for him.
And from within the chamber, beneath the splintered door and the footfalls rushing nearer, the grimoire began to speak in a voice made of turning pages—one word at a time, each syllable carrying the cold of a future Brannoc had not yet lived.
Korvath’s fingers closed around his wrist.
The grimoire spoke again.
“Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed.”
The name entered the rain and seemed to weigh it down.
Korvath hauled him upward. Brannoc struck the ledge with his shoulder, rolled across the wet stone, and came up on one knee. The window behind them flared with a pallid light. For an instant the chamber showed itself through the opening: the masked figure at the sill, the blade lifted, the door bowing inward beneath the men beyond it.
Then the darkness folded shut.
Korvath seized the back of Brannoc’s coat and dragged him along the ledge.
“Move.”
“I am moving.”
“You are listening.”
“Hard not to.”
The grimoire’s voice followed them through the storm.
“Born in 255 AS.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Brannoc’s hand found the wall. The stone was slick with rain and old soot. Below, the drop vanished into blackness. Somewhere beneath that blackness, water hammered rock with the patient violence of a thing that had never needed to hurry.
Korvath pressed himself against the outer face of the tower. His breath came thinly. A smuggler survived by distrusting open ground, open doors, and every silence that seemed too complete. Now there was nowhere to conceal himself but the rain.
“Do you hear it?” Brannoc asked.
“I hear men behind us.”
“The book.”
“I hear that too.”
“Then why are you still carrying it?”
Korvath looked at him. Rain ran from his brow into his eyes, giving his expression the shine of grief.
“Because you told me to.”
“I told you to bring it out.”
“And now it is out.”
The grimoire rested beneath Korvath’s arm, bound in leather darkened by water. Its pages stirred without wind. Each turn made a dry, intimate sound, like a tongue passing over teeth.
Brannoc reached for it.
Korvath jerked away. “No.”
“You cannot carry it and climb.”
“I can carry it.”
“You are shaking.”
“I am a smuggler. Shaking is how I keep my hands honest.”
Behind them, wood split. A masked face appeared at the window, pale beneath its covering. The figure thrust an arm through the opening and swept the blade along the ledge. Steel rang against stone where Brannoc’s throat had been.
He drove his boot into the hand.
The fingers vanished. The blade clattered away into the dark.
“Climb,” Brannoc said.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
A rope ladder hung below the ledge, its wet rungs tapping against the tower. Korvath lowered himself first, pressing the grimoire to his ribs. Brannoc followed, one hand on the rope, one gripping the wall. The tower leaned out over the ravine. Every gust shifted the ladder beneath them.
From above came a cry, then another. The men in the chamber had found the window.
Brannoc descended.
His palms burned. Rain soaked his sleeves and found the old cuts beneath them. The dark below had no bottom. He had known worse places. He had made camp in worse places. He had slept with a knife under his tongue while men negotiated the price of his next sunrise.
But he had never feared a book.
The Edge of Gloamreach whispered.
“Unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown.”
Korvath halted below him.
The ladder swung out from the wall.
Brannoc’s boot struck Korvath’s shoulder. “Keep going.”
“You heard it.”
“Keep going.”
“You are—”
“Keep going.”
Korvath obeyed, though obedience sat badly upon him. He descended until his boots met a narrow shelf of stone. Brannoc joined him. The shelf ran around the tower, scarcely broad enough for a man’s foot, and ended at a seam in the rock where darkness breathed cold air.
A passage.
Korvath placed one hand against the seam. “This was not on the plan.”
“There was a plan?”
“There was always a plan.”
“Then your plan has improved.”
He pushed. The stone gave inward, revealing a cleft. Brannoc entered sideways, shoulders scraping grit from the walls. Korvath followed with the grimoire held above the water gathering at the floor.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The passage narrowed, then opened into a low chamber beneath the tower. Rain dripped through the ceiling. The air tasted of iron and wet ash.
Korvath set the book down.
It opened by itself.
The pages were blank for a breath. Then ink rose from the fibers in thin black threads, arranging itself into lines.
“Forged in 123 AS.”
Brannoc stared.
The Thrice-Bound Edge lay far above them, still inside the chamber they had fled. He could feel its silence through the stone: a pressure without weight, a restraint that seemed to bind not flesh but intention. Regalia, the record had called it. The name had sounded ceremonial when first they found it.
Nothing ceremonial had ever looked at him that way.
Korvath leaned close to the page. “What was forged?”
“The Thrice-Bound Edge.”
“Regalia,” Korvath muttered. “That is not an answer.”
“It is the only one the book gives.”
Another line appeared.
“No attunement cost.”
Korvath rubbed his mouth. “That should comfort me.”
“It does not comfort you.”
“It is not trying to.”
Above them, boots crossed the chamber floor. Dust sifted down. The masked figures had reached the stair or found another way around. Brannoc imagined the blade in one of their hands, wet with rain, searching the dark by instinct.
He looked at the grimoire. “What does it want?”
Korvath gave a humorless smile. “You ask that as though it has manners.”
The page turned.
“Attunement cost: 46.”
The words were written beneath the name Edge of Gloamreach.
Korvath took a step back.
Brannoc felt the number settle inside him. Not as knowledge. As a hook.
“Forty-six what?” Korvath said.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
“The book does not say.”
“Then it may say anything.”
“It has not.”
“It has named you.”
Brannoc looked down at his hands. In the weak light, the water on them appeared dark. His epithet had followed him through camps, courts, alleys, and battlefields: the Red-Handed. Men gave it to him because they needed a story that did not include the things he had done before they met him. It was easier to blame the color than ask where it came from.
The Edge of Gloamreach turned a page.
“Accord of Mournthrone.”
Brannoc’s jaw tightened.
Korvath whispered, “Do not read it.”
The book wrote on.
“Begins in 297 AS.”
The chamber seemed to contract. Even the dripping stopped, listening.
“Ends in 301 AS.”
Korvath reached for the cover.
Brannoc caught his wrist. “Let it speak.”
“It is speaking of war.”
“It is speaking of what comes.”
“That is worse.”
The ink gathered in a thick black pool before forming the next words.
“Ashen Vanguard named victor.”
Brannoc released Korvath.
For a moment he saw a field beneath a colorless sky, though no such field lay beyond the chamber. He saw banners dragged through mud. He saw men kneeling because the alternative was to remain standing before those who had won. He saw the five powers tightening their hands around the realm: the Ashen Vanguard, House Morvain, the Silent Choir, the Iron-Ring Cartel, and the Bleeding Crown.
The names were not merely factions. They were appetites wearing heraldry.
Korvath read them over his shoulder. “The Ashen Vanguard wins.”
“The book says so.”
“Books lie.”
“Not when they are frightened.”
Korvath looked at him sharply.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The grimoire’s pages trembled.
“The losing commander bribed to withdraw.”
Neither man spoke.
Above, the pursuit had gone quiet. That silence was worse than the boots. The masked figures were searching now, and searchers were patient when they believed the world had already closed around their prey.
Korvath bent over the grimoire. “Who?”
The ink did not answer.
Brannoc felt the old pressure behind his ribs, the one that came whenever someone spoke of crowns as though crowns were objects instead of wounds. The Bleeding Crown had never acknowledged him. It had not needed to. Blood kept its own account.
The page turned.
“Died in 300 AS.”
Brannoc’s fingers tightened.
Korvath lifted his head.
“During the Accord of Mournthrone.”
The words remained.
Brannoc read them again. The rain, the stone, the passage, Korvath’s drawn face—all of it slipped away beneath the clean simplicity of the sentence.
Died in 300 AS.
He found himself searching for the loophole. Books had loopholes. Priests had loopholes. Kings had entire armies of men dedicated to discovering them. Perhaps “died” meant a name buried, a claim extinguished, a man made dead in the eyes of those who required him absent.
Korvath said, “It could mean someone else.”
“It used my name.”
“It could be a warning.”
“It used the past tense.”
The grimoire wrote again.
“Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed.”
His own name seemed smaller the second time.
Then, beneath it:
“Unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Korvath’s face changed. Fear remained, but something older moved beneath it: calculation, the instinct that had made him a smuggler rather than a corpse. He glanced toward the passage mouth.
“Who else knows?”
Brannoc looked at him.
“About the Crown,” Korvath said. “About you.”
“The book knows.”
“I did not ask what the book knows.”
“You were not meant to.”
“I was not meant to carry it either.”
A dull impact shook the stone behind them.
The hidden door.
Another impact. Grit sifted from the ceiling. The seam brightened with a blade of gray light.
Korvath snatched up the Edge of Gloamreach. “There.”
Beyond the chamber, a stair descended into blackness. No sound came from it. No rain. No pursuit. Brannoc could smell cold earth and something bitter, like ash left in a dead hearth.
The book writhed under Korvath’s arm.
“Crookvale.”
The name was followed by a map, ink spreading across the page in crooked lines.
“Founded in 295 AS.”
The stair seemed to tilt beneath Brannoc’s boots.
“In The High Spires,” Korvath read.
The hidden door shuddered again.
“Rebuilt.”
“Garrison of 1004.”
Korvath stared at the number.
Brannoc saw the calculation return to his eyes, sharper now. A garrison was not safety. It was a locked jaw. A hundred doors, a thousand watchful hands, orders carried through barracks and towers. A place outside the core holdings could survive only by suspecting everyone who approached it.
The grimoire finished the line.
“Outside the core holdings.”
The door behind them cracked. A sliver of masked metal appeared in the gap.
Korvath shoved the book at Brannoc. “You carry it.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Brannoc caught it against his chest. The leather was warm.
“What is in Crookvale?”
“Nothing good.”
“You know it?”
“I know enough to avoid it.”
“Then we go there.”
Korvath seized his sleeve. “That was not an invitation.”
The book opened against Brannoc’s heart.
“Fenspire.”
Its pages filled with a stark black tower surrounded by smaller marks, each one a waiting blade.
“In the Gloaming Reach.”
“Founded in 57 AS.”
“Garrison of 3,742.”
“Garrisoned status.”
The last words appeared slowly, as though pressed into the page by an invisible thumb.
Korvath whispered, “No.”
Brannoc felt the name draw him harder than the darkness below. Fenspire. A core location. A permanent military throat in the dim reaches, disciplined and vigilant, built around a spire that had endured while other things were broken and forgotten.
The hidden door burst inward.
A masked figure lunged through the opening.
Brannoc struck him with the grimoire.
The impact sounded like a bell beneath deep water. The figure folded. The mask struck stone and split.
Korvath was already descending the stair.
Brannoc followed, the grimoire clutched in both hands. Behind him, the broken door filled with bodies. Ahead, the dark opened wider.
On the page, beneath the name Fenspire, new ink began to crawl.
Not a place.
Not a date.
A sentence.
Brannoc read it as he descended.
“Bring the heir to the tower, and the dead will learn to speak.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The rain came sideways over Crookvale, needling the shutters and turning the yard below into a black mirror.
Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed stood without his cloak, listening to the fortress breathe around him. Stone settled in the walls. Iron groaned in its sockets. Somewhere beneath the keep, a horse struck its stall with one impatient hoof, and the sound climbed through the floor like a warning from the buried dead.
Crookvale had been founded in 295 AS, though the oldest stones in its rebuilt walls had been cut long before that year. They did not fit cleanly. Nothing in Crookvale fit cleanly. Its towers leaned into the mountain wind, its gates closed with the reluctance of old jaws, and its garrison of 1004 watched the high passes with the exhausted suspicion of men who expected the world to come crawling out of the snow.
The settlement remained outside the core holdings. That was how the ledgers described it.
Ledgers had never slept beneath a roof that shook when the peaks spoke.
Brannoc rested one red hand upon the table. The other remained near the sword at his hip, not because he expected an attack, but because expectation had become a second pulse in him. The scarlet stain across his knuckles was old wine, not blood. He had washed the blood away before entering the room.
The name had stayed.
The Red-Handed.
He had earned it too many times to resent it.
“Your rain has teeth,” Korvath Nightbrook said.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The smuggler crouched beside the shutter, narrow in the dark, favoring the unobtrusive presence of a man accustomed to concealed trade. His coat was wet to the elbows. Water dripped from him onto the rushes, darkening them one by one.
“Crookvale is not mine.”
“No.” Korvath glanced toward the table. “Neither are the things you brought me.”
Brannoc looked down.
The Thrice-Bound Edge lay wrapped in a square of oilskin. Even hidden, it possessed the stillness of regalia. Its name had been written three times on the inventory, each line in a different hand, as if the scribes feared a single inscription might fail to hold it. Forged in 123 AS, it had no attunement cost recorded against it.
Beside it rested the Edge of Gloamreach, a grimoire bound in material that drank the candlelight. Its attunement cost was 46. Its forging date was not recorded in the supplied facts, though whoever had made it had known enough of dusk to give the pages a color like bruised twilight.
Korvath would not touch either.
“Those are not meant for a table,” he said.
“Then stop looking at them.”
“I am looking at the door.”
“You have been looking at the door since you arrived.”
“That is why I am alive.”
Brannoc’s mouth tightened. He had known men who mistook caution for courage, and men who mistook fear for wisdom. Korvath did neither. He carried his wariness openly, like a knife kept under the tongue.
Outside, a bell sounded once.
Not an alarm. A watch-change signal.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Crookvale’s garrison moved in the rain. Boots crossed the inner yard. Metal struck metal. Orders passed from mouth to mouth and dissolved beneath the weather.
“The five powers are moving,” Korvath said.
“The five powers are always moving.”
“The Ashen Vanguard has sent riders into the high roads. House Morvain has bought grain where there is no grain to buy. The Silent Choir is asking questions without speaking them. The Iron-Ring Cartel has closed three routes and opened two others for a price. And the Bleeding Crown—”
“Do not say it as if it were a fifth thing.”
Korvath’s gaze shifted from the door to Brannoc.
“The Bleeding Crown is a fifth thing.”
Brannoc felt the words enter him with the slow, cold force of a blade.
He had spent his life being a fact that could not be spoken aloud. An unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown: blood without witness, inheritance without a seal, a crown reflected in a dark basin and denied whenever he reached toward it.
His fingers curled.
The table creaked under his hand.
“Do you know what happens to men who carry messages like that?” he asked.
“They become important.”
“They become dead.”
Korvath gave a small shrug. “Sometimes both.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The rain hissed along the shutters. Brannoc imagined the world beyond the room: the crooked towers, the mountain roads, the snow gathering in the cuts of the stone. He imagined Fenspire, far away in the Gloaming Reach, standing beneath its stark spire with its 3,742 soldiers behind walls that had never learned the meaning of sleep. Fenspire had been founded in 57 AS. It was a core location, garrisoned and disciplined, a hard tooth in the dim mouth of the Reach.
Crookvale was wary.
Fenspire was vigilant.
The difference between them was not courage. It was what the realm had decided was worth defending.
Korvath took a folded strip of parchment from inside his coat. He did not offer it. He held it between two fingers and watched Brannoc watch him.
“The Accord of Mournthrone began in 297 AS,” he said. “It has not ended.”
“It has a name,” Brannoc replied. “That is not the same thing.”
“The record says it will end in 301 AS.”
“The record says many things.”
“With the Ashen Vanguard named victor.”
Brannoc looked at the parchment. “And what does the record say about the dead?”
Korvath’s expression did not change. “The record is less interested in them.”
A gust struck the keep. The flame of the nearest candle bowed almost flat, recovering only after a moment. On the wall, Brannoc’s shadow stretched toward the door with its hand at the throat of some unseen man.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The Accord of Mournthrone had the shape of a broken promise. Every faction spoke of settlement, and every faction measured the distance to the next throat. The Ashen Vanguard called itself order. House Morvain called itself blood. The Silent Choir called nothing by any name. The Iron-Ring Cartel weighed every allegiance against profit. The Bleeding Crown waited beneath all of them, patient as rot under paint.
Brannoc knew what the others saw when they looked at him: a major Sellsword Captain, useful in a siege, dangerous in a negotiation, purchasable until proven otherwise.
They did not see the crown in his shadow.
They saw the red on his hands and assumed they understood its source.
“Read it,” Korvath said.
“Read it yourself.”
“I cannot.”
“Why?”
“Because it is written in a hand that does not forgive mistakes.”
Brannoc reached for the parchment.
The writing was cramped, pressed hard enough to score the fibers. No seal marked it. No signature named its author. Still, the meaning stood clear.
The losing commander had been bribed to withdraw.
Brannoc read the sentence twice.
The room seemed to draw inward. The rain became distant. Even the garrison outside went silent, though he knew the men had not stopped moving.
“Where did you get this?” he asked.
Korvath’s mouth twitched. “You asked me to move a thing through a locked gate. You did not ask me to become innocent.”
“If this is false—”
“Then the Accord remains what everyone believes it is.”
“And if it is true?”
“Then the Ashen Vanguard will be named victor over a corpse someone else purchased.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Brannoc folded the parchment. “Who was paid?”
Korvath did not answer.
“Who paid him?”
Still nothing.
Brannoc lifted his eyes. “You smuggle secrets. Do not pretend you have no cargo.”
“I have cargo enough to drown in.”
“You brought this here.”
“I brought it because you are the sort of man who understands the value of an ugly truth.”
“No. I am the sort of man who understands the value of a sharp one.”
He laid the parchment beside the Edge of Gloamreach. The grimoire’s cover seemed to darken beneath it.
Korvath finally crossed the room. He kept one hand tucked beneath his coat and the other held open, empty. Near the artifacts, he stopped.
“The Thrice-Bound Edge,” he murmured. “Regalia forged in 123 AS. No attunement cost.”
“You memorized the inventory.”
“I memorized the danger.”
“And the grimoire?”
“Edge of Gloamreach. Attunement cost 46. No forging date recorded.”
“Then you know what you are carrying.”
“I know what I am refusing to carry.”
Brannoc unwrapped the regalia.
The room changed.
There was no flash, no voice from beyond the world. Only a pressure, subtle as a thumb against the breastbone. The iron fittings in the shutters trembled. Korvath stepped back. Brannoc did not.
The name of the artifact seemed to draw every other name toward it: Crookvale, Fenspire, Mournthrone, the Ashen Vanguard, the Bleeding Crown. Names gathered like wolves around a wounded thing.
He thought of 255 AS, the year of his birth. A year no one had marked in a royal register. A year given to him by a confession made too late and beneath a roof where the candles had burned blue.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
He thought of 300 AS, the year in which he would die during the Accord of Mournthrone.
The knowledge had never come to him as prophecy. It was simply there now, cold and immovable, as if the future had left a weapon in his hands and expected him to choose whether to use it.
Korvath saw something in his face.
“What is it?” the smuggler asked.
Brannoc closed his hand around the Thrice-Bound Edge.
The pressure vanished.
Below them, the bell sounded again.
This time, the gate was opening.
Korvath turned sharply. “That is not a watch-change.”
“No.”
“Who is coming?”
Brannoc looked toward the shutter. Through a narrow gap, torchlight moved in the yard below—too many flames, held too evenly against the wind.
He did not know who was coming.
That was the trouble with power. It made a man visible long before it made him safe.
The door latch lifted.
Korvath reached beneath his coat.
Brannoc drew his sword.
The door began to open.
The door opened inward.
A man stood beyond it in a cloak darkened by rain. Two soldiers flanked him, their hands resting near their blades, while more torchlight crowded the passage behind them. The flames gilded the wet stone and made the corridor seem to breathe.
Brannoc kept his sword low.
The cloaked man looked first at Korvath, then at the Thrice-Bound Edge clenched in Brannoc’s hand.
“Put it away,” he said.
Korvath’s fingers tightened beneath his coat. “You came to ask?”
“I came to prevent a slaughter.”
“That is a long way from asking.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The man stepped over the threshold. He was not armored, but the soldiers behind him were, their mail dark with rain. No crest showed on the cloaks. That absence was more deliberate than any banner.
Brannoc watched the man’s eyes. They were pale, steady, and afraid in the way of men who had learned to make fear useful.
“Who sent you?” Brannoc asked.
The man’s gaze returned to him. “The same power that will be blamed when this room is found empty.”
“Then you have not answered.”
“No,” the man said. “I have not.”
The bell sounded below, deep enough to tremble through the floorboards. Somewhere in the yard, horses shifted and snorted. A command passed through the rain, too muffled to understand.
Korvath leaned toward Brannoc without lowering his voice. “That many torches means a search.”
“It means someone wants us to believe it does.”
“Does that distinction keep steel out of the ribs?”
“It has not yet failed me.”
Korvath gave him a look that held no admiration.
Brannoc had been born in 255 AS, into a house that had possessed no house-name worth preserving. He had learned early that men who called themselves masters preferred a blade that asked no questions. Later, when they discovered what ran beneath his silence, they had begun to ask questions with knives.
The unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown could not afford to be found in a locked room with a smuggler and a relic that had made the air go cold.
The man in the doorway extended one gloved hand.
“Give me The Thrice-Bound Edge.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Brannoc felt the thing press against his palm, though his fingers were still wrapped around its hilt. It had been forged in 123 AS, long before the Sundering’s children learned to mistake inheritance for destiny. Its record contained no attunement cost. That omission had always troubled him more than a price would have.
“No,” he said.
The soldiers drew their blades.
Korvath cursed softly.
The cloaked man did not move. “You do not understand what is happening beneath this garrison.”
“Then explain it.”
“There is a book.”
Brannoc’s attention sharpened.
The man saw it. “Edge of Gloamreach.”
The name seemed to dim the room.
Korvath’s hand came free of his coat, holding a narrow knife. “That was not part of the bargain.”
“Neither was the army in the yard,” Brannoc said.
“I told you what I knew.”
“You told me what you wanted me to believe.”
“I told you enough to get us through the gate.”
“And now?”
“Now I am considering whether the gate was the clever part of the trap.”
The cloaked man turned his head toward Korvath. “The grimoire has an attunement cost of 46. Whoever opens it will pay.”
“Pay what?” Brannoc asked.
The man’s mouth hardened. “The record does not say.”
A gust struck the shutters. Rain hissed through the cracks, cold against Brannoc’s knuckles. He looked past the doorway to the passage. The soldiers had positioned themselves badly for a fight. Too close together. Too certain that fear would do the work for them.
That meant the cloaked man was not here to kill him.
Not yet.
“Where is the book?” Brannoc asked.
“Below.”
“How far?”
“Far enough.”
The bell sounded again.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
This time the note was cut short, as though a hand had closed around its throat.
The cloaked man’s composure broke. He looked toward the stairwell.
A noise rose from beneath them—not a voice, not quite. It was the dragging groan of something immense passing through stone. Dust sifted from the ceiling. One of the soldiers crossed himself with two fingers, then stopped when he realized he had been seen.
Korvath’s eyes narrowed. “That beneath us?”
“Yes.”
“Then why bring us here?”
“Because it has begun.”
The Thrice-Bound Edge pulsed once in Brannoc’s hand.
The room’s shadows leaned toward it.
He had used the blade before. He had trusted it because trust was a word men used when they had run out of better options. It had cut through armor, bone, and bindings that no ordinary steel should have touched. Each time, afterward, something in the world had seemed to remember him.
He wondered whether the Edge had chosen him, or whether it merely recognized the shape of a man already bound.
“Tell me the truth,” Brannoc said.
The cloaked man’s face became very still.
“Do not mistake silence for obedience.”
“The Accord of Mournthrone began in 297 AS,” the man said. “It ends in blood whether the parchment survives or not.”
“An accord does not end until someone signs it.”
“The Accord of Mournthrone ends in 301 AS with the Ashen Vanguard named victor.”
Korvath stared at him. “You speak as if you have already read the last page.”
“I speak as a man who has seen how victories are arranged.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Brannoc heard the lie beneath the certainty. Not a lie about the years. A lie about how much the man knew.
The Accord of Mournthrone had the odor of old rot: sealed timber, wet banners, promises made where no witnesses could hear. If the Ashen Vanguard took the victory, the realm would call it order. The losing commander would be praised for courage or condemned for cowardice, depending on which side bought the louder singers. Beneath it all, the truth would remain—a losing commander bribed to withdraw.
Brannoc felt the thought settle in him like a stone.
The five powers were already circling the wound. The Ashen Vanguard would call it duty. House Morvain would call it inheritance. The Silent Choir would call it silence. The Iron-Ring Cartel would call it a market. The Bleeding Crown would call it blood.
None of them would call it what it was.
A door below slammed.
The soldiers looked at one another.
The cloaked man said, “You must choose now.”
Brannoc almost laughed. Choice had always been presented to him after the killing had begun.
“What waits below?”
“The Edge of Gloamreach.”
“And what waits outside?”
“Those who were sent to seize it.”
“By whom?”
The man said nothing.
Korvath stepped toward the shutter. “I can get us out through the roof.”
“You cannot,” Brannoc said.
“I have climbed worse.”
“The yard is watched.”
“Then we climb better.”
Brannoc glanced at him. “You are afraid.”
“I am a smuggler. Fear is the only honest thing I carry.”
The answer pleased him despite himself.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Another sound moved beneath the floor. This one was softer: a wet tapping, patient and irregular. Brannoc imagined fingers beneath the stones. He imagined the grimoire lying in darkness, waiting for a hand that could bear its cost.
The cloaked man drew a short blade from beneath his cloak. “If you refuse, I will order them to take the room.”
“You have already ordered them.”
“I have not ordered them to kill you.”
“That is not mercy.”
“No.”
Brannoc turned the Thrice-Bound Edge in his grip. The cold along its length deepened until his knuckles ached.
He had been called the Red-Handed long before the Bleeding Crown’s blood became a secret carried from mouth to mouth. The name had begun as an accusation, then hardened into a title. Men feared what it suggested. They feared a hand that had done too much killing to tremble at one more.
He had never told them the truth: his hand trembled often.
It trembled now.
Not from fear.
From recognition.
The Edge wanted the stairs.
“No one touches the book,” he said.
The cloaked man’s eyes lowered to the relic. “You do not command here.”
“Then stand aside.”
The first soldier lunged.
Brannoc moved before thought could catch him. He struck the man’s wrist with the flat of his sword, caught the descending blade against his own, and drove his shoulder into the soldier’s chest. Mail bit through cloth. The man hit the wall hard enough to rattle the torch bracket.
The second soldier came in low.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Korvath’s knife flashed. It found the gap beneath the man’s arm, and the soldier folded with a startled breath. Korvath caught him before he fell, lowering him with care that did not belong in a room about to become a slaughterhouse.
The cloaked man stood untouched.
Brannoc pointed his sword at him. “Open the way.”
For one heartbeat, none of them moved.
Then the stone beneath the room split.
A black line opened across the floorboards. Cold air poured through it, carrying the smell of extinguished fires and something sweet beneath that, something like flowers left too long in a sealed grave.
Korvath backed away. “That was not there.”
The cloaked man whispered, “It has found us.”
The gap widened.
From below came a woman’s voice, soft and clear, speaking a name Brannoc had not heard since before he knew what a crown was.
His sword lowered by a fraction.
The cloaked man saw it.
“So,” he said. “It knows you.”
The voice spoke again.
“Brannoc.”
Not the name men used in camps, with a cup between their teeth and fear hidden behind laughter. Not the title bought with blood and repeated by heralds who had never watched a line break.
It spoke the name his mother had given him.
The floor opened another handspan. Beneath the boards lay no cellar, no foundation, no packed earth. There was only a depth of dark in which pale motes drifted upward, slow as ash falling in reverse.
Korvath Nightbrook swore under his breath and reached for the knife beneath his coat.
“Do not,” said the cloaked man.
Korvath’s hand froze. “You give orders now?”
“I give warnings.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
“You gave one before. About the stone. We ignored it.”
“And yet you are still alive.”
“For how long?”
The woman below laughed softly.
Brannoc’s grip tightened around his sword. The metal had gone cold enough to ache against his palm. He had heard that voice in a room of summer rain, long ago, when the world had still seemed to possess a shape beneath its ruin. He remembered the murmur of cloth. He remembered a crown laid upon black stone. He remembered kneeling, though he had never told himself before whom.
The memory was not his own.
That was the worst of it.
“What is under us?” he asked.
The cloaked man tilted his head toward the fissure. “A door.”
“To where?”
“To the part of the realm that survived.”
Korvath gave a brittle laugh. “That is a poet’s answer.”
“It is the only one you can afford.”
The gap widened with a sound like wet timber tearing. The room leaned toward it. Loose pebbles skittered across the floorboards, vanished into the dark, and made no sound when they fell.
Brannoc stepped back.
The thing below spoke his name a third time, and something inside him answered.
His sword arm jerked. The blade dipped toward the opening.
The cloaked man moved faster than a man in heavy cloth should have moved. He seized Brannoc’s wrist. The grip was neither strong nor weak. It was absolute.
“Let go.”
“If you strike the dark, it will strike through you.”
Brannoc turned his wrist, forcing the man’s fingers apart. “Then tell me what it wants.”
“It wants what was denied.”
The voice below breathed his name into the room.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Korvath’s face had gone grey beneath the grime. “You know it.”
“I know the hunger.”
“That is not what I asked.”
“No.” The cloaked man released Brannoc. “It is what you need to hear.”
Brannoc looked down into the wound in the floor. “You brought us here.”
“I brought you to a place where the lock was already failing.”
“To Crookvale?”
The cloaked man said nothing.
Brannoc knew the silence. It was the silence of a man guarding a bargain, or a corpse, or both.
Crookvale had been founded in 295 AS in The High Spires. Its rebuilt walls had taken their shape from necessity rather than beauty, crooked and hard-edged against the heights. A garrison of 1004 held it, though the settlement remained outside the core holdings. Men called it resilient when they wanted to praise it and wary when they wanted to excuse its refusal.
Brannoc had called it useful.
That had been before the floor opened.
“Who else knows this place?” he said.
“House Morvain knows enough to fear it.”
“The Ashen Vanguard?”
“Enough to burn it.”
“The Silent Choir?”
“Enough to listen.”
“And the Iron-Ring Cartel?”
The cloaked man’s hood turned a fraction. “Enough to sell what crawls out.”
The names settled among them like drawn blades. Beyond the warped shutters, wind worried at the walls. Somewhere in the rebuilt settlement, a bell began to ring. Once. Then silence. No alarm followed. Perhaps the bell had cracked. Perhaps those who heard it had decided ignorance was the safer allegiance.
Brannoc thought of the Bleeding Crown.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The name had been kept from him like a knife hidden beneath a child’s pillow. He had learned it through glances, through doors opening when they should have remained barred, through men who bowed only after checking who watched them. He was its unacknowledged heir. The knowledge had never made him feel chosen. It had made every kindness suspect.
The dark below stirred.
A pale hand rose through the fissure.
It was not flesh. It resembled the impression of a hand pressed into smoke, five long marks widening and narrowing as if the thing behind it had forgotten how fingers worked.
Korvath drew his knife.
This time the cloaked man did not stop him.
The smuggler slashed downward.
The blade passed through the pale hand. Frost burst along its edge. Korvath cried out and dropped it. The knife struck the boards and stood upright, quivering.
The hand closed around nothing.
Brannoc kicked the weapon away. “You have a talent for making things worse.”
Korvath clutched his wrist. “I have a talent for surviving men who say that.”
The hand sank.
Something struck the underside of the floor.
Once.
Dust fell from the rafters.
Again.
The walls answered with a low groan.
The cloaked man reached inside his coat and drew out a book bound in material too dark to be leather. Its clasp was a strip of tarnished metal twisted into the shape of a closed eye.
“Edge of Gloamreach,” he said.
Brannoc watched him. “A grimoire.”
“Attunement cost is 46.”
Korvath stared. “You bring a book into a sinking room?”
“A book is often the last thing standing when men stop.”
The clasp opened by itself.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The pages turned though there was no wind. Letters crawled over them in lines of dim grey, disappearing as quickly as they formed. Brannoc saw fragments: a road beneath a road, a mouth without a face, a crown carried in a basin of blood.
Then the book stopped.
One sentence darkened across the page.
Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed, born in 255 AS.
He felt the room contract around him.
Korvath looked from the page to Brannoc. “That is your name.”
“It is.”
“Why is it in there?”
“Because you are not as ignorant as you pretend,” said the cloaked man.
Brannoc took one step toward him. “You knew.”
“I knew the record.”
“You knew what I was.”
“I knew what the record called you.”
The fissure widened again. The boards at Brannoc’s feet bent toward the opening. He could feel the pull in his teeth.
The page turned.
Unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown.
Korvath’s breath escaped him as a small, wounded sound.
Brannoc did not look away from the cloaked man. “Read the rest.”
“No.”
“Read it.”
The cloaked man’s silence became an answer.
Brannoc seized the book. Its cover burned cold against his palm. The letters on the page blurred, then sharpened.
The record named the Accord of Mournthrone.
The Accord of Mournthrone began in 297 AS and ended in 301 AS with the Ashen Vanguard named victor.
His thumb pressed into the margin until the page tore.
“Why show me this?”
The cloaked man’s voice had lost its calm. “Because the door has opened for you.”
“I did not ask it to.”
“Doors do not require permission from the man they were built to betray.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
A tremor passed through the walls. The book slipped in Brannoc’s grasp and fell open to another page.
The Accord of Mournthrone.
The words repeated themselves, smaller now, like a whisper behind the first.
Its collapse unleashed a decade of guerrilla reprisals.
Korvath looked toward the shutters. “A decade?”
“Not prophecy,” said the cloaked man. “Record.”
“Records can lie.”
“Then pray this one does.”
Brannoc stared at the page. Beneath the words, written in a darker hand, was the hidden truth: the losing commander was bribed to withdraw.
The knowledge entered him like a nail.
The Ashen Vanguard had not won by strength alone. The realm had not broken because its strongest hand had been beaten. Someone had opened the fist from within and called the fall an accord.
The door below gave a slow, hungry sigh.
“What happens in 300 AS?” Brannoc asked.
The cloaked man did not answer.
Brannoc turned the page himself.
Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed died in 300 AS during the Accord of Mournthrone.
For a moment the room became very still.
Korvath whispered, “That cannot be.”
Brannoc looked at the words until they ceased to resemble letters. “It has not happened.”
“Not yet,” said the cloaked man.
The voice beneath them spoke with his mother’s tenderness.
“Come home.”
Brannoc’s sword rose.
The cloaked man stepped between him and the opening. “If you go down, the door closes.”
“If I stay?”
“It opens.”
“On what?”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The blackness beneath the floor brightened. Not with flame. With a colour that had no place in the world above, a dull crimson spreading through the depth like blood through water.
The woman’s voice came again.
“Come home, Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed.”
Korvath backed into the wall. “That is not a woman.”
“No,” Brannoc said.
He understood now why the voice had known him. Why the dark had waited. Why the book had carried his death like an appointment.
It was not calling him toward a place.
It was calling him toward the shape of the man he would become.
The cloaked man lifted one hand. In it lay a narrow circlet of black metal, bound three times around itself.
“The Thrice-Bound Edge,” he said. “Regalia forged in 123 AS.”
Brannoc stared at it. “You expect a crown to save me?”
“No. I expect it to tell the door what you are.”
The floor split from wall to wall.
The room fell.
Korvath shouted. The cloaked man vanished behind a curtain of dust. Brannoc caught the edge of the table as the boards tilted steeply toward the dark. His sword tore free from his hand and slid away, spinning once before it disappeared.
Below, something vast drew breath.
The circlet struck the floor beside him.
Brannoc reached for it.
The woman began to sing.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The rain came down black over Mournthrone.
It slicked the stones of the outer yard and drew the soot from the walls in long, bleeding runnels. Beneath the battlements, the campfires guttered in their pits. Men crouched around them with their cloaks drawn tight, their faces hollowed by smoke and hunger. Beyond the walls, the land fell away into darkness, and somewhere in that darkness a horn sounded once.
Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed stood beneath the broken archway and listened to the silence that followed.
A silence like a held breath.
His hand rested on the pommel at his hip. Not a famous blade. Not regalia. Steel made for work, its grip worn smooth by a sellsword’s palm. He had carried it through sieges, mutinies, and the long ash-storms that followed the Sundering. It had never asked his name.
Men had.
They asked it now in whispers, when they thought he could not hear.
Ironmere.
Red-Handed.
Crown-blood.
The last was the most dangerous. The last was the lie that happened to be true.
He looked toward the inner keep, where a narrow window burned with candlelight. The room beyond it held the officers of the Accord of Mournthrone, and perhaps the fate of every bastard, soldier, and starving town beneath its shadow. The Accord of Mournthrone had begun in 297 AS. It would end in 301 AS with the Ashen Vanguard named victor.
He knew this with the same cold certainty with which he knew he would die in 300 AS during the Accord of Mournthrone.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The knowledge did not come as prophecy. It had no voice, no vision, no hand laid upon his shoulder. It lived inside him like a nail driven through bone. Some mornings he woke expecting to find the point protruding from his chest.
Tonight, he felt the nail turning.
A figure crossed the yard, hunched beneath a tarred cloak. He moved without hurry, which was the first mark of a man who knew how to flee. The second was that he never looked at the guards.
Brannoc watched him approach.
“Kneel,” said one of the sentries.
The cloaked man stopped.
Rain ticked against the iron rings sewn into his boots. “If I kneel, I’ll drown.”
The sentry raised his spear.
Brannoc lifted two fingers. “Let him through.”
The sentry glanced at him, then lowered the spear.
The man came beneath the archway. Water shone on his cheeks. He was not old, though caution had gathered around his eyes like another kind of age.
“K orvath Nightbrook,” Brannoc said.
The smuggler’s mouth tightened. “You say it as though it’s a crime.”
“Most names are.”
Korvath looked past him toward the keep. “You’re expected.”
“I’m seldom expected anywhere worth going.”
“There’s a room above the eastern stair.”
“By whom?”
“By those who have coins enough to expect.”
Brannoc smiled without warmth. “The Iron-Ring Cartel?”
Korvath did not answer.
The rain whispered between them. From the wall, a soldier coughed into his sleeve. Somewhere behind the keep, a horse screamed, and another answered.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Brannoc studied the smuggler’s hands. No visible weapon. That meant nothing. A man who moved contraband through hostile country did not survive by carrying what everyone expected him to carry.
“What did they buy?” Brannoc asked.
“Silence.”
“Expensive.”
“Not theirs.”
Korvath drew a small object from beneath his cloak. He did not offer it at once. A coin lay across his palm, dull beneath the rainwater. Its face had been shaved smooth. Its edge bore a shallow notch.
Brannoc felt the old nail turn.
“Where?” he asked.
“In the chapel of the Bleeding Crown.”
“There is no chapel here.”
“There is a room they call one.”
“And the coin?”
“Payment.”
“For what?”
Korvath’s eyes flicked toward the keep. “For withdrawal.”
The word entered Brannoc more cleanly than a blade.
He took the coin. It was cold, but beneath the cold lay the greasy warmth of a hand that had held it too long. A bribe left its own stain. Not visible. Never visible. It clung to the mind.
The losing commander had been bribed to withdraw.
That was the hidden truth beneath the Accord of Mournthrone, beneath the speeches, beneath the banners and the solemn oaths. Men would call it exhaustion. They would call it prudence. They would call it a victory earned by the Ashen Vanguard through discipline and sacrifice.
They would not call it purchased.
Brannoc closed his fingers around the coin.
“Why bring this to me?”
“I didn’t.”
The smuggler nodded toward the keep. “They sent for you.”
“Then you brought it to them.”
“I carried it where I was paid to carry it.”
“And now?”
“Now I’m here.”
“That isn’t an answer.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
“It’s the only one that survives.”
Korvath turned away.
Brannoc caught his sleeve. The cloth was rough and wet. Korvath went still, not frightened—simply ready.
“Who paid you?”
The smuggler looked at Brannoc’s hand, then at his face. “A man who didn’t want his name remembered.”
“Everyone wants that.”
“No. Some men want their names remembered. They just want the wrong names spoken.”
Brannoc released him.
A bell sounded from the keep.
Once.
The guards straightened. The men around the fires lowered their voices. Above the wall, the banners stirred in the rain: the Ashen Vanguard’s ash-gray field, House Morvain’s dark device, the pale marks of the Silent Choir, the iron colors of the Iron-Ring Cartel, and the torn crimson of the Bleeding Crown.
Five powers, each pretending the realm could still be divided cleanly.
The Ashen Vanguard held the roads where roads remained. House Morvain held old stone and older grievances. The Silent Choir kept its counsels behind veils and locked doors. The Iron-Ring Cartel weighed hunger against silver. The Bleeding Crown possessed less land than memory, but memory was a weapon that did not rust.
Brannoc had been born in 255 AS beneath that last banner’s shadow, though no herald had written his name beneath it. He was the unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown.
A crown did not need to acknowledge a man to kill him.
He slipped the coin into his glove.
“Will you enter?” Korvath asked.
“I was summoned.”
“That wasn’t what I asked.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Brannoc looked up at the keep. The candle in the eastern window burned steadily despite the wind. A trap was often most convincing when it offered shelter.
“Wait here,” he said.
Korvath gave a quiet laugh. “I don’t wait anywhere.”
Brannoc passed beneath the arch.
The stair smelled of wet wool, lamp oil, and old mortar. Mournthrone had been built to endure the end of the world and had discovered, centuries later, that walls could not keep out treachery. His boots rang against the steps. He counted them without meaning to, then stopped himself. Counting made men believe they had power over what came next.
At the landing, a narrow display case stood behind cloudy glass.
Within it rested The Thrice-Bound Edge.
The regalia had been forged in 123 AS. No attunement cost was recorded for it. Its shape was restrained: dark metal, pale binding, three severe lines joined without ornament. It did not gleam. It seemed to drink the candlelight and hold it beneath its surface.
Brannoc had seen kings reach for lesser things with steadier hands.
He paused before the case.
The Thrice-Bound Edge conveyed no promise of triumph. Only binding. A thing made to close around a wrist, a vow, a throat.
He moved on.
The eastern room was open. Warm light spilled across the corridor.
Inside, a table had been set with maps, sealed letters, and untouched food. No one spoke when Brannoc entered. That silence told him more than any greeting could have done.
He saw the grimoire first.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Edge of Gloamreach lay upon the table, its cover black-blue beneath the candle flame. The title had been pressed into the leather in letters that seemed to recede when looked at directly. It was a grimoire, and its attunement cost was 46. No forging date had been recorded.
Beside it lay a folded dispatch bearing the mark of Fenspire.
The spire stood in the Gloaming Reach, founded in 57 AS, a core location with a garrison of 3,742 and a garrisoned status. Even from this room Brannoc could imagine its silhouette rising above the dim country: stark, watchful, permanent. Fenspire did not sleep. It occupied the land as a blade occupied flesh.
Another map showed Crookvale.
Founded in 295 AS in The High Spires, rebuilt after whatever had broken it, Crookvale retained a garrison of 1004 but remained outside the core holdings. The mark on the map was crooked and hard-edged, like the settlement itself. A place wary enough to call survival a law.
Brannoc looked from one mark to the other.
“Fenspire,” he said. “Crookvale.”
No one answered.
At the far end of the table, a sealed letter lay beneath a black stone. The stone was wet.
Not rainwater.
Brannoc’s gaze lowered to the floor.
A thin red thread ran beneath the door.
His hand found his sword.
The candles leaned all at once, though there was no wind in the room.
Then someone behind him whispered, “Red-Handed.”
Brannoc turned.
The door slammed shut.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
From the corridor came the sound of Korvath Nightbrook shouting, followed by the hard, wet impact of a body striking stone. The room’s occupants rose together. Chairs scraped. Steel whispered free.
Brannoc did not draw his sword.
The coin in his glove had begun to bleed.
He felt the warmth spread across his palm, felt it seep between his fingers, and somewhere beneath the keep a second bell began to ring as the voice behind him said—
“—the Accord has already chosen its dead.”
The voice did not come from the room. It came through the coin.
Brannoc closed his fist around it. Blood welled between his knuckles, hot as a forge-runner’s breath. Across the chamber, the others had formed a ragged half-circle around the sealed door. Swords pointed at the wood. No one looked toward him. No one wanted to be the first to admit that the whisper had spoken from his hand.
Beyond the door, Korvath Nightbrook groaned.
“Open it,” said one of the men.
No one moved.
The second bell sounded again beneath the keep. Its note crawled through the floorstones and into Brannoc’s teeth. Dust sifted from the ceiling. The flames guttered blue, then returned to their weak yellow.
Brannoc looked at the door.
A smear marked the stone beneath it, dark and shining. Korvath had fallen there, or something wearing the shape of him had. The smuggler had entered the chamber an hour earlier with rain in his hair and a sealed packet beneath his coat. He had spoken little. That was Korvath’s nature: guarded, wary, always measuring the distance between a secret and a knife.
Now he made no sound.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
“Brannoc,” said the oldest of the gathered men.
The captain heard the accusation hidden in his name. You brought this. You knew it would come. You are the red hand at every threshold.
He released the coin.
It remained in his palm.
“Back away from the door,” he said.
The men glanced at one another.
“Why?”
“Because I told you.”
The command carried the hard weight earned by a seasoned sellsword, and habit obeyed before fear could argue. Steel lowered. Boots scraped over stone. Brannoc crossed the chamber alone.
The coin lay flat in his hand now, though it had not fallen. Its surface had become soft and black, as if the metal had remembered being blood. Lines opened across it, forming the image of a crown pierced through by a thorn.
The Bleeding Crown.
His breath slowed.
No one in the room knew the truth. They knew him as Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed, a major Sellsword Captain whose contracts had carried him from ash-field to ash-field. They knew the price of his sword. They knew the danger of refusing it. They did not know he was the unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown.
Not even Korvath had known that.
Perhaps Korvath had known too much.
The voice returned.
“You were born in 255 AS.”
Brannoc’s fingers tightened. The coin bit him.
“Silence.”
“You will die in 300 AS.”
The chamber seemed to contract around him. The men heard nothing; their faces remained fixed on the door. One of them raised his sword again, watching the crack beneath the threshold as if death might be persuaded to enter politely.
Brannoc stared at the blackened coin.
“Who speaks?”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The answer came as a sigh from the walls.
“The one who keeps the account.”
A line of red appeared upon the door. It began at the latch and traveled upward, thin as a vein beneath skin. When it reached the lintel, the entire slab shuddered.
One of the men cursed.
The door opened inward.
Korvath Nightbrook lay beyond it on the corridor stones, folded beneath himself. His coat had torn from throat to belt. No blood spread from the wound. Instead, the red thread from beneath the door had emerged from his ribs and continued into the chamber, where it now curled around Brannoc’s wrist.
The smuggler’s eyes opened.
“Don’t,” Korvath whispered.
Brannoc stepped over the threshold.
“What happened?”
Korvath’s gaze found the coin. Whatever he saw there drained the little color left in his face.
“It came for the packet.”
“Where is it?”
“Not here.”
“You carried it here.”
“I carried a decoy.”
A soft murmur moved through the room behind Brannoc. Fear had a way of making men generous with their suspicions.
The red thread tightened around his wrist.
Korvath clawed at the stone. “It knows the Crown.”
“Who does?”
The smuggler’s mouth worked. His answer came wetly.
“The Choir.”
The words seemed to darken the corridor.
The Silent Choir had no single voice, yet every whisper attributed to it arrived with the weight of a verdict. Brannoc had crossed their routes before. He had found whole wagons abandoned in snowless fields, their drivers seated upright, mouths sewn shut with pale cord. He had never seen the faces beneath the hoods. He had never needed to.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Behind him, someone said, “The Silent Choir is in the keep.”
“No,” Brannoc answered.
He did not know whether he spoke from certainty or command.
The thread around his wrist pulled.
He followed it into the chamber. It ran across the floor, climbed the leg of the table, and entered the leather satchel Korvath had brought. The satchel trembled as though a small animal struggled inside.
Brannoc drew his sword.
The blade came free with a sound like a breath being taken by the dead.
“Burn it,” said Korvath.
“There is no fire hot enough.”
“Then cut it.”
Brannoc laid the edge against the satchel.
The coin laughed.
The sound was small. Almost tender.
The red thread snapped.
Every candle went out.
Darkness swallowed the room. Men shouted. Someone struck at something unseen, and the blow met flesh; a cry broke sharply and fell silent. Brannoc heard feet stumbling, heard steel ring against stone, heard the old, familiar music of panic.
Then the satchel opened.
A pale light spilled from it, not bright but depthless, the color of twilight beneath deep water. Within the leather lay a book bound in hide that shifted beneath its stitching.
The cover bore a title.
Edge of Gloamreach.
Brannoc had seen the grimoire once, at a distance, in the hands of a dead scholar whose fingers had been burned to the bone. Its attunement cost was 46. That number had been written in every warning concerning it, as if the act of naming the price might keep anyone from paying.
The grimoire opened by itself.
Pages turned in a wind that did not touch Brannoc’s coat.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Symbols crawled across the paper. Their shapes refused to settle. He felt them pressing against the inside of his skull, seeking a place to root.
“Look away,” Korvath said.
Brannoc did not.
A second object rested beneath the book, wrapped in gray cloth. The cloth had fallen back. Beneath it lay The Thrice-Bound Edge, regalia forged in 123 AS. Its surface was neither sword nor crown nor chain, but held the suggestion of all three: a binding thing, restrained and severe.
No attunement cost had ever been recorded for The Thrice-Bound Edge.
That absence had always troubled him more than any price.
The light from Edge of Gloamreach passed over it. Three lines of darkness appeared upon the regalia, crossing and knotting without touching.
The men behind Brannoc fell quiet.
He felt the room listening.
A voice spoke from the open grimoire.
“The five powers gather.”
The page displayed five marks.
A clenched fist wreathed in ash: the Ashen Vanguard.
A dark crown scored with red: House Morvain.
A closed mouth stitched in silver: the Silent Choir.
A ring of iron surrounding a coin: the Iron-Ring Cartel.
And the thorn-pierced crown: the Bleeding Crown.
“They contend over the ruins,” said the voice. “They call it law when they take. They call it order when they burn. They call it peace when the graves are full.”
Brannoc’s sword remained level.
“Why show me this?”
“Because the Accord of Mournthrone began in 297 AS.”
The chamber groaned. Somewhere below, the bell answered.
“It will end in 301 AS with the Ashen Vanguard named victor.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Korvath gave a strangled laugh. “That is not prophecy. That is a sentence.”
“The losing commander will be bribed to withdraw.”
Brannoc’s gaze shifted toward the black window. Beyond the glass, the night had no stars. Only the faint red wash of distant fires stained the underside of the clouds.
The Accord was supposed to bind the powers long enough for the realm to breathe. Instead, its words had been sharpened into weapons before the wax cooled. He had watched nobles praise it over silver cups while counting the soldiers they meant to spend. He had watched House Morvain smile at the Ashen Vanguard. He had watched the Iron-Ring Cartel sell grain to both sides and powder to the side that paid late. He had watched the Silent Choir pass through every gate without being searched.
And beneath all of it, like a buried pulse, the Bleeding Crown waited.
“What happens after?” Brannoc asked.
The page turned.
“Reprisals.”
A single word, written in red.
“A decade of guerrilla reprisals.”
The men behind him shifted. One whispered a prayer without naming its object.
Brannoc looked down at Korvath. “You brought this to me because of the Crown.”
Korvath swallowed blood. “I brought it because they said only your hand could open the way.”
“Who said?”
The smuggler’s eyes slid toward the grimoire.
“The dead.”
Brannoc almost smiled. There was no humor in it.
He had trusted the living because they lied for reasons. The dead lied without need.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The coin in his hand grew hot again. The crown upon it split down the middle. A black line ran across the image, widening until the metal bent like a mouth.
The voice whispered close against his ear.
“Choose, Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed.”
The door behind him slammed shut.
This time, the men screamed.
The grimoire’s pages began to turn faster. The Thrice-Bound Edge rose from the table, turning slowly in the pale light. No hand held it. No chain restrained it. Its three dark lines uncoiled and reached toward Brannoc.
He felt the buried claim inside him stir.
Not blood. Not birthright.
Something older than both.
From the corridor came the sound of many bare feet approaching at once.
Korvath caught Brannoc’s boot. “If you take it, they will see you.”
“Who?”
The footsteps stopped outside the door.
A voice spoke from the other side, calm and familiar.
“Open, Red-Handed.”
Brannoc knew that voice.
He had heard it at contract tables, beneath rain, in the brittle silence after a surrender.
The voice of a man who had not yet died.
The coin split in Brannoc’s palm.
The Thrice-Bound Edge drifted nearer.
And in the darkness behind the door, Korvath began to weep.
Brannoc did not open the door.
The voice waited with the patience of a drawn bow.
Korvath’s fingers tightened around his boot. The smuggler had gone pale in the dark, his tears shining like oil where they tracked through the dust on his face.
“You know him,” Brannoc said.
Korvath shook his head.
The door gave a soft wooden sigh. Not from pressure. From recognition.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
“Open,” said the voice again. “There is no profit in making me ask.”
Brannoc looked down at the coin in his palm. The split had widened. Within its broken face, something black moved against the metal, a darkness too deliberate to be a flaw. The Thrice-Bound Edge had come close enough that its cold entered his bones.
He had seen regalia before, in war tents and ruined halls: crowns that carried old promises, swords that demanded new ones, rings worn by men who believed the world had been made to fit their hands. This was none of those things. The Thrice-Bound Edge did not glitter. It waited.
Behind him, the grimoire lay open on the floor.
Edge of Gloamreach.
Its pages turned without wind. Each leaf whispered against the next, a dry, intimate sound, like a tongue testing a wound. The script upon them was not written in ink. It was written in the bruised color beneath the skin.
“Tell me who stands outside,” Brannoc said.
Korvath’s breath came thin and fast. “A dead man.”
“That is not a name.”
“It is enough of one.”
The feet in the corridor shifted. Many of them. Bare soles upon old stone. No one spoke. Their silence was worse than a crowd’s anger. It had the obedience of a congregation.
Brannoc rose from his crouch.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The claim inside him stirred again—not blood, not birthright, but something older than both. It moved through his chest with the slow certainty of a buried wheel. He had spent years strangling that sensation whenever it surfaced. A man could survive a blade. A man could survive treachery. A man could even survive learning that the crown he had served had never meant to acknowledge him.
What he could not survive was wanting it.
The Bleeding Crown had endured as an idea longer than any living claimant. Its name had crossed battlefields in whispers, passed from hand to hand beneath cloaks, offered to captains who understood the difference between authority and fear. Brannoc had been its unacknowledged heir, though no oath had ever been spoken over him, no seal pressed into wax for him, no court had opened its doors.
He had been born in 255 AS.
The knowledge came now with no memory attached to it. A bare fact, cold as a nail.
Korvath stared at him. “Do not take the edge.”
“You told me that before.”
“I was hoping you had not heard.”
“You are a smuggler, Korvath Nightbrook. Hope is a poor trade for you.”
A broken laugh escaped the man. It died quickly.
Outside, the familiar voice said, “You always did mistake refusal for strength.”
Brannoc’s hand went to the hilt at his side. The gesture was useless. His sword had been left somewhere beyond the chamber, along with the rest of the world that still obeyed ordinary distances.
“Why are you here?” Brannoc called.
“To collect what was promised.”
“No promise was made.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
“There is always a promise. Sometimes it is made by the hand. Sometimes by the blood. Sometimes by the coward who waits behind a door.”
Korvath pressed his forehead to the floor.
Brannoc glanced at him. “You brought me here.”
“I carried you here.”
“You brought me.”
“I was paid to find the passage.”
“By whom?”
Korvath’s lips trembled. “You know.”
The answer struck harder than a confession.
The Iron-Ring Cartel had paid men to move weapons through places no map admitted existed. House Morvain had paid men to forget what they saw. The Silent Choir had paid in favors that outlived coin. The Ashen Vanguard paid in law, when law could still be found. And the Bleeding Crown—if the old stories were more than the fevered invention of dispossessed soldiers—paid in inevitability.
Brannoc looked again at the coin.
“Who paid you?”
Korvath’s eyes lifted. “The voice.”
The door opened.
No hand touched it.
The chamber beyond was not the corridor Brannoc remembered. There was no torchlight, no fallen plaster, no cramped passage crowded with bare feet. A long hall stretched into darkness beneath a ceiling lost in shadow. Pale figures stood along its walls, their heads bowed. Their mouths had been sewn shut with black thread.
At the far end stood a man in a weather-darkened coat.
Brannoc knew the posture before he knew the face. The slight forward tilt of the shoulders. The habit of keeping one hand near the belt, not from fear but from arithmetic. The stillness of a commander who had learned that every motion was witnessed and every hesitation priced.
The man’s face remained indistinct.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
That was the cruelty of it. Brannoc knew the voice, the gait, the shape of the silence around him, but the face had been taken away.
“Step through,” the man said.
The figures along the hall bowed lower.
Brannoc did not move.
The Thrice-Bound Edge drifted past his shoulder. It entered the hall without touching the floor, without making a sound. The moment it crossed the threshold, the sewn mouths opened.
A single breath passed through them.
The chamber filled with the smell of wet ash.
Korvath made a small, broken noise. “You see? It knows you.”
“It knows what I am.”
“No.” Korvath crawled backward. “That is worse.”
Brannoc turned toward him. “What did you bring me to?”
The smuggler’s gaze fixed upon the open grimoire. “Fenspire.”
The name seemed to draw the darkness tighter.
Fenspire stood in the Gloaming Reach, founded in 57 AS, its stark spire raised above a land where daylight always seemed to arrive wounded. It was a core location, garrisoned by 3,742, and whatever stood beyond this door carried its discipline: the cold vigilance of a place that had learned to sleep with its weapons in hand.
But Brannoc had never seen Fenspire like this.
He had seen its outer walls once from a distance, under a sky thick with black weather. He had seen the watchfires and the ordered movement of soldiers. No one had spoken of a hall beneath it, or a congregation with sewn mouths, or a regalia that floated like a patient executioner.
Korvath said, “The book opened the way.”
“You opened the book.”
“I touched the clasp.”
“And then?”
“And then it knew your name.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The voice at the end of the hall softened. “Names are such small doors.”
Brannoc stepped across the threshold.
The dead—or whatever passed for dead within that place—did not look at him. Their heads remained bowed. Their hands hung at their sides, palms turned outward. Each palm bore a dark line from wrist to finger, as if a blade had once been drawn there and had left a road for something to follow.
Behind him, Korvath whimpered.
Brannoc did not turn. “Stay.”
“Where?”
“Here.”
“I cannot.”
“You can.”
“I cannot.”
The hall’s darkness leaned toward them.
Brannoc advanced, and the voice came with him, though the man at the far end did not move.
“You served the Ashen Vanguard,” it said.
“I sold my sword.”
“To the Ashen Vanguard.”
“To whoever paid.”
“You speak as though coin absolves the hand.”
“It keeps the hand fed.”
“And when the hand is asked to crown?”
Brannoc stopped.
The Thrice-Bound Edge hovered before him, its shape now clearer: not a sword, not a crown, but a length of dark metal bound three times by pale bands. No edge could be seen, yet the air near it parted in narrow, trembling lines.
“Who asks?” Brannoc said.
The man at the end of the hall inclined his head.
Behind the figures, something scraped along the walls.
“Every power that has survived the Sundering,” the voice said. “The Ashen Vanguard. House Morvain. The Silent Choir. The Iron-Ring Cartel. The Bleeding Crown.”
“They do not ask for the same thing.”
“They never have.”
“Then why show me?”
“Because you are the place where their demands meet.”
Brannoc felt the buried claim turn within him.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
He hated the voice for finding it. Hated Korvath for bringing him here. Hated the dead for bowing as if they had been awaiting his arrival since before he was born.
“What do they want?”
“The Vanguard wants a victor. House Morvain wants a puppet. The Choir wants silence. The Cartel wants a market. The Crown wants a body.”
“And you?”
The man’s blurred face tilted.
“I want the truth to remain expensive.”
A tremor passed through the hall.
