chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Brannoc seized the stranger by the front of his coat and dragged him over the threshold. The man’s
shoulder struck the wall. Dust fell from the beam overhead.
“Names,” Brannoc repeated.
The stranger’s breath rasped. “You were not called to bargain.”
“No,” Brannoc said. “I was called because someone has run out of men willing to die in his place.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The lantern-bearer shut the door behind them. His hand never left the hilt at his belt.
For one moment, no one spoke. Rain whispered against the window. Somewhere below, the house
groaned in its foundations.
Then the lantern-bearer said, “You mistake the shape of your inheritance.”
Brannoc’s fingers tightened.
There it was. Not the Crown, not the summons. The word behind both.
Inheritance.
Korvath’s gaze flicked toward him. Brannoc felt the question arrive and die unasked.
The lantern-bearer continued. “You are the unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown.”
The sentence fell with the weight of a stone dropped into deep water.
Brannoc had heard it in fragments before. In taverns where men drank too quickly. In the mouths of dying
captains. In the silence of those who recognized his blood and prayed he had not recognized theirs.
But never spoken plainly in a locked room.
He released the first messenger.
The man stumbled, caught himself, and rubbed his wrist. “There is no shame in what you are.”
“Shame?” Brannoc said. “You crossed a wet city with knives to tell me I was born inconvenient.”
“You were born dangerous.”
“Those are not the same.”
“To the Crown, they are.”
The name of the Bleeding Crown seemed to stain the air. Brannoc looked down at the folded message. Its
wax had cracked beneath his grip. He imagined the hand that had pressed it there, the hand that had
written of summons and duty without once writing the word blood.
On the table, Korvath had spread a map.
It showed the shattered realm in ink faded to the color of old bruises. The Ashen Vanguard held its central

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
roads. House Morvain’s territories were marked with black thorns. The Silent Choir had no borders at all,
only pale circles drawn around places where sound was said to die. The Iron-Ring Cartel had marked its
routes in red thread. Beyond them, beneath a crown-shaped blot, lay the territories of the Bleeding Crown.
Five powers contended over the ruins, and every one of them called its hunger necessity.
Korvath tapped the map with one finger. “If they want him moved, they will need a road.”
“The road exists,” said the first messenger. “Crookvale.”
Brannoc leaned over the map.
“Crookvale was founded in 295 AS,” the man said. “In The High Spires. It has been rebuilt. Its garrison is
1004. It remains outside the core holdings.”
Korvath gave a low, humorless laugh. “A hundred and four ways to be noticed.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
“1004,” Brannoc corrected.
The smuggler glanced at him.
Brannoc did not explain. Numbers had teeth. A garrison of 1004 was not a wall; it was a message.
Someone wanted the settlement held, watched, and ready.
“Crookvale is not a road,” Brannoc said. “It is a throat.”
“It is the only passage the Crown can trust.”
“No passage trusts anyone.”
The lantern-bearer lifted the black cloth from his lantern. Light spilled over the table. Beneath the map,
another sheet had been folded into quarters. He opened it carefully.
“Fenspire,” he said.
The name drew Brannoc’s attention.
“Fenspire stands in the Gloaming Reach. It was founded in 57 AS. It is a core location, garrisoned, with a
garrison of 3,742.”
Korvath’s face hardened. “That is not a passage.”
“It is a destination.”
“No.” Brannoc studied the marks on the paper. “It is a cage with a spire above it.”
“Every fortress is a cage.”
“Only if you are inside.”
The lantern-bearer’s eyes lifted toward him. “The Bleeding Crown wants you in Fenspire.”
Brannoc looked again at the map. A thin line ran from Crookvale toward the Reach, then vanished beneath
a smear of black ink. No route was drawn onward.
He touched the hidden grimoire through his coat.
The Edge of Gloamreach had come into his possession without a history. Its leather smelled of dust,
smoke, and something colder. Its attunement cost was 46, a number written in the margin by a hand that
had left no name. He had not opened it since the message arrived. He had feared the book less than what it
might show him.
Now the fear moved.
“Why?” Korvath asked.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The first messenger flexed his injured wrist. “Because the regalia recognizes you.”
Brannoc felt the folded thing against his chest.
The Thrice-Bound Edge.
Regalia forged in 123 AS. Its record contained no attunement cost. It had lain silent beneath his coat until
the messenger spoke of the Crown. Now its presence seemed deliberate, restrained, as if three unseen
bindings had drawn taut around his heart.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
“Recognizes me as what?” Brannoc asked.
Neither messenger answered.
Brannoc drew the regalia free.
It was not bright. Nothing in the Ashen Era had earned the right to brightness. Its surface held the color of
old iron beneath ash, its edges severe and unadorned. The room’s lantern flame bent toward it.
Korvath swore.
The first messenger took one step back.
Brannoc noticed. Fear had a posture. This was not fear of the weapon. It was fear of what the weapon
might confirm.
He broke the folded wrapping.
The instant his fingers touched The Thrice-Bound Edge, the grimoire beneath his coat opened by itself.
Pages scraped against cloth.
A cold wind moved through the room, though the window was shut. The lantern guttered. Ink bled across
the nearest page, gathering into a dark pool. Brannoc pulled Edge of Gloamreach free and let it fall open
on the table.
The page showed no words at first.
Then a year surfaced.
297 AS.
The ink spread into a crown split down the center. Beneath it, another line appeared.
The Accord of Mournthrone began in 297 AS.
Brannoc stared.
A second year burned into the paper.
300 AS.
The letters that followed were cramped, almost frantic.
Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed died in 300 AS during the Accord of Mournthrone.
His breath stopped.
The room returned in pieces: Korvath’s hand near the crossbow, the strangers frozen beside the door, the
rain threading the dark glass. His own name remained on the page, colder than any epitaph.
He read the next line.
301 AS.
The Accord of Mournthrone ended in 301 AS with the Ashen Vanguard named victor.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The lantern flame rose sharply. Shadows climbed the walls.
More writing crawled from the margin.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Its collapse unleashed a decade of guerrilla reprisals.
Below that, the final sentence formed.
The losing commander was bribed to withdraw.
No one moved.
Korvath came around the table. “What does it say?”
Brannoc shut the book.
The cover resisted him.
He pressed harder. The leather buckled beneath his palm, and the letters of its title seemed to deepen:
Edge of Gloamreach.
“What does it say?” Korvath asked again.
“That the future has poor manners.”
The first messenger’s face had gone pale beneath the hood. “You opened it.”
“I noticed.”
“You were not meant to—”
Brannoc struck him across the mouth.
The man hit the wall. The lantern-bearer drew his sword, but Korvath’s crossbow rose with it, the quarrel
aimed at his eye.
Brannoc placed The Thrice-Bound Edge on the map.
Every mark trembled.
Far away—or beneath the floor, or inside his blood—something answered.
The regalia’s three bindings tightened around nothing visible. The map’s ink began to run from the
borders of Fenspire toward Crookvale, from Crookvale toward the black crown.
The Bleeding Crown.
Brannoc heard, beneath the rain, the slow drag of a blade being drawn.
The hooded messenger wiped blood from his lip. “If you refuse, the Crown will come for you.”
Brannoc looked at the page where his death remained written.
“Let it come.”
The door behind them clicked.
Not from the latch.
From the other side.
Korvath turned. The crossbow wavered for the first time.
A voice spoke through the wood.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
“Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed.”
The same voice that had called him before.
Only now it was closer.
And the grimoire opened again.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Chapter 6
Fenspire rose through the mist like a black nail driven into the mountain.
Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed watched it from the lower road while rain silvered the ash beneath his
boots. The tower had no beauty in it. Beauty belonged to things that expected to survive. Fenspire had
been built to endure being hated.
A banner hung above the gate, sodden and dark. Its device was lost in the weather, but the men beneath it
were plain enough: helms, hooked spears, crossbows held beneath oilskin. The garrison numbered 3,742,
and every one of them seemed to know that the Reach was waiting for a weakness.
“Fenspire was founded in 57 AS,” Korvath Nightbrook said beside him.
Brannoc did not look at the smuggler. “You say that as if the stone remembers.”
“Stone remembers better than men.”
“Stone has no tongue.”
“It has cracks.”
Korvath’s voice was soft, almost swallowed by the rain. He dressed in the color of wet soot, without badge
or ornament, and kept his hands hidden beneath his cloak. A face made for forgetting. The sort of face a
guard saw, searched, and lost before the next bell.
Brannoc had trusted such men before. He had buried more than one.
The road climbed toward the gate. Behind them, the Gloaming Reach dissolved into gray folds of heather
and black water. Ahead, Fenspire’s walls were wet as old bone. The tower rose within them, narrow and
severe, its upper windows glowing with the weak amber of watchfires. No smoke drifted from the
chimneys. The wind pressed it flat and sent it crawling along the battlements.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Brannoc’s gloved hand rested on the pommel of his sword. The leather was stiff with rain. Beneath the
glove, the old color of his hand had been washed clean, but the name remained.
The Red-Handed.
Names did not need blood to keep their shape.
“Are you afraid?” Korvath asked.
Brannoc glanced at him then. “Of Fenspire?”
“Of what waits inside it.”
“That depends what waits.”
Korvath’s mouth twitched. It might have been a smile, though there was no warmth in it. “The Bleeding
Crown waits everywhere.”
The words entered Brannoc like a cold blade slipped between ribs.
He looked again at the tower.
His crown. His inheritance. His shame.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The claim had never been proclaimed before a court, never carried in a sealed writ, never blessed by a
priest of any power. It lived in whispers and bloodlines and the careful silences of those who had known
his mother. It lived in the way certain old soldiers watched him when they thought he was not watching
back. Unacknowledged did not mean unreal. A bastard could be denied. A blade could not be denied once
it had opened the body.
“Do not speak that name here,” Brannoc said.
“Which name?”
“You know which.”
Korvath’s gaze slid toward the gatehouse. “The one that makes men kneel?”
“The one that makes men kill.”
A bell sounded above them.
Not loud. Not urgent. One measured toll, then another.
The gatehouse stirred. Shutters opened in the walls. Crossbows tilted downward.
Brannoc felt the soldiers’ attention pass over him, weighing sword, cloak, posture, the expensive restraint
of his equipment. A Sellsword Captain was never merely a man at a gate. He was a question with steel at
his hip. Who had bought him? Who had failed to? How long until his loyalty became a debt?
Korvath stepped forward.
“Hold,” called a voice from above.
Brannoc saw no face, only the dark slit beneath the parapet.
“Names.”
“Korvath Nightbrook.”
The pause that followed was brief but deliberate.
“And the other?”
Brannoc could have given a false name. It might have bought him an hour, perhaps a night. But false
names were like false coin: useful only where no one cared to test them.
“Brannoc Ironmere.”
The gatehouse went still.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Rain ticked against his shoulder plates. Somewhere beyond the walls, a dog began to bark, then stopped as
though struck.
“And the epithet?” the voice asked.
Brannoc’s jaw tightened.
Korvath turned his head a fraction. “They know you.”
“They know a story.”
“The story has teeth.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
“Open the gate,” Brannoc called.
“State your business.”
“To see someone.”
“Who?”
Brannoc looked at the black slit overhead. “If I knew that, I would not be here.”
That earned him movement. Men shifted along the wall. Metal scraped against stone.
Korvath leaned close enough that Brannoc smelled rainwater and bitter root on his breath. “You were
meant to say you carried a message.”
“I carry no message.”
“You carry a war.”
“I carry myself.”
“That may be worse.”
The gate opened a handspan, then stopped. A man in a hooded mantle appeared in the gap. He held no
visible weapon, which meant there were weapons close enough to reach them. His face was narrow and
bloodless, his eyes fixed on Brannoc with the exhausted hatred of someone examining a familiar wound.
“You are expected,” he said.
Brannoc felt the muscles across his back draw tight. “By whom?”
The man’s eyes moved to Korvath. “Not by you.”
“Then open the gate.”
“You cannot enter armed.”
Brannoc almost laughed. The sound would have been ugly.
“I am a Sellsword Captain.”
“You are Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed.”
“That is what I said.”
“And you were born in 255 AS.”
The rain seemed to thin around him.
He had heard the year spoken in ledgers, in curses, in the mouths of men who had counted his life against
the shape of a prophecy. To hear it from this stranger made it feel less like a birth and more like a
sentence.
Korvath’s hand emerged from his cloak. Not a weapon. A small iron token rested between his fingers, its
surface blackened by use.
The gatekeeper saw it.
His expression changed.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Brannoc noticed. “What is that?”
“Something you were not meant to see,” Korvath said.
“You have made a habit of that.”
“I survive by habits.”
The gatekeeper reached through the gap and took the token. His thumb passed over its face. For the first
time, something like fear showed in his features.
“Give up your sword,” he said.
“No.”
“Then remain outside.”
Brannoc looked beyond him, through the narrow opening. Fenspire’s inner court lay drowned in rain.
Figures crossed it beneath cloaks. At the far end, a stair climbed toward the tower. On the top landing
stood a woman in a pale veil, motionless beneath the eaves.
He could not see her face.
He knew she was watching him.
“Who is that?” he asked.
The gatekeeper did not turn. “You were expected by her.”
“Her name.”
No answer.
The woman lifted one hand.
The gesture was small. The gatekeeper bowed his head.
Brannoc hated her immediately.
Not for the mystery. Mystery was a currency, and he had spent much of his life among debtors. He hated
the ease of the command. The assumption that the world would move when she moved.
He had seen that assumption before in the courts of the Bleeding Crown, where men wore red beneath
their collars and called obedience peace.
The gate opened wider.
“Your sword,” said the gatekeeper.
Brannoc drew it halfway. Rain ran down the blade in a black line. The weapon had no grand name, no
forged history fit for a song. It was steel made honest by use. He held it out hilt first.
The gatekeeper reached for it.
Brannoc did not release it.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
For a moment the two of them stood joined by the sword, the rain beating between their hands.
“If this is an ambush,” Brannoc said, “you will need more than a wall.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The gatekeeper met his eyes. “If this were an ambush, you would already be dead.”
“Then you have failed to impress me.”
“Not yet.”
Brannoc let go.
The man took the sword and stepped aside. Korvath passed through first, his shoulders hunched, his face
emptied of interest. Brannoc followed.
Fenspire smelled of wet iron, boiled grain, and old ash. The stones beneath his boots sloped toward
channels cut in the courtyard, where rainwater ran red-brown from the walls. Soldiers watched from
covered walks. Their faces were young in some places and ancient in others. Every man carried the same
narrow stillness, the patience of those who had been taught that danger announced itself only after it
arrived.
Brannoc counted the exits without meaning to.
One gate behind him. Two covered passages. A stair to the battlements. The tower entrance guarded by
four men who pretended not to guard it.
His hand felt wrong without the sword.
The Thrice-Bound Edge lay somewhere inside the tower, if the whispers had not lied. Regalia forged in
123 AS, bearing a name that sounded less like a weapon than a sentence imposed upon one. No record
named an attunement cost. That absence troubled Brannoc more than any price could have. Everything
that bound a man asked payment. If the record was silent, perhaps the payment had been hidden.
Korvath glanced back. “You are staring.”
“At the tower.”
“You should stare at the people.”
“I know what people do.”
“And the tower?”
“It has not yet lied to me.”
They reached the foot of the stair. The veiled woman waited above them.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Up close, she seemed neither old nor young. The pale cloth concealed everything but the shape of her
mouth. Rain whispered from the eaves. Behind her, the doorway stood open upon darkness.
“You came late,” she said.
Brannoc looked toward the sky, though no light showed through the cloud. “You gave no hour.”
“I gave a summons.”
“I received a rumor.”
“Rumors travel farther.”
“Then your message was poorly made.”
The mouth beneath the veil curved. “You speak like a man who believes he has choices.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
“I speak like a man who has survived without your permission.”
Something moved behind the doorway.
Not a soldier. Something quieter. A dry rustle, like pages shifting in a sealed room.
Korvath’s posture changed.
Brannoc noticed. “What is inside?”
The veiled woman ignored him. “The Accord of Mournthrone is not finished.”
“It ended.”
“It ended for those who signed it.”
“The Ashen Vanguard named itself victor.”
“Named itself,” she said. “There is a difference.”
The words struck close to truths Brannoc had kept buried beneath campaigns, coin, and drink. The Accord
of Mournthrone had begun in 297 AS and ended in 301 AS, but endings were courtly things. Men declared
them while soldiers still bled in ravines. A victory could be purchased as easily as a withdrawal. A
commander could be bribed, and a host could vanish from the field beneath the respectable cloak of
strategy.
He had seen enough of war to know that banners lied better than men.
“What do you want from me?” he asked.
The woman turned toward the dark doorway. “What you were denied.”
His breath caught before he could stop it.
Korvath said, “Do not.”
The woman looked down at him. “You brought him here.”
“I brought a blade.”
“You brought the heir.”
The courtyard seemed to contract around them.
Brannoc heard the soldiers breathing. Heard rain dripping from the tower stones. Heard, from somewhere
below, the faint scrape of his confiscated sword being carried away.
He climbed one step.
The woman did not move.
“The Bleeding Crown has no heir,” he said.
“Then why did you come?”
“I came for an answer.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
“No. You came because a part of you still believes blood can make a door open.”
The darkness behind her stirred again.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
A smell spilled from it—dust, bitter herbs, and something colder, touched by twilight. On a table within,
half-seen beneath a cloth, lay a broad black volume bound in material that seemed to drink the candlelight.
The Edge of Gloamreach.
Brannoc had heard of the grimoire in campfires and sealed rooms. Its attunement cost was 46. He had
never believed the number mattered until he saw the book waiting in the dark, its spine marked by a thin
seam of gray light.
The veiled woman descended one step toward him.
“Take off your glove,” she said.
Brannoc’s bare fingers flexed beneath the leather.
“No.”
“Your hand has been named.”
“My hand has been wounded.”
“By whom?”
He thought of old steel, old treachery, old oaths spoken over cups that tasted of ash. He thought of the
crown he had never worn and the men who would rather see it burned than see it rest on his head.
The woman reached for him.
Brannoc seized her wrist.
Every soldier in the courtyard raised a weapon.
Korvath whispered, “Brannoc.”
The woman did not struggle. Beneath the veil, she smiled again.
From the open doorway, the black grimoire opened by itself.
And somewhere inside Fenspire, the bell began to toll.
The woman’s wrist was cold beneath his grip.
Not cold as skin went cold in winter, nor as a corpse cooled beneath a shroud. The chill of her ran inward,
a thin, deliberate current that entered through his palm and climbed his arm. His wounded hand answered
with a pulse of pain.
The soldiers’ weapons remained raised.
Korvath stood three paces away, his face gone narrow and bloodless. He had the look of a man who had

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
found a door in a wall and understood, too late, that something on the other side had already opened it.
“Release me,” the woman said.
Her voice had not changed. That was the worst of it. No strain. No fear. No anger. It carried the mild
patience of someone waiting for a servant to finish making a mistake.
Brannoc tightened his fingers.
The bell tolled again.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Its sound came down through the stones of Fenspire, vast and black. Dust shivered from the archway. In
the courtyard, one of the horses screamed and reared against its tether, showing the wet ruin of its mouth.
No one moved to calm it.
The grimoire’s pages turned.
They did not flutter. They turned with purpose, one after another, their edges scraping together like small
knives being drawn. The book lay open on the flagstones inside the doorway, untouched by wind. Its
cover was blacker than the shadows around it, its shape severe and old.
“Edge of Gloamreach,” Korvath whispered.
The name passed through Brannoc like a hook.
The woman’s gloved hand rose. The fingers of it touched the back of his bare wrist. He felt the pressure
through the scarred flesh, and beneath that pressure something searching, patient as a root beneath stone.
“Take your hand from me,” she said.
“Tell them to lower their weapons.”
“They will not.”
“Then they may keep them raised until their arms rot.”
A soldier shifted near the well. Brannoc heard the leather of his grip creak. He did not look at him. Every
man in the courtyard had become a line of force, a bowstring drawn to the point where courage and terror
were indistinguishable.
Korvath said, “Brannoc, the book is speaking.”
“No book speaks.”
From the doorway came a sound like a breath dragged through a dead throat.
The pages stopped.
Ink gathered upon the open leaf. It rose from the fibers in black beads, joined itself into strokes, and began
to write.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Brannoc could not read it from where he stood. He saw only the movement: the crawling script, the
cramped columns, the sudden blackening of the page. Then the letters brightened—not with light, but with
the pallor of old bone.
The woman watched him watching the book.
“You know what it wants.”
“I know what books want. To be burned.”
“Not this one.”
“Especially this one.”
A faint smile touched her mouth beneath the veil. “You mistake being named for being chosen.”
The words found something soft beneath his ribs.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
He had lived among men who spoke of names as if names were chains. Sellswords gave false ones at
gates, kept true ones from taxmen, and died beneath names borrowed from better men. His own had been
carried across battlefields in whispers, scraped from contracts, muttered over cups. Brannoc. Ironmere.
The Red-Handed.
A name could buy a blade.
A name could open a grave.
The grimoire turned another page.
This time the writing was large enough for him to see.
BRANNOC IRONMERE THE RED-HANDED
The letters stood alone at the top.
His hand opened.
The woman’s wrist slipped half an inch in his grasp, but he caught it again. The soldiers raised a collective
breath. Somewhere behind him, a buckle clicked.
Below his name, the ink continued to form.
BORN IN 255 AS.
His jaw locked.
The courtyard seemed to recede. The wall, the soldiers, the doorway, the woman—all of it drew away
beneath the bell’s tolling, leaving only the page and the black strokes that crawled over it.
He had never told the men here when he was born. He had never told most men anywhere. Birth was a
weakness if it could be counted, a measure by which another man might decide how long one had left to
be useful.
The grimoire wrote on.
DIED IN 300 AS.
The next bell-strike did not come.
Silence fell so completely that Brannoc heard the horse breathing through its nose. He heard the scrape of
his own thumb against the woman’s glove. He heard the blood working inside his wounded hand.
For one instant, the line refused meaning.
Then it entered him.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Not as fear. Fear was clean. Fear had a blade’s edge and a direction. This was heavier. It was the sensation
of standing in a room where everyone had already mourned him and no one had thought to tell him.
His eyes went to the woman.
She did not look surprised.
“You knew.”
“I had read the page.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
“And you brought me here to show it.”
“I brought you here because the page was sealed.”
“By whom?”
Her silence was answer enough to make the soldiers uneasy.
Korvath took one step toward them. “What does it say?”
Brannoc turned his head.
The smuggler stared at the grimoire as though it were a hungry animal. His guarded manner had broken
apart, revealing the old caution beneath: not the caution of a coward, but of a man who survived by
knowing when not to be present.
“It says my name,” Brannoc said.
Korvath’s eyes flicked to the woman. “That is not an answer.”
“It is the only one you’re getting.”
The woman’s fingers moved beneath his grip.
Brannoc felt a hard object press into his palm. A sliver of metal, thin and cold. He glanced down.
The thing was no larger than a fingernail, dark at its center and pale along one edge. It had not been there
before. He had felt no motion, seen no trick of hand.
Her voice lowered.
“Give it to the book.”
“Why?”
“Because it has remembered you.”
“Books remember nothing.”
“Then let it forget.”
The shard bit him.
His blood welled around it, bright against the black metal. The old wound in his hand opened with a wet
sting. A drop fell to the flagstones.
The grimoire answered.
Every page lifted at once.
A wind burst from the doorway, though the courtyard air remained still. It struck Brannoc in the chest and
drove the smell of dust, iron, and distant rain into his lungs. The soldiers cried out. One loosed his
weapon; the bolt struck stone and spun away. Another dropped to one knee.
The woman did not move.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The black leaves of Edge of Gloamreach turned in a single roaring wave. The ink on the open page spread
outward, consuming the words. His name dissolved. The line beneath it remained.
DIED IN 300 AS.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The letters began to drip.
Brannoc’s wounded hand burned. He looked at the shard. It had sunk beneath his skin, not deep, but deep
enough that the edges had vanished. Black veins traced outward from it, fine as cracks in ice.
He tried to pull it free.
Pain flashed white.
The woman caught his hand.
“Do not.”
He nearly struck her. The impulse came up through him swift and trained, the old answer to restraint. He
stopped only because the soldiers would fire, and because her grip had become impossibly strong.
“Take it out.”
“If you tear it loose, the book will open the rest.”
“The rest of what?”
She leaned close. Her veil smelled faintly of soot.
“The part that tells you who kills you.”
For the first time, her calm broke.
Not much. A tremor touched the final word. But Brannoc heard it.
He studied her covered face. “You’re afraid.”
“I am careful.”
“Same disease, different coat.”
The book slammed shut.
The force of it struck the doorway. Black sparks crawled along the threshold and vanished into the stone.
The soldiers flinched as one. Korvath swore under his breath and reached inside his coat.
Brannoc saw the motion.
“Don’t,” he said.
Korvath’s hand stopped.
“You brought that thing here,” Brannoc said.
“I carried it.”
“That is not the same defense.”
“I was told it had to reach Fenspire.”
“By whom?”
Korvath looked at the woman.
There it was again: the silence, the refusal, the shape of an allegiance neither of them would name.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Brannoc turned his grip until the woman’s wrist bent. She made no sound, but her shoulder tightened.
“Who sent you?”
“No one.”
“Everyone is sent by someone.”
“Not the dead.”
His hand stilled.
The courtyard darkened though the sky above the walls had not changed. A shadow passed over the
stones, too broad to belong to any bird. The black grimoire trembled once inside the doorway.
The woman said, “You have very little time.”
“For what?”
“To decide whether you want to die as yourself.”
A bitter laugh scraped out of him. “The book has already decided.”
“The book has written a fact.”
“Facts can be altered.”
“Not all.”
He looked again at the page visible between the grimoire’s covers. The ink had soaked through, staining
the leather beneath. His name was gone, but he could still see the pressure of the letters in the paper, the
grooves left by whatever hand—or thing—had written them.
Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed died in 300 AS.
The sentence settled inside him with the weight of a stone dropped into deep water.
He saw no battlefield. No assassin. No grave. The book had given him no face to hate, no weapon to
avoid, no path by which a man might cheat the dark. Only the date. Only the certainty.
He had spent his life refusing other men’s endings.
The woman’s wrist was still in his grasp.
“Why show me this?” he asked.
“You asked to know who had named your hand.”
“And?”
“I did not say the name came from the living.”
The bell began to toll again.
This time it rang from beneath them.
The stones under Brannoc’s boots shuddered. A seam opened between the flagstones, a black line

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
widening toward the doorway. The soldiers broke formation. Some shouted for the gates; others backed
into one another, weapons wavering. Korvath drew the thing from his coat at last—not a blade, not any
weapon Brannoc recognized, but a small iron ring held between two fingers.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The woman tore her wrist free.
Brannoc caught only the edge of her glove.
She stepped backward toward the open doorway.
“Wait.”
The word left him before pride could stop it.
Her veiled head tilted.
He hated her for hearing the plea inside it.
“Come with me,” she said.
Behind her, Edge of Gloamreach opened once more.
A hand rose from between its pages. It was made of ink, thin and jointed, and it reached across the
threshold toward Brannoc.
The ink hand touched his palm.
Cold entered him without breaking the skin. It was not the cold of winter, nor of steel left beneath rain. It
was the absence of warmth—the place where warmth had been scraped away. His fingers opened against
his will.
The hand folded itself around them.
Brannoc struck at the wrist with his free hand. His blow passed through blackness and found the edge of
the doorway. Pain flashed up his arm. The soldiers nearest him cried out as though he had struck them
instead. One loosed an arrow. It vanished into the open grimoire with a wet, sucking sound.
The woman did not flinch.
“Come with me,” she said again.
“What is on the other side?”
“An answer.”
He looked past her veil.
There was no corridor beyond the door. No chamber, no stair, no sky. The pages of Edge of Gloamreach
had opened upon a depth that refused shape. Pale ash drifted through it, rising instead of falling. Far away,
something vast moved behind a membrane of darkness, its passage bending the dimness as wind bent long
grass.
Brannoc had lived among men who sold certainty by the measure. Priests sold it in white halls. Captains

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
sold it over maps. Kings sold it with wax seals pressed into blood. He had learned to distrust any answer
that did not come with a price.
The hand tightened.
His knees nearly gave.
Korvath Nightbrook was staring at him. The smuggler’s face had gone slack, all its guarded slyness
burned away. In his fingers, the little iron ring looked dull and harmless. Brannoc knew better now. It had

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
the stillness of a shut eye.
“Do not take another step,” Korvath said.
The woman’s head turned by a fraction. “You brought him here.”
“I brought you the book.”
“You brought the door.”
“I brought what I was paid to bring.”
“Then be paid.”
Korvath’s mouth tightened. “That was not the bargain.”
The soldiers heard the exchange, or enough of it to understand that the world had become a marketplace in
which they were the merchandise. Their fear changed shape. Fear of the unnatural could still be endured;
men had endured it since the Sundering. Fear of being cheated was older, and more immediate.
A spearpoint pushed between the soldiers. It trembled toward the woman’s veiled face.
“Shut the book,” its owner said.
The ink hand pulled Brannoc forward.
He caught the spearshaft before it reached her. His grip closed. Wood groaned.
“Lower it.”
The soldier looked at him, bewildered. “Captain—”
“Lower it.”
The spear dipped. Brannoc shoved it aside, and the man stumbled against his fellows.
The woman watched him. Though her face was hidden, he felt her attention settle on the place beneath his
ribs where old secrets had grown teeth.
“You have already chosen,” she said.
“I chose not to watch a frightened boy die for the sake of your pride.”
The soldier was not a boy. Brannoc knew that. He had seen the man’s beard, his scars, the hard calluses
where a weapon had been carried too long. But terror stripped years from the face. It made every soldier
young.
“And what do you call the choice you made before that?” she asked.
He said nothing.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The room smelled of singed wool, iron, and the bitter mineral scent rising from the pages. His coat
dragged against the threshold. Beneath it, his heart beat with the brutal steadiness of a marching drum.
He had spent his life walking toward doors other men barred against him.
The Bleeding Crown had never acknowledged him. Its silence had been more elaborate than denial. There
were seals that opened for him and mouths that closed when he entered. There were old hands that
lingered too long over his face, searching for a resemblance no one dared name. He had learned the shape

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
of his inheritance through absences.
Now the doorway offered him no crown, no army, no proclamation. Only darkness wearing the manners
of invitation.
The ink hand crawled higher.
Black fingers crossed his wrist. They left no stain, but he felt words forming under his skin, each letter a
small, deliberate wound.
Korvath stepped nearer. “Brannoc.”
It was the first time the smuggler had spoken his name.
The soldiers heard it. Their eyes shifted toward him. Some had known. Some had guessed. Others
understood only that Korvath Nightbrook had addressed a Sellsword Captain without title, and that the
name itself seemed to have disturbed the air.
Brannoc did not look away from the doorway.
“How do you know me?”
Korvath swallowed. “I know what people pay to move.”
“People?”
“Secrets.”
“Mine?”
“Yours are too heavy for one man.”
A laugh came from somewhere in the formation. It died at once.
The woman lifted her hand. The iron ring in Korvath’s grasp answered with a faint chime. Not metal
striking metal. Something more distant, like a bell heard beneath deep water.
The doorway widened.
The edges of Edge of Gloamreach darkened. Its pages flexed, their corners lifting as though the book
breathed. The threshold drew the room toward itself. Loose ash skittered over the floor. A dropped knife
slid across the stones and disappeared into the dark.
Brannoc planted his boots.
For a moment, he held.
Then the hand beneath his skin pulled.
He had been wounded by men with axes, hooked blades, sharpened farm tools. He had been stitched in

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
darkness and cauterized by fire. Pain had always been a thing with a border. It entered, it raged, it passed.
This had no border.
The letters under his skin were moving toward his elbow.
“What happens if I refuse?” he asked.
“Your body remains,” said the woman.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
“And the rest?”
She did not answer.
That was answer enough.
Brannoc looked back at the room. The soldiers stood in a broken ring, their weapons lowered but not
abandoned. They were waiting for him to make the kind of decision men could obey. They wanted him to
become solid again—to give an order, name an enemy, place himself between danger and those paid to
follow him.
He had done that all his life.
The Ashen Vanguard would have called it duty. House Morvain would have called it leverage. The Silent
Choir would have called it a vow. The Iron-Ring Cartel would have measured it and sent an invoice.
The Bleeding Crown would have called it nothing.
Brannoc’s gaze found Korvath.
“You knew this would happen.”
“No.”
“You knew enough to fear it.”
“Yes.”
“And you brought me anyway.”
Korvath glanced at the ring. His fingers had begun to bleed where its edge bit into them. “I was told the
book would open for a man with a claim.”
“What claim?”
The smuggler’s eyes moved to Brannoc’s hand.
The hand of ink had reached his forearm.
The soldiers shifted. A murmur ran through them, low and ugly.
Brannoc felt the old heat stir in his blood. Not magic. Not anything so clean. Anger, perhaps. Shame. The
instinct to kill the nearest witness before the truth could find a tongue.
He had never told Korvath the truth.
Few had been allowed close enough to hear it.
The woman said, “You may leave him here.”
Korvath’s jaw worked. “That was not the bargain.”
“You have said that.”
“And I mean it.”
Something moved in the depth beyond the doorway. The vast shape turned. For an instant, Brannoc saw a

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
pale curve that might have been a face or the underside of a wing. He saw hollows where eyes could have
been. He saw a crown—not worn, but embedded in the thing’s darkness like a wound that had forgotten

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
how to close.
His breath stopped.
The Bleeding Crown was not there. He knew that. The crown was stone, blood, history, a power
contended over by hands that had forgotten what it meant to rule. Yet the shape beyond the pages had
summoned it from him, and that was worse than seeing any relic.
The woman took his hand.
Her glove was warm.
The warmth broke him.
Brannoc surged backward, wrenching against the ink hand. The threshold screamed—not loudly, but
inwardly, through his teeth and behind his eyes. Every soldier in the room dropped to one knee. The book
slammed its pages together around the doorway, then opened again with Brannoc half-drawn across the
sill.
Korvath shouted something.
Brannoc did not hear it.
He struck the stone with his shoulder. His fingers clawed at the floor. Blackness streamed between the
cracks beneath his nails. The letters in his arm flared, and for an instant the words became clear.
Not his name.
Not any name.
A command.
He read it, and the reading entered him like a hook.
The woman leaned close. Through the veil, he smelled smoke and crushed leaves.
“If you cross,” she whispered, “you will learn why they hid you.”
“Who hid me?”
Her silence returned.
Behind him, Korvath made a choked sound.
Brannoc turned his head.
The smuggler had dropped the iron ring. It lay on the floor, upright now, spinning without motion. Within
its hollow was not the stone beneath it but a narrow glimpse of red light, pulsing in time with Brannoc’s
heart.
The soldiers were no longer watching the woman.
They were watching him.
His hand had become ink to the elbow.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
There would be no returning to the room as the man who had entered it. Perhaps that was the answer she
had offered. Perhaps every door was merely a mouth waiting for the traveler to understand he had already
been swallowed.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Brannoc fixed his stare on Korvath.
“If I go,” he said, fighting for breath, “close the book.”
Korvath stared at him.
“Do you hear me?”
“I hear you.”
“Close it when I tell you.”
“And if you do not tell me?”
Brannoc looked into the depth beyond the threshold, into the ash that rose and the shape that waited
without impatience.
“Then decide what kind of coward you are.”
Korvath flinched as though struck.
The woman pulled.
Brannoc’s shoulder crossed the threshold. The darkness took him to the bone. He tasted old blood.
Somewhere far behind him, men began to pray—not to the Silent Choir, not to any power they could
name, but to the simple mercy of remaining themselves.
The woman’s hand closed around his.
This time, he did not resist.
The pages of Edge of Gloamreach rose on either side of him like black wings.
And from the room beyond, Korvath whispered, “Brannoc, that is not the book’s other side.”
The doorway began to close.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Chapter 7
Rain worried the shutters of the tower as though it had been sent to pry them loose.
Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed stood with one hand on the table and watched the black water slide
down the narrow glass. Beyond it, Crookvale crouched beneath the weather, rebuilt stone shouldering
against the dark. Its roofs had been laid in uneven tiers, its walls repaired in colors that did not belong
together. Survival had made the place ugly. Survival had made it stubborn.
A lamp guttered behind him.
“Say it again,” Brannoc said.
The man at the table swallowed. “The offer is sealed.”
“Offers are sealed when they are buried.”
“The Iron-Ring Cartel will provide coin.”
“Coin for what?”
The man’s mouth tightened. He wore no colors. That was a color of its own.
Brannoc lifted his hand from the table. The knuckles were scarred, the skin darkened by old blood that no
soap had persuaded to leave. He had not earned the name Red-Handed by killing one man, or ten. Names
grew in the mouths of others, fed by fear and repetition. They had called him captain before they called
him dangerous. They had called him dangerous before they called him heir.
The last name had never been spoken in a room with a locked door.
“Coin,” Brannoc said, “for what?”
“For the withdrawal.”
The rain hissed in the chimney.
Somewhere below, a guard laughed too loudly, then stopped. Brannoc imagined the man touching the hilt
of his weapon afterward, embarrassed by the sound he had made. In Crookvale, even laughter had to prove
it belonged there.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
“The Ashen Vanguard has already named itself victor,” said the courier. “The Accord of Mournthrone is
finished in all but language.”
“Finished?”
“The Accord began in 297 AS. It ends in 301 AS.”
“Then it has not ended.”
The courier glanced toward the shutters. “It will.”
Brannoc leaned closer. The man smelled of wet wool, lamp oil, and the sour fear of someone carrying a
message that could outlive him.
“Who paid you to tell me this?”
“No one.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
“That is a poor answer.”
“It is the true one.”
“Truth is not improved by being poor.”
The courier’s fingers pressed flat against the table. “The losing commander was bribed to withdraw.”
There it was. Not a rumor, then. Not merely the kind of rot that rose from a battlefield when too many
dead men lay under too little earth. The words entered the room and found a place to sit.
Brannoc looked again through the rain-blinded glass.
The Ashen Vanguard. House Morvain. The Silent Choir. The Iron-Ring Cartel. The Bleeding Crown.
Five powers, each pretending the realm could be stitched without reopening the wound. Five hands
reaching into the same ash, each certain the cinder that burned belonged to it.
“And you expect me to believe the Cartel is buying a victory already won?”
“The Cartel is buying what comes after.”
“After the accord?”
“After the name.”
Brannoc’s thumb rubbed the edge of the table. The wood had been planed smooth, but one splinter
remained. He worried it until it pierced the callus.
The decade of guerrilla reprisals had not yet begun. He knew that because the roads still carried wagons,
because men still wore uniforms instead of hiding their faces, because a messenger could enter a tower
and speak of withdrawal without having his tongue cut out for bringing the word. Yet he could feel the
future crouched beneath the floorboards.
“Where is the commander?” Brannoc asked.
The courier’s eyes hardened. “I was not told.”
“Was he bought before the battle or after?”
“I was not told.”
“You have been told very little.”
“I have been told enough to keep breathing.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Brannoc smiled without warmth. “That is a skill. Not a virtue.”
The courier looked at his hand. “They say you are the Bleeding Crown’s heir.”
“They say many things.”
“They say unacknowledged.”
“Then they have heard the word correctly.”
The man flinched, almost imperceptibly. There were people who feared the Crown, and people who feared
what might claim it once the Crown began to bleed. Brannoc had spent his life among both kinds. Born in
255 AS, he had learned early that blood could be a door, a chain, or a blade held to the throat. His had

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
been all three.
He turned from the window.
“Leave.”
“The answer?”
“You have not yet made an offer.”
“The Cartel wants—”
“The Cartel wants everything. It is the only prayer merchants know.”
The courier rose, but did not move toward the door. “If you refuse, the Ashen Vanguard will take
Crookvale.”
“Crookvale is outside the core holdings.”
“It still has a garrison of 1004.”
“Numbers are not walls.”
“They are men behind walls.”
“Men can be paid.”
“Not all men.”
“No,” Brannoc said. “Some must be frightened.”
The courier’s face went pale.
Brannoc almost pitied him. Almost. Pity was a warm drink, and warm drinks made a man careless. He had
watched captains die with their hands wrapped around cups. He had watched lords bargain away villages
while discussing the quality of the wine. He had watched men kneel to the Bleeding Crown and rise
believing themselves taller.
On a shelf beside the lamp lay a packet of copied records, bound in black thread. Brannoc had not opened
it since dusk. The top page had worked loose, exposing a line of cramped script.
The Thrice-Bound Edge was forged in 123 AS.
He touched the page with one finger.
The artifact was named as regalia, though the record offered no attunement cost. Its title had been written
three times in three different hands, each one more careful than the last. The Thrice-Bound Edge. A
restrained name for something made to bind. A blade, perhaps. A crown. A promise shaped until it could
cut.
He had seen men kill for less than a promise.
The courier followed his gaze. “That is not what I came to discuss.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
“No,” Brannoc said. “You came to discuss what men will do when promises fail.”
A low sound rolled through the tower. Not thunder. A horn from the outer wall.
The courier turned sharply.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Brannoc did not.
Another horn answered from the dark.
The room seemed to narrow around them. The lamp flame bent, then steadied. Brannoc reached for the
sword at his side, not drawing it, only resting his fingers against the hilt. Steel had its own language. It
spoke more plainly than heralds.
“How many?” he asked.
“I don’t know.”
“Then find out.”
The courier moved at last, but Brannoc caught his sleeve.
“If the Cartel has men outside the walls—”
“It does not.”
“You sound certain.”
“I was told there would be no—”
Brannoc twisted the sleeve until the man’s breath broke. “You were told very little.”
The tower door shook beneath a fist.
“Captain!” called a voice from the stairwell.
Brannoc released the courier. “Enter.”
The door opened. A guard stood there, rainwater shining on his shoulders. He was young enough to still
believe armor could make a man whole.
“Movement below,” the guard said. “No banners. Three groups at the east road. More in the gullies.”
“Are they attacking?”
“Not yet.”
“Then they are waiting to see whether we are frightened.”
The guard looked at the courier.
Brannoc saw the calculation begin. It was the simplest arithmetic in the realm: one stranger, one secret,
one tower threatened. The answer was usually blood.
“Seal the inner gate,” Brannoc said.
“Captain—”
“Do it.”
The guard hesitated. Brannoc let him.
A seasoned sellsword captain needed no crown to command a room. He needed only the willingness to
make the first wound.
“Go,” Brannoc said.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The guard went.
The courier stood beneath the open door, listening to boots strike the steps below. “If they are the Ashen
Vanguard—”
“They are not.”
“How can you know?”
“Because the Vanguard would have shown its colors.”
“Perhaps they want us to think—”
“Perhaps you want me to think.”
The courier’s fear sharpened into anger. That was better. Anger had edges. Fear only had weight.
Brannoc gathered the copied records and folded them beneath his coat. The page bearing the line about
The Thrice-Bound Edge brushed his ribs. Forged in 123 AS. Older than the rebuilt stones. Older than
Crookvale. Older than most claims men now called ancient. The knowledge pressed against him like a
hidden coin.
Outside, the rain thickened. Its sound filled the pauses between horns.
“Take me with you,” the courier said.
“You are safer here.”
“You mean to leave me.”
“I mean to leave you alive.”
“Then let me go.”
Brannoc looked at him.
The man understood his mistake before Brannoc spoke. A smuggler might have found a way through the
gullies. A priest of the Silent Choir might have passed unseen beneath the rain. A servant of House
Morvain might have lied with more elegance. But this courier had arrived with a sealed offer and no name
behind it. He was not a messenger. He was bait that had learned to walk.
At the far end of the tower, something struck the outer wall.
Dust sifted from the ceiling.
The courier whispered, “They have begun.”
“No,” Brannoc said, drawing his sword.
The blade came free with a soft, intimate sound.
“They have only knocked.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
A second impact shuddered through the stone. The lamp flame rose tall and blue. Below, men shouted.
Metal rang against metal. From the eastern wall came the sudden roar of frightened horses, followed by a
cry that ended too quickly.
Brannoc stepped toward the stair.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Behind him, the courier said, “If Crookvale falls, the reprisals will spread.”
“They will spread whether it falls or stands.”
“The Accord can still be preserved.”
“The Accord is a word men use when they want corpses to wait politely.”
He descended one step.
The courier moved after him.
Brannoc turned the sword in his hand, letting the lamplight run along its edge. “Stay.”
“I can fight.”
“You can carry a message.”
“To whom?”
Brannoc glanced at the black-windowed dark, at the unseen roads leading toward the High Spires, toward
the Gloaming Reach, toward every throne built upon ruin.
“To anyone who still believes the future is something they can purchase.”
He went down.
The stairwell smelled of wet stone and old smoke. Below, the garrison was waking in fragments: buckles
drawn tight, boots slipping into iron, curses whispered against the dark. Brannoc passed through them
without slowing. Men moved aside because they knew his name, or because they knew his hand, or
because they had heard what happened to those who stood between him and a decision.
At the bottom, the inner gate trembled.
A captain in the courtyard shouted for oil.
Brannoc raised his sword.
“Open it.”
The shouting stopped.
Rain streamed through the murder slits. Beyond the gate, shapes moved among the ruins—too many to
count, too patient to be raiders. No colors. No torches. The dark itself seemed to have taken positions.
One of the soldiers stared at him. “Captain, the gate—”
“Open it.”
“Those are enemies.”
“Then they have come far enough to meet us.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The winch groaned. Chains shifted overhead. The gate began to rise, stone grinding against stone, and the
rain blew in sideways, cold as a hand laid upon a grave.
Brannoc stepped beneath the lifting arch.
On the road beyond, someone called his name.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Not captain.
Not Red-Handed.
The other name.
The one the Bleeding Crown had never acknowledged.
Brannoc’s sword lowered by a fraction as the darkness answered—
The word struck deeper than any challenge.
Brannoc stopped beneath the rising gate. Rain streamed from the ironwork above him and broke against
his shoulders, darkening the leather there. Behind him, men shifted along the parapet. He heard the small
noises soldiers made when courage was being measured and found wanting: a buckle drawn tight, a thumb
testing a blade, breath taken through the teeth.
Again the voice came from the road.
“Unacknowledged heir.”
The soldiers heard it this time.
A murmur passed through them, low and ugly. Someone laughed, but the sound died quickly. Brannoc felt
the old wound open beneath his ribs—not pain, precisely. Pain was clean. This was a hand reaching into
him and closing around the thing he had spent his life pretending was not there.
He stepped beyond the gate.
The darkness on the road shifted. Figures emerged by degrees, not from concealment but from the rain
itself. Cloaks without colors. Faces veiled. Steel held low. They did not advance. That was the first thing
that frightened him.
Raiders came hungry.
Assassins came quickly.
These had come to be witnessed.
Behind Brannoc, the gate chains shrieked. “Captain,” one of the soldiers called. “Come back under stone.”
Brannoc kept his sword lowered.
“Tell me who sent you.”
The nearest figure tilted its head. A hood concealed the face, though rain ran from its hem in steady
threads. When it spoke, the voice was neither old nor young.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
“The one who knows what you are.”
“That knowledge has not improved anyone’s life.”
“The Bleeding Crown knows.”
At the name, the men behind him went still.
The Crown had been spoken of in taverns as a curse, in halls as a claim, in battlefields as a promise that
never arrived. Brannoc had learned to hear it without turning his head. He had learned to sleep while
others whispered of bloodlines and succession. He had learned to let them call him Red-Handed, as though

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
the epithet had been forged in battle and not hammered over the mouth of a secret.
“The Bleeding Crown has never acknowledged me,” he said.
“No.”
The figure raised a gloved hand.
Something moved behind the line of cloaks. A case was carried forward, narrow and blackened, its surface
shining with rain. It was set upon the road between them.
Brannoc’s soldiers muttered. The men who had brought it stepped away.
“Open it,” said the hooded voice.
“Open it yourself.”
“We did not come to touch what waits inside.”
“Then you have brought me a corpse.”
“No.”
Brannoc looked at the case. Its clasps were made of dull metal, each shaped like a closed eye. No crest
marked the lid. No wax sealed it. The absence felt deliberate, more threatening than any royal device.
He glanced back at the gate. The arch had risen high enough to admit a mounted man. Beyond it, the fort’s
lamps burned weakly through the wet. His men watched him with the naked devotion of those who had
mistaken habit for loyalty. They would follow him into a killing ground if he gave the order. They would
also remember the order.
“Stay where you are,” he said.
He crossed the road.
The rain softened the world. It blurred the cloaked figures, the gatehouse, the wounded lights. It made a
private chamber of the space between him and the case.
His boots struck the lid’s shadow before they struck the case itself.
A scent rose from the road: wet ash, old leather, something bitter beneath. Brannoc crouched. The clasps
released under his fingers with a faint click.
Inside lay a book wrapped in oilskin.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Not a weapon. Not a head. Not a letter bearing the seal he had feared since boyhood.
He peeled back the covering.
The binding was gray-black and swollen, its surface marked by lines that seemed to move when the rain
touched them. Along the spine, letters had been impressed into the hide.
Edge of Gloamreach.
Brannoc did not touch it.
He had seen the title once before, in a room where men with clean hands debated the value of forbidden
things. The grimoire had been described there in voices lowered by greed. Its attunement cost was 46. The
number had stayed with him—not because it meant anything to him, but because the men speaking it had

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
looked afraid of the price.
A soldier behind him whispered, “Captain?”
Brannoc lifted the book from its case.
The cold entered through his gloves.
Not the cold of rain. This was older, a depth without weather. The marks on the cover tightened beneath
his palm. Somewhere in the dark, one of the cloaked figures drew breath sharply.
The book opened by itself.
Its pages were pale as old bone, though no script appeared upon them. The blankness pressed against his
eyes. Brannoc felt a pull in his wrist, then in his shoulder, as if the book were trying to turn him toward
some unseen horizon.
He closed it.
The figures did not move.
“Why bring this to me?”
“Because it will open for you.”
“Then you are fools.”
“Perhaps.”
The answer unsettled him more than defiance would have. Men who came armed into a fortress did not
usually make room for uncertainty. Men who spoke in the name of the Bleeding Crown made less.
Brannoc rose with the grimoire in his hand.
“Who are you?”
“We are the remainder.”
“Of what?”
The hood inclined toward the fortress behind him.
“Of the promise made when the realm broke.”
That was poetry, and poetry was a kind of lie. Brannoc had spent too long among captains and claimants
to mistake beautiful words for anything but a sheath around a knife.
He turned his head slightly. “You heard that? They call themselves a remainder.”
No answer came from the gate.
He looked back at the road. The hooded figure stood close enough now that he could see the rain beading
on the leather of its gloves. Beneath the hood, the face remained shadowed.
“Tell me what you want.”
“You.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text: The old wound opened wider.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
“Dead?”
“Not yet.”
The word passed through the rain with the quiet certainty of an execution order.
Brannoc smiled, though there was no humor in it. “You crossed the dark to tell me I may live?”
“We crossed it to tell you that living will cost more.”
“Everything costs more when men cannot afford to say what they mean.”
“You mean the Crown.”
He said nothing.
“The Bleeding Crown has an heir,” the figure continued. “The realm knows this, though the realm has not
been told.”
“The realm knows nothing.”
“The realm knows hunger. It knows the smell of a lord’s panic. It knows which men look away when your
name is spoken.”
Brannoc’s fingers tightened around the grimoire. The cover seemed to pulse once beneath the leather.
He remembered all the eyes that had measured him. All the smiles that ended before reaching the mouth.
All the bargains in which he had been offered silver, land, absolution—anything but recognition. An
unacknowledged heir was useful. A named heir was dangerous. Between those truths lay the whole shape
of his life.
“You want me to claim it,” he said.
“We want you to survive what comes.”
“That is not the same thing.”
“No.”
A sound came from the ruins beyond the road.
Metal scraping stone.
The soldiers at the gate raised their weapons. Brannoc turned, grimoire still in hand. The shapes among the
broken walls had tightened their circle. He could no longer see open ground between them.
“How many?” someone called from the parapet.
Brannoc did not answer.
The cloaked figure spoke behind him. “They are not ours.”
“Then whose?”
“Everyone’s.”
A bolt struck the gatehouse.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
It hit one of the soldiers in the throat. He folded without a cry, his hands fluttering at the wound while the
men around him shouted and recoiled. Another bolt clattered against the stone. Then the road erupted with

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
motion.
The figures in the dark surged forward.
Brannoc threw the grimoire back into its case and kicked the case toward the gate. It skidded through mud.
A soldier seized it by the handle, dragging it clear as arrows hissed overhead.
“Close the gate!” Brannoc roared.
The chains began to move.
He met the first attacker beneath the arch. Steel rang. The impact jarred his arm to the shoulder. The
attacker wore no colors and fought without sound, blade cutting from the hip in a flat, efficient stroke.
Brannoc turned it aside, stepped in, and drove his pommel into the veiled face.
Bone gave.
The figure fell, and another came over it.
Rain ran into Brannoc’s eyes. He wiped it away with the back of his hand, leaving red across his cheek
though he could not tell whose blood it was. Behind him, men shouted for room. Before him, the darkness
pressed closer.
The hooded messenger had vanished.
Brannoc saw the absence and understood it as a betrayal.
“Coward!” he shouted.
Something answered from near the case.
Not the messenger’s voice.
His own.
“Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed.”
He turned.
The grimoire lay open in the mud.
Its pages were no longer blank. A black line had appeared across the nearest sheet, thin as a crack in ice.
Beneath it, letters gathered slowly, bleeding into being.
The sword in Brannoc’s hand felt suddenly heavy.
The gate descended behind him with a thunderous grinding, cutting off the fort, the soldiers, the lamps,
and every retreat he had not yet admitted he needed.
On the page, the final word formed.
Heir.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Then the darkness lunged, and Brannoc reached for the impossible—
The darkness struck him without weight.
It entered through his eyes.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
For one breath Brannoc saw nothing but blackness, and in that blackness he felt the shape of himself being
taken apart—not flesh from bone, but certainty from certainty. His sword vanished first. Then the mud
beneath his boots. Then the iron taste of the air.
He reached for the ground and found a page.
It buckled beneath his palm, warm and damp as skin.
Letters crawled beneath his fingers.
BRANNOC IRONMERE THE RED-HANDED.
He tried to wrench his hand away. The ink had already climbed into the lines of his palm. It burned there
with a cold so complete that his knuckles seemed to belong to someone else.
“Name your price,” he said.
His voice came back from every direction.
PRICE.
“Gold.”
PRICE.
“Blood.”
The word shuddered through the dark.
BLOOD.
Brannoc shut his hand. Somewhere beyond the page, something breathed with the patience of a buried
king.
He had seen men bargain with demons, saints, and starving armies. They all made the same mistake. They
believed the thing across from them wanted what they possessed.
The grimoire wanted what he had not yet given himself permission to become.
A pale seam opened before him.
Through it came the smell of snow on stone.
Then the world returned in a rush.
He stood upon a high road under a colorless sky. Below, the rebuilt walls of Crookvale clung to the
mountainside, their crooked towers shouldering one another against the wind. Smoke dragged low over
the settlement. Men in the garrison’s colors watched from the battlements, too distant to be faces. A
banner snapped above them, then tore loose and vanished into the ravine.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Brannoc knew the place. He knew it with the intimacy of a wound he had never suffered.
“Crookvale,” he whispered.
The road answered with no echo.
A number had been cut into the nearest milestone.
1004.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
He placed his hand over it. The stone was warm.
Crookvale had been founded in 295 AS. The knowledge did not arrive in his mind; it surfaced through
him, as though the grimoire had dredged it from some drowned chamber in his blood.
He looked toward the walls.
No sentry moved.
Below, the gate stood open. Beyond it, the street descended through rebuilt houses and shuttered
workshops. The place had the hush of a settlement waiting to hear whether it was still alive.
“Why show me this?”
A figure stood beside the milestone.
Korvath Nightbrook wore the same guarded stillness he had carried at the fort, but the road had hollowed
him. His cloak hung wet around him. His hands were empty.
Brannoc’s fingers found the hilt that was no longer there.
“You’re dead,” Brannoc said.
Korvath glanced toward the open gate. “That is an ambitious conclusion.”
“Where is my sword?”
“Where you left it.”
“I left it in my hand.”
“You leave many things there.”
The old anger rose cleanly. Brannoc welcomed it. Anger had edges. It could be held.
He struck at Korvath.
His fist passed through the smuggler’s chest and closed on winter.
The road buckled. The walls of Crookvale folded inward like paper touched by flame.
When the world steadied, Brannoc stood beneath a vast black spire.
Fenspire rose from the Gloaming Reach, its stone vanishing into low cloud. Every window burned with a
pinprick of watchful fire. Lines of soldiers moved along the walls in ordered silence. Behind the
battlements, weapon racks filled the courtyards. The garrison was not merely present; it was the shape of
the place.
3,742.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The number appeared in the air above the gate.
Brannoc read it twice.
“Core holding,” he said.
Korvath stood several paces away now, his face turned toward the spire. “A garrisoned one.”
“Who holds it?”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The answer came from the stone.
THE ASHEN VANGUARD. HOUSE MORVAIN. THE SILENT CHOIR. THE IRON-RING
CARTEL. THE BLEEDING CROWN.
The five names rolled over one another like armies marching beneath the earth.
Brannoc looked up at the tower. “All of them?”
“Not in the same room.”
“Then put me in the room.”
Korvath’s mouth twitched, though it was not quite a smile. “You have spent your life trying to enter rooms
that were built to exclude you.”
“My life.”
The words caught.
A strip of parchment appeared across the sky. Its surface was gray and marked with a single line of script.
BORN IN 255 AS.
The cold sharpened.
Brannoc stared at the words until they blurred.
He had never known his birth year. Not truly. There had been whispers, ledgers altered by careful hands, a
woman who would not speak of the night he first cried. Men had called him many things before they
called him captain. Bastard. Stray. Red-Handed. The grimoire offered the number without pity.
“Who wrote that?”
Korvath did not answer.
Another line formed beneath it.
UNACKNOWLEDGED HEIR TO THE BLEEDING CROWN.
Brannoc laughed once.
The sound died at his feet.
“No.”
The spire’s windows went dark one by one.
“No,” he said again, louder. “An heir is named. An heir is witnessed. An heir is given a place at the table
before someone decides the table must burn.”
The parchment remained.
He struck it with his palm. The sheet split around his hand, but the words did not tear. They sank into him.
The Bleeding Crown.
The name had followed him through camps, alleys, and battlefields, never spoken plainly, always

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
crouching behind another man’s silence. He had taken coin from lords who looked at him too long. He had
killed for commanders who never learned his face. He had thought the hunger in him came from poverty,

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
from violence, from the years spent being useful to men who found usefulness cheaper than trust.
The grimoire had found a simpler answer.
Korvath said, “You knew.”
“I suspected.”
“That is not the same thing.”
“It is when suspicion keeps you alive.”
A bell sounded within Fenspire.
Not an alarm. A summons.
The stone beneath Brannoc’s boots opened.
He fell into a hall lined with banners.
The Ashen Vanguard’s cloth hung scorched and stiff. House Morvain’s standard drooped as if it had been
soaked in rain that never dried. The Silent Choir had no colors at all—only white fabric marked by a black
vertical seam. The Iron-Ring Cartel displayed interlocked iron circles, each one painted over the last.
Above them all hung the banner of the Bleeding Crown, its red field split down the center.
Five chairs stood around a table.
Four were occupied.
The fifth waited.
Brannoc recognized no faces. That was worse than recognizing enemies. The figures had been stripped of
age, station, and feature. Their voices emerged from the banners behind them.
“The Accord of Mournthrone begins in 297 AS,” said one.
A second voice followed. “The Accord ends in 301 AS.”
“Named victor: the Ashen Vanguard.”
The table cracked between them.
“Collapse.”
The banners stirred though there was no wind.
“Ten years of guerrilla reprisals.”
Brannoc looked from one empty face to another. “That has not happened.”
“It will.”
“Then why tell me?”
The fourth figure leaned toward the vacant chair. “Because the losing commander is bribed to withdraw.”
A purse appeared on the table.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text: It was small. Plain. Heavy enough to drag the cloth toward it.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Brannoc saw no hand take it. He heard no terms. Yet the betrayal filled the hall, rank and intimate. Armies
would die believing they had been defeated by steel. Villages would burn believing they had chosen the
wrong oath. Men would whisper of cowardice when the truth was that someone had counted the price of
retreat.
“Who paid him?” Brannoc asked.
The figures turned toward him.
“Sit.”
The fifth chair was made of black iron.
He approached it slowly. On its back, three cuts had been carved into the wood. The markings resembled
the bindings of The Thrice-Bound Edge, though the weapon itself was nowhere visible.
He touched the chair.
Pain opened in his wrist.
A final line appeared above the table.
BRANNOC IRONMERE THE RED-HANDED DIES IN 300 AS DURING THE ACCORD OF
MOURNTHRONE.
He withdrew his hand.
For a moment, the hall became very quiet.
Then Brannoc began to laugh.
It was not a pleasant sound. It had no joy in it, only disbelief hammered thin enough to ring.
“Not yet,” he said.
The figures watched him.
“Not in this room.”
The page beneath the chair darkened. Ink pooled around his boots.
He drew back, but the floor seized him. Black tendrils rose from the boards, winding around his ankles,
his calves, his knees. They did not feel like rope. They felt like written commands.
The grimoire’s name appeared across the table.
EDGE OF GLOAMREACH.
The letters shone with a twilight glow.
Brannoc dragged one foot free. Skin tore. No blood came. Only ink.
“I have no oath to you.”
The empty chair creaked.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
From somewhere above, beyond the sealed roof, a woman’s voice spoke—not Korvath’s, not his own.
“Everyone has an oath.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
He looked toward the sound.
At the far end of the hall, a door stood open.
Beyond it was not another chamber, but the fort he had left: mud, lamps, barred gate, the messenger’s
body—or perhaps only the messenger’s shadow—waiting beside the case. The soldiers were still shouting.
Time had not moved there.
Brannoc could return.
The grimoire did not say what would follow.
He looked back at the table. At the purse. At the empty chair. At his own death written in a hand that had
never trembled.
Then he saw a sixth mark beneath the names of the five powers.
A smear of red.
Not ink.
His blood.
The door to the fort began to close.
Brannoc lunged.
The black bindings climbed to his waist. The hall tilted. The empty chair slid nearer across the floor, its
legs groaning against the stone.
He reached through the doorway and caught the edge of the world.
For one heartbeat, his hand rested on the mud outside.
A soldier screamed his name.
Brannoc looked down at the black letters burning across his palm.
HEIR.
The door narrowed to a slit.
He bared his teeth and pulled.
Something on the other side pulled back.

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
Chapter 8
The wind came down from the High Spires with teeth in it.
It worried the walls of Crookvale, found every seam in the rebuilt stone, and filled the watchtowers with a
thin, ceaseless moan. Below, the settlement crouched beneath the dark like something that had survived a
beating and expected another. Fires burned behind narrow shutters. Iron shutters, iron doors, iron bands
around every gate. Crookvale had remade itself in the image of fear.
I stood upon the western wall and watched the road vanish beneath the snow.
My hand was clean.
That bothered me more than blood would have.
Men had given me the name Red-Handed because names were cheaper than truth. A captain needed an
emblem, a rumor, something that would reach a camp before he did. The name had served. It had opened
gates, emptied purses, and silenced mutinies before mutiny could form a mouth.
But tonight my hands were clean, and the thing I had come to do could not be washed from them.
Behind me, boots scraped over the wallwalk.
“Captain.”
I did not turn. “If you have come to tell me the weather is foul, save your breath.”
“The weather is foul.”
“Then save it anyway.”
The guard halted a few paces away. He smelled of wool, lamp oil, and the sour fear of a man who had
been ordered to deliver a message without being told its meaning.
“Korvath Nightbrook has arrived.”
That name moved through me like a knife entering an old scar.
“Alone?”
“Yes.”
“No horse?”
“No.”
“No escort?”
The guard hesitated. “He says he has none.”
“He says many things.”

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
The man shifted his weight. Stone creaked under his boots. “He was found beneath the south gate. He
knew the old smuggler’s cut.”
Of course he did. Korvath Nightbrook made a profession of knowing where walls were weakest. He
worked in the dark spaces between law and hunger, carrying whatever could be hidden and selling it to
whoever did not ask where it came from. His face had the forgettable quality of a shut door. His clothes

chunks.doc_title: The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
chunks.text:
were plain. His eyes were not.
“Put him in the lower chamber,” I said. “Search him twice.”
“He has already been searched.”
“Then search him by someone who knows what a book looks like.”
The guard frowned.
“Anyone can hide a knife,” I said. “The clever ones hide the reason for carrying it.”
He left. The wind returned to me.
Crookvale had been founded in 295 AS. I had repeated the words when I first entered the place, because
facts were a way to keep the mind from surrendering to the shape of a place. Founded in 295 AS. Rebuilt
after ruin. A garrison of 1004. Outside the core holdings, and therefore always waiting for the hand that
would claim it—or the blade that would cut it loose.
Numbers had no mercy in them. They did not care how many had frozen in the passes, how many walls
had fallen, how many men had been hanged from the gate beams until the crows learned their faces. A
place was founded in a year. A garrison held a number. A dead man remained dead.
I looked down at my right hand.
